comments.body:
🤖 # Job Summary: Aug Hero Run — 535B-A23B MoE (d6144), 18T tokens

Full-scale EP64 MoE pretrain: d6144, **535.3B total / 22.76B active** params, **18.0T tokens** (~**2.70e24** train FLOPs, fwd+bwd), on GB200 with our hand-rolled pooled-wave expert-parallel all-to-all. Data is the two-phase Harrier mixture on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store. Below: model, optimizer, training/topology, the MFU optimizations, the scaling ladder, and outputs.

## 1. Model

### Hyperparameters
| | |
|---|---|
| hidden_dim | 6144 |
| num_layers | 48 |
| num_heads | 48 · head_dim 128 |
| num_kv_heads | 12 stored — **local 12 / global 6** (GQA 4:1 local, 8:1 global) |
| num_experts / top-k | **384 / 8** |
| intermediate_dim (expert FFN) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| latent_dim (LatentMoE) | 3072 (= hidden/2) |
| shared experts | 2 dense SwiGLU, width 3072 |
| vocab_size | 128,256 |
| max_seq_len | 4096 · sliding_window 2048 · global_every 4 |
| capacity_factor / transport cf | 1.15 / 1.15 · num_expert_waves 3 |
| qk_mult | 1.3 · rope θ=10000 (fused, half-RoPE) |
| sconv | sites k/attn/mlp, kernel 4 |
| init | 0.5/√hidden = 0.006379 (uniform, truncated normal) |
| active / total params | 22.76B / 535.3B |

### Features
All structural (always on) unless noted.
- **All-MoE**: every block's MLP is a QB-routed `MoEMLP`; no dense-only layers.
- **GQA, split local/global KV**: sliding-window (local) layers keep 12 KV heads, full-causal (global) layers 6; K/V are sliced/aligned per layer via `lax.cond`, so global layers pay less KV compute.
- **QB routing (histogram estimator)**: router takes top-(K+1) on biased logits; the (K+1)-th logit is the per-token threshold `alpha`, the first K are selected. Each expert's threshold `beta` is the **(1−K/E) upper quantile of the margins `score−alpha`**, read from a **10k-bin histogram over the live global `[min, max]` range** (a `pmin`/`pmax` this step sets the grid; a summed-histogram cumulative count gives the per-expert quantile). The router bias `−beta` is applied on the **next step** as a zero-mean stop-gradient offset — balances expert selection without touching gradients. The histogram estimator is a smoother global quantile than a per-device top-k.
- **Sigmoid combine weights**: combine weights are `sigmoid(unbiased selected logits)`, rescaled so the K weights sum to a fixed 2.5 (not softmax).
- **LatentMoE + learnable latent RMS-norm**: tokens are compressed `hidden→latent (3072)`, passed through a **learnable RMSNorm (`latent_norm`, per-dim gain)** to decouple the expert-input scale from the down-projection init, then dispatched to experts **entirely in latent space**, and projected `latent→hidden` after the weighted combine. The router still reads the full-width token. (Also halves the all-to-all payload — see §4.)
- **Shared experts**: 2 dense SwiGLU experts run on every token in parallel with the routed path; their output is added before the residual.
- **RMSNorm on embeddings and readout**: a learnable-gain [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594) is applied to the token embeddings ([`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223)) and before the untied `lm_head` ([`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1165)), in addition to the per-block `rms_attn`/`rms_mlp`; the GatedNorm below wraps each of these.
- **GatedNorm**: learnable `x·sigmoid(silu(x·w_down)·w_up)` gate (rank-128 bottleneck) applied after **every** RMSNorm (attn, mlp, embed, final).
- **XSA (Exclusive Self-Attention)**: per head, subtract the component of the attention output parallel to its own value vector: `z = y − (yᵀv/‖v‖²)v` — removes the copy-through component so each head learns new information rather than passing V unchanged.
- **Attention head gate**: each head's attention output is scaled by a learned `2·sigmoid(x·attn_gate)`, one scalar per head; `attn_gate` is zero-initialized (gate starts at 1).
- **RMS qk-norm**: Q and K are RMS-normed (non-parametric) per head before RoPE.
- **Partial (half) RoPE, fused**: rotary is applied to **only the first half of head_dim**; the second half is rope-free on every layer. Single-pass fused kernel (θ=10000).
- **Rope-free global layers**: every 4th layer + the last are full-causal and **rope-free** (NoPE, qk_mult-only); the others are sliding-window with RoPE. One per-layer boolean drives mask, KV-head count, and rope together.
- **ShortConv (SConv)**: depthwise causal 1-D conv (kernel 4), identity-init, packed-document segment-masked, at three sites — after K, on the attention-branch output, on the MoE-branch output.
- **Embeddings**: `token_embed` fully replicated + shard-local lookup; `lm_head` (`output_proj`) FSDP+model-sharded; **untied**.
- **Logit z-loss**: the final-logit logsumexp is penalized (`logsumexp_weight = z_loss_weight = 1e-4`) and **added to the training loss** (fused into the CE) — controls gradient-norm growth at long token horizons (the fix the prior scaling ladder surfaced). Distinct from the router z-loss, which is logging-only.
- **Monitoring** (logged, not in loss): per-layer routing entropy, load-balance loss, router z-loss, and sender/receiver token-drop fractions.

## 2. Optimizer — MuonH / AdamH / Adam (compute-scaled)

Three groups via `optax.multi_transform` + a path mask:
- **MuonH** — attention, expert-MLP, shared-expert, latent, and GatedNorm **matrices**. Newton–Schulz orthogonalization (bf16, `backend_steps=5`, quintic coeffs, nesterov momentum 0.95) → **Frobenius-hyperball** scale-invariant step (moves along the direction, projects back onto the param's Frobenius sphere; norms in fp32). Orthogonalization is distributed **intra-rack only** (never crosses DCN); 4D expert stacks are handled without gathering the matrix dims.
- **AdamH** — the **lm_head readout**: Adam moments give the direction, then the same norm-preserving hyperball projection. Gets the MuonH LR, not `adam_lr`.
- **Adam** — `token_embed`, router, router_bias, `attn_gate`, 1-D norm gains, and the tiny SConv kernels.

### Hyperparameters (@ 18T budget)
| | |
|---|---|
| MuonH LR | 0.003291 |
| Adam LR | 0.000759 (MuonH = 13/3 × Adam = 4.33×) |
| beta1 / beta2 | **0.90** / 0.95 |
| epsilon | 6.04e-15 (Adam) · muon_epsilon 1e-8 |
| momentum / nesterov | 0.95 / true |
| use_syrk | true (Blackwell SM100 symmetric GEMM for X·Xᵀ) |
| LR schedule | linear · warmup 1% · min_lr_ratio 0.05 |
| max_grad_norm | none (no global clip) |
| z_loss_weight | 1e-4 (logit z-loss, fused into CE) |

The MuonH/AdamH groups carry **no decoupled weight decay** — they regularize purely through the norm-preserving hyperball projection. LR / beta2 / epsilon are compute-scaled from the Aug hero refit (issues #7856 / #8003, R²=0.978, seq_len=8192): `adam_lr = 0.087571 · tokens^-0.3461 · hidden^-0.3448 · √(tokens_per_batch)`, `beta2 = clip(0.999^(tpb/131072), 0.95, 0.9999)`, `epsilon = 9.676e-18 · √(tokens/tpb)`.

## 3. Training & topology
- **Hardware**: 11× GB200 NVL72 racks. **EP64 within each rack** (expert axis = 16 nodes × 4 GPUs), **data-parallel replication across the 11 racks over DCN**. Mesh `(replica_dcn=11, data, expert=64, model)`; token/batch sharded over `(replica_dcn, data, expert)`.
- **batch_size** 11,264 seqs (1024 × 11 racks) · **seq_len** 4096 · **num_train_steps** 390,139 · **total_tokens 18.0T** · **791 tokens/active-param**.
- **compute_budget** ≈ 2.70e24 FLOPs (analytic, fwd+bwd, latent-corrected).
- **mixed_precision** `params=bf16, compute=bf16, output=bf16`, with **fp32 pinned-host master params** + **offloaded optimizer state** (see §4). Router path kept fp32 before top-k/softmax/QB stats.
- **data**: two-phase Harrier mixture (15T pretrain + 3.75T cooldown, phase-1 at 80% of steps) on the fuzzy-deduped datakit store, marin tokenizer; simulated epoching against the 18.75T reference with a ≤8-epoch cap (max cell exposure ~2.1). 4k-seq pretrain deliberately (2× sequences/batch for expert balancing; token-drop grows sharply at longer context).

## 4. MFU / performance optimizations
- **Hand-rolled fixed pooled-wave all-to-all EP** — every device packs sends into one fixed `[expert_shards, pool_capacity]` pool and receives into fixed per-wave `[local_experts, receiver_cap, H]` buffers; all sizes are compile-time constants so the `all_to_all` runs on fully static shapes. Chosen over `ragged_all_to_all` to avoid a metadata/offset collective and dynamic shapes; **expert IDs ride in-band** as packed header rows in the same activation collective (no separate metadata collective). [EP writeup](https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/moe-fixed-wave-a2a-384/2026.08.17/index.html)
- **Static waves (3)** stripe each destination pool round-robin by rank, shrinking per-wave buffers; each wave is rematerialized to cap activation memory. **Round-robin receiver allocation** keeps overflow drops unbiased across senders.
- **LatentMoE halves EP transport bytes** — the all-to-all carries latent-width (3072) rows both directions instead of hidden (6144). FLOP accounting is corrected for this so MFU isn't overstated.
- **gpu_fa4_cute FA4 attention** — bf16 CuTe segmented flash attention with per-token key lower bounds (no materialized `[B,S,S]` mask, no THD compaction), real GQA, custom CUTLASS backward, grug-tuned 64×64 tiles for B200/head_dim-128. **Sliding-window vs full-causal is just a different lower-bound array feeding the same kernel** → cuts attention FLOPs on the ~3/4 local layers. Bounds are precomputed **outside** the layer scan.
- **Fused linear-softmax cross-entropy (bf16 backward)** — `implementation="xla_fast_bwd"`: streams the whole 65,536-token rank shard over `v_block=4096` vocab blocks with online logsumexp (never materializes the `[B,128k]` logits), and runs both **backward GEMMs in bf16 on tensor cores** (vs fp32/TF32) for ~2.3× on the hero CE shape; the logit z-loss is fused as `logsumexp_weight·lse²`. `v_block=4096` is the dominant MFU lever for the 128k vocab.
- **Fused depthwise causal ShortConv (Pallas)** — the SConv sites dispatch to a fused **Pallas Triton depthwise causal conv** kernel on GPU (forward and `dx` bit-identical to the pad-and-shift reference, `dw` as accurate; pad-and-shift fallback off-GPU). Shard-local (depthwise, no cross-channel/cross-shard term → no collectives); the channel dim is FSDP-sharded so its gradient reduce-scatters.
- **Muon symmetric-GEMM (QuACK SM100) Newton–Schulz** — the two `X·Xᵀ` products in each Newton–Schulz iteration go through a **QuACK symmetric CuTe GEMM** (`use_syrk`) that computes only one triangle of the symmetric output (`A = X·Xᵀ`, then `B = b·A + c·(A·Aᵀ)`) instead of a full dense matmul — roughly halves the matmul FLOPs per iteration on the batched 4D expert stacks, where orthogonalization is the bulk of the optimizer's compute.
- **Padded + resharded distributed Muon (intra-rack)** — the stacked leaves are orthogonalized in parallel across the rack instead of gathered to one device: 3D non-expert stacks **zero-pad the leading (layer) axis** so it divides the intra-rack shard count, then reshard the padded stack over the batch mesh axes (one matrix per shard, `vmap`'d, resliced back after); 4D expert stacks `[layers, experts, fan_in, fan_out]` reshard over the `expert` axis (or the largest batch-axis subset that divides `layers·experts`) and run under a `shard_map` **without ever gathering the `fan_in×fan_out` matrix dims**, then reshard back to the parameter's own spec. All of this is pinned **intra-rack only** — the reshards deliberately exclude the `replica_dcn` axis so Newton–Schulz never runs a collective over the slow inter-rack DCN link.
- **ArrayStacked + `jax.lax.scan`** — all 48 blocks are one compiled body scanned over the layer axis, cutting compile time and HBM; router/QB collectives are structured around the scan.
- **Heterogeneous global/local layers under one homogeneous scan** — `lax.scan` needs a single compiled body, so the ways global (full-causal, rope-free) and local (sliding-window) layers differ can't be Python branches — each rides in as a traced per-layer scalar and is selected *inside* the body:
  - **RoPE diff** — global layers run rope-free. Rather than branch, RoPE is **always computed** and then selected with `jnp.where` on a per-layer `disable_rope` scalar, so both layer kinds compile to the same body.
  - **GQA diff** — local layers keep 12 KV heads, global layers 6. K/V are stored at the max (12) width and sliced-then-`align_kv_heads`'d to the per-layer count via `lax.cond(is_global, …)`, so global layers pay less KV compute without changing the stacked parameter shape.
  - **Mask diff** — the full-causal and sliding-window FA4 bound arrays are precomputed **outside** the scan and the per-layer one is picked with `jnp.where` (the sliding window is a static mask field the body can't vary), so the window rides in as the selected bounds.
- **remat `recompute_all`** — the whole block is recomputed in backward (lowest memory); a `save_moe` mode is available to keep the MoE dispatch tensors and skip re-running the EP collectives.
- **Capacity-factor token dropping (1.15)** bounds expert compute and transport buffers regardless of routing imbalance; drops are counted/logged as sender/receiver fractions.
- **use_syrk** routes the optimizer's `X·Xᵀ` through QuACK's SM100 symmetric GEMM; Newton–Schulz runs in bf16 (halved all-gather bytes) and **intra-rack only**.
- **offload_opt_state + FP32_PINNED_HOST master** — optimizer state and fp32 master weights live in pinned host RAM, shuttled device↔host each step, to leave HBM for the pooled all-to-all buffers. (The pinned-host restore is fixed in [#8443](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8443) and memory-bounded in [#8480](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8480); the hero now writes an hourly temporary checkpoint and resumes from it after a preemption.)
- **XLA/runtime flags** — latency-hiding scheduler on, collective-overlap limit 4, CUDA async allocator, 192GB host-memory limit, PGLE off, GPU command buffers disabled.

## 5. Scaling ladder (why, and the rungs)
Runs at 5 widths on one iso-ratio recipe (**791 tokens/active-param**, same mixture + simulated epoching + per-cell epoch structure), ≈1% of total compute, to (a) project performance vs prior recipes and catch bugs, (b) watch grad-norm and token-drop dynamics across scale (the last ladder caught grad-norm growth → the logit z-loss fix), and (c) project evals across the ~100-day trajectory.

| rung | racks | batch | steps | tokens | active |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| d768 | 1 | 1024 | 11,420 | 48B | 61M |
| d1024 | 2 | 2048 | 15,276 | 128B | 162M |
| d1536 | 6 | 6144 | 15,128 | 381B | 481M |
| d2048 | 11 | 11,264 | 20,072 | 926B | 1.2B |
| **d6144 (hero)** | 11 | 11,264 | 390,139 | **18.0T** | 22.8B |

## 6. Code (at run commit [`12d8b6f`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be))

**Model** ([`model.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py)) — [`GrugModelConfig`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L160)
- All-MoE routed FFN: [`MoEMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L907) · shared experts [`DenseMLP`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L637)
- QB routing (histogram estimator): threshold/beta [`_qb_beta_hist`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L874), histogram build [`_histogram_from_expert_counts`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L820), applied next-step as stop-grad bias
- Sigmoid combine + renorm-to-2.5: [`_ROUTING_RENORM_SUM`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L58), [combine](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L980)
- LatentMoE + learnable latent RMSNorm: [`latent_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1046)
- RMSNorm on embeddings/readout: [`embed_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1223), [`final_norm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1203); [`RMSNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L594)
- GatedNorm: [`GatedNorm`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L612)
- XSA (exclusive self-attention): [subtract V-parallel component](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L573)
- Attention head gate (zero-init): [`attn_gate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L583)
- RMS qk-norm: [`rms_norm(q)`,`rms_norm(k)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L534)
- Partial (half) RoPE, fused: [`_rope`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L553), [`rope_fused`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L541); rope-free global layers via per-layer bounds [L1252](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- ShortConv: [`ShortConv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L420) → fused Pallas [`short_conv`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L52)
- Attention (FA4-cute): [call](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L572), [`fa4_cute_segment_bounds`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1252)
- Untied embeddings: [`token_embed`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1160), [`output_proj`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1163)
- Homogeneous global/local scan (rope diff + GQA diff): [`ArrayStacked` scan body](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1262), rope-free select via [`jnp.where(disable_rope)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L568), per-layer KV-head [`lax.cond(is_global)`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L521), per-layer mask-bounds [select](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/model.py#L1268)

**Optimizer** — MuonH/AdamH/Adam
- Group mask (which param → which group): [`create_mask`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/12d8b6f09f96ad4f0277445765c1a00dbc81d5be/experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/optimizer.py#L195)

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
## Raw Data

On the raw data side, our pool for this hero run is logged at this frozen commit of [our data provenance table on hugging face](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marin-community/token-counts/commit/3612ddc3350212e38ce8a50b99c3df7ea10b44a9). The raw (pre-dedupe) pool contains 25.6 trillion tokens from 292 sources (though >100 of those are a variety of rollout datasets courtesy of @penfever!).

## Deduplication & Decontamination

For this run, we removed 2.494T tokens through a combination of  fuzzy deduplication and n-gram based decontamination w.r.t many common benchmarks in LM-eval-harness + the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index (~250k documents were removed) for a final count of 23.106T tokens. 

Fuzzy duplication used a combination of MinHash deduplication and heuristics among linked pairs within connected component clusters. Examples of duplicates can be found here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/rav/dedup-pair-browser/2026.08.18.2/index.html

## Bucketing

We then embedded all documents with [Harrier 0.6b](https://huggingface.co/microsoft/harrier-oss-v1-0.6b). 

For topic labels, documents were grouped into 40 semantic buckets by first performing K-means with 5000 clusters (using a sample of 2.56 Million documents) and then doing agglomerative clustering over those 500 clusters to get 40 buckets.

For quality labels, documents were labeled using GLM 5.2 for quality and these labels were distilled into a "Faster Transformer" classifier using both the harrier embedding and the token distribution of the document.

You can see samples from each bucket + distributions from source -> topic x document buckets here: https://storage.googleapis.com/marin-public/held/harrier-k40-cluster-overview/2026.08.18/index.html?revision=uniform-sampling

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Comparing our scaling law to prior runs. The main differences here is that the May recipe is at compute optimal, this run is at ~12x overtrained, and the 67B-A2B scaling law was at 100x overtrained. The 67B-A2B ran at 8k seqlen, and was therefore given a lower asympotote of 1.4 instead of 1.5. The May fit also inaccurately has an asympotote at 1.6 instead of 1.5. Main architecture change is we dropped from 4/256 level of sparsity to 4/192 level of sparsity (25% fewer total parameters, to fit on GB200 at this scale. Several other small features added. Overall, the scaling law looks reasonable and nothing looks off in the training dynamics or data. Grad norms look stable over the run, peaking at 25% into the run. These runs ran at oversized batch sizes, which may be slightly suppressing the gradient. Expecting the grad norm to climb higher on the hero run, but still peak at the same ~25% into the run. This will be good metric to monitor for issues. Drop rate jumps to 10 pct at very start, then drops to 0, then climbs to ~4pct over the run. Slightly increasing as we scale. Predicting we wont have that 10 percent spike for the hero, because our warmup (1 percent) will cover a much larger number of steps since the hero is at a higher step count. I think most likely scenario is the hero runs around 2 percent dropping, but up to 8 percent seems plausible bsaed on the data at 4k seqlen.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: Also noting- the d2048 scaling ladder rung failed at 81%. Chose not to resume to add more time to Hero Run. The dynamics look clear from the first 81 percent, and we can cleanly extrapolate the last 19%. From a practical perspective, we will not actually be running the end of the run at 4k seqlen, and the datamix may update midrun. So the utility of the scaling law is more around the first 50 percent of the run and ensuring the projection is reasonably within expectation (which it is).

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
From model perspective, main risk points during the run:

1. First 3%. Can we get through LR warmup and reach steady dynamics? If we see gradient run away/large issues here, we likely need to revisit initialization, or potentially initial batch size. Or increase capacity factor if the issue involves high dropping.
2. 30% mark. Gradient may peak, and we will see if gradient keeps climbing, or if its starts to cooldown. Indication that it keeps climbing indefinitely could indicate we need stronger logit z loss, lower token dropping, or revisit some of the norm constraints.
3. Context Extension. How will token dropping respond? See initial Issue desc.
4. Very low loss regime. If training plateaus or acts strange near end of run only, first things to check will be the numerics.

Health checklist:

1. Is total grad norm oscillating steadily? In our May 16B active run, the grad norm grew steadily to 1.5 and training was still very smooth. So I am less concerned with the absolute magnitude, and more concerned with the rate of change. Hyperball makes comparing absolute magnitude not apples to apples with AdamW runs.
2. Are all Hyberball constrained parameters actually respecting the constraint? In past we have seen bug where JAX does norm calculation incorrectly, due to some transient sharding issue. This has been updated to a more explicit calculation that seemed to resolve that issue, but issues of a similar nature may arise.
3. Is token dropping following similar trend as scaling ladder?
4. Is loss decreasing steadily?
5. Are evals decreasing steadily?
6. Is our router bias terms behaving steadily?
7. Does router entropy stay near max?
8. Is embed norm growth reasonable?
9. Is MFU holding constant?
10. Is LR schedule (both Adam and MuonH params) actually following the correct schedule?
11. Does the entire wandb config look accurate?
12. Are we hitting the projected eval targets at each 5 percent?

Thanks for sharing this work.  
I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body: @windsornguyen we can share lots of metadata for data mix but we're unable to grant direct access to data. What are you looking for?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
> Thanks for sharing this work. I have a question regarding the motivation behind LatentMoE. Since the training system uses GB200 NVL72 with high-bandwidth NVLink, I am curious why a latent representation is introduced before expert dispatch. Is LatentMoE mainly motivated by reducing communication overhead at larger scales (e.g., beyond a single NVLink domain), or does it also provide benefits beyond communication optimization, such as improving model capability? Thanks!

On its own, LatentMoE halves the comms cost. We found that putting a learnable RMSNorm on the latent projection improved model capability as well, so LatentMoE w/ norm performed better than no latent MoE. Without this learnable RMSNorm, we run into activation scaling issue and see 30 percent worse quality. We also found going from top 4 of 192 to top 8 of 384 (half sized) gave 15 percent quality gain. But it doubles comms cost. So one way to view latentMoE is it enables 4/192->8/384 without change to either comms or compute.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks for the detailed reply! I have a few follow-up questions after looking through some of the previous Marin experiments.
1. Alternating dense/MoE vs shared experts.
I noticed #6443 already implemented an alternating dense/MoE architecture with no shared experts in the MoE blocks, which looks quite similar to the design later used in MAI-Thinking-1, but I couldn't find final results. Was that direction abandoned because of quality, systems efficiency, or simply because the runs weren't completed?
More broadly, do you think dense FFN layers can replace much of the functional role of shared experts? MAI's results suggest that dense layers can carry the common computation while the MoE layers specialize, while also eliminating all-to-all communication on half of the FFN layers. Since the current Hero model uses shared experts partly as a backbone against token dropping, would this design become more attractive once routing is fully dropless?
2. Relative position on local layers + NoPE on global layers.
I also saw the negative Inkling relative-position experiment in #7208. One slightly different variant I'm curious about is using learned relative position only on the sliding-window layers, while leaving global-attention layers completely NoPE. My intuition is that local layers can learn precise relative ordering, while global layers remain position-independent for better long-context extrapolation. Do you think the #7208 result argues against this variant as well, or would it be meaningfully different?
3. AdamH for token embeddings.
In #5203, moving token_embed to AdamH with unit-variance initialization seems to have worked across all four tested scales. However, the current Hero recipe puts token_embed back in Adam. Was that result later invalidated by the MuonH recipe / newer embedding ablations (#6442), or was there another reason it wasn't carried forward?

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: > Thanks for the detailed reply! I have a few follow-up questions after looking through some of the previous Marin experiments. 1. MAI Thinking makes their dense layers only have num_neurons = hidden_dim, which is roughly 3x smaller than normal. This to me a is a bit awkward at first glance because attn is still full capacity every layer. So the normal behavior of attention fetch info, mlp process it is a bit imbalanced (of course if one has data that an idea is good, that it seeming awkward doesn't matter, but it made me more hesitant to spend the time collecting that data instead of working on other things). At very small scale if I do an exact active:total replica (dense 3x width hidden instead of 1x), I get same quality and 20% better MFU than our baseline. But small scale alone is poor signal here, because dense models look much better at small scale in general. We never ended up doing large scale ablation here, since I was more worried about token dropping dynamics. Also the way we are using jax scan makes it a awkward to have different behavior per layer. I am less optimistic about alternating dense/moe long term, because with mature mixture-of-kittens kernels the MFU hit of MoE is probably not that high anyways. 2. Hmm I separately saw some early positive results from Inkling relative position embedding that gave lower loss. But our kernel was not quite fast enough to justify. And perhaps more importantly, the kernel was a bit buggy if I changed sliding window length. I think it should be good on global layers too, since its limited to just the most recent X (512 or 1024) positions. I am more bullish on relative position embedding + MLA. Since MLA has very janky approach to RoPE, which requires replicating 64 head dims across every head. Relative position embedding fixes this. Have to be a bit careful with ablations here because at very small scale RoPE on global looks much better than NoPE on global. (but this fades with scale) 3. So initial AdamH on embed looked good. But later I did learning rate sweep, and if LR was 40% too high, was seeing grad spikes up to 20. I think what was happening (guessing) was rare tokens were having their norm driven to near zero, and then getting massive grad when they finally ended up in the batch. (we have rms_norm on embed that will apply high growth multiplier to small vocab embeds) Dont want any features in the model that require perfectly optimal hypers. So reverted it.

comments.author: MythosAd
comments.body:
Thanks, this is really helpful.

My motivation for alternating dense/MoE is less about the current MFU gap and more about separation of concerns: dense layers handle common computation, while MoE layers handle specialization. Keeping them as two clean execution patterns seems to leave more room for independent kernel, scheduling, and parallelism optimization, even if MoE kernels improve substantially.

For position encoding, my preference for learned relative PE on local layers + NoPE on global layers is mainly to avoid positional extrapolation entirely. With a fixed local window, the relative-position range never changes as context grows, while global attention stays purely content-addressed. I agree this probably needs larger-scale ablations to judge properly.

comments.author: yonromai
comments.body:
🤖 ## Finding and recommendation

Keep the ongoing Hero run on its current router arithmetic.

Using BF16 operands with FP32 accumulation and output reduced saved-input router score RMS error from `0.0074565` to `0.00002808` against an FP64 reference. It matched the reference top-8 order for all 324 valid saved entries; current arithmetic changed the order for 80 entries. On the restored step-126000 training batch, the arithmetic change altered top-8 order for `8.9853%` of routed tokens and changed the selected expert set for `2.6479%`.

The more accurate dot was about `1.5–2%` slower per training step in two short launch orders. Across all 30 paired post-compile steps, its median throughput ratio was `0.98245` and its median iteration-time ratio was `1.01436`. Peak HBM was unchanged at `115.5375 GiB` in the checkpoint-writing pair.

The 20-step paired continuation stayed finite and had almost identical mean training loss: preferred minus current was `-0.00000127`. The runs still followed different trajectories. Router gradients and pending query-bias state diverged, and mean sender drops increased by `5.55%` under the preferred arithmetic. Receiver drops remained zero. Expert-load summaries showed no notable systematic skew over this short run.

The corrected fixed-current-arithmetic Paloma evaluation applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. The preferred-trained checkpoint was higher by `0.00072265` macro loss and `0.00029618` macro BPB after 20 steps. Fifteen of 16 subset losses were higher. This difference is too small and too early to establish lasting quality harm.

The evidence shows a real numerical and routing-policy change with a small runtime cost and no demonstrated benefit for a mid-run transition. A fresh-run ablation remains reasonable.

## Limits

All full-model experiments used one 16-node B200 NVL72 rack. This preserves Hero's EP64 geometry, but uses one data-parallel replica and batch 1024 instead of the production run's 11 racks and global batch 11,264. It does not exercise cross-rack reductions. The query-bias histogram also sees 1024 sequences instead of 11,264.

The continuations cover only 20 optimizer steps. They can show immediate route and state divergence, but they do not establish long-term benefit or harm. The speed delta is also close to the one-rack noise floor, so `1.5–2%` is an approximate cost rather than a precise forecast for the 11-rack run.

<details><summary>Evidence and reproduction</summary>

### Source and code identities

- Observed production source: [`e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/e8460b35bd6b312b62799b12ae363b3981af3c83)
- Complete native source checkpoint: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-main-step121638/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints/step-126000`

- Experiment branch: [`yonromai/goal/hero-training-router-01a0c066`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/tree/goal/hero-training-router-01a0c066)
- Final experiment commit: [`a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40`](https://github.com/yonromai/marin/commit/a00cb77a491f4777a2c66edce54f47ff7b255c40)

Both continuation jobs and both corrected Paloma jobs completed all 16 tasks without failures or preemptions.

The earlier fixed-evaluation `a1` runs omitted each checkpoint's pending query-bias update. They are superseded by the corrected `a2` runs above. The separate evaluation-path problem is tracked in [#9352](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9352).

### Saved-input accuracy

The fixture contains 324 valid layer-15 entries representing 32 byte-distinct activation vectors. The production-shape probe tiles the entries to 65,536 rows and preserves their captured frequency.

| Arithmetic | Score RMS error | Maximum error | Top-8 order versus FP64 reference | Isolated forward | Isolated backward |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- | ---: | ---: |
| Current BF16 output, then FP32 cast | `0.0074565` | `0.0311123` | 80/324 entries changed | 14.07 ms | 14.43 ms |
| BF16 operands, FP32 accumulation/output | `0.00002808` | `0.00007003` | all 324 matched | 14.07 ms | 14.48 ms |
| FP32 operands | `0.00000416` | `0.00002373` | all 324 matched | 18.20 ms | 23.26 ms |

The isolated timing covers only the saved-input router dot and gradient. It is not a whole-step measurement.

### Continuation measurements

| Post-compile metric, 19 real batches | Current | Preferred FP32 accumulation | Preferred minus current |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Median train throughput | 275,523 tok/s | 271,399 tok/s | -1.50% by ratio of medians |
| Median full iteration | 16.3871 s | 16.5275 s | +0.86% by ratio of medians |
| Final cumulative peak HBM | 115.5375 GiB | 115.5375 GiB | 0 |
| Mean train loss | 1.24572355 | 1.24572228 | -0.00000127 |
| Mean sender drops | 684,900 | 722,882 | +37,983 (+5.55%) |
| Mean routing entropy | 5.945189 | 5.945129 | -0.000060 |
| Mean expert-count CV | 0.097451 | 0.098131 | +0.000680 |

The corrected Paloma macro losses were `2.22016478` for the current continuation and `2.22088742` for the preferred continuation. The runs used current router arithmetic for both checkpoints and applied each checkpoint's pending query-bias state. This common policy removes evaluation-time router rounding as a direct difference. It also evaluates the preferred-trained checkpoint under arithmetic different from its training policy, so the sign is not a clean estimate of long-run preferred-policy quality.

comments.author: mindscanlabs
comments.body:
**An independent forecast of the final loss, with a law found from the data (no fixed form)**

I forecast the run's final `eval_dropless/paloma/macro_loss`: the last eval logged in the lineage at step 387,000 or later, as W&B records it (expected at 16K packing). I used only public W&B data, up to step 302,999 (snapshot of 2026-10-21, 22:58 UTC).

| forecast | data | value | 90 % interval |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| A | ladder + the hero's own evals | **1.979** | [1.965, 1.994] |
| B | ladder only | **1.935** | [1.915, 1.963] |

**Method in brief.** NAI, the symbolic-regression system I develop, finds a law L(C, fraction of training) from the table, with no form given: no floor and no power law are assumed. C is your lm_head-excluded compute.
- B is the ladder-only law at the hero's compute and the end of training.
- A adds the hero's post-swap 4K evals to the table and takes the level from its 16 evals at 16K.
- The intervals are NAI's forecast band, nominally 90 %.

B is 0.10 below the Aug 19 pre-registration from the same ladder, because the law NAI found has no fixed floor.

The formulas are sealed. Their SHA-256 digests and the scoring rules, fixed in advance: https://github.com/mindscanlabs/NAI-track-record/blob/main/forecasts/marin-535b.md

I'll post the formulas and the scored comparison after the run ends. Thanks for running this in the open: it makes a forecast like this possible.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body: A measurement for anyone checking forecasts made while the evals packed at 4K (Marin's Aug 19 forecast of 2.039, and mine in #9977): the switch to 16K lowered the Paloma macro by about 0.031 on nearly the same weights. The `qk16k-a1-step252k` arm restored step 252,000 with the hero's post-switch settings (16K, `qk_mult` 1.48) and logged 2.0929 and 2.0926 at steps 252,049 and 252,099, against 2.1234 for the hero's 4K eval of that checkpoint, logged at step 251,999. With `qk_mult` left at 1.3 (`qk16k-a0-step252k`), the drop is about 0.028. The hero's own step from 254,999 to 257,999 looks smaller (0.024) because WikiText's dip at 254,999 lowered the last 4K eval; without WikiText it is 0.032 over those 3,000 steps. The top-level `macro_loss` instead averages the zeros in ([eval.py#L611](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8577d258214dd0dcb992c04458ee4eb10496d4e5/lib/levanter/src/levanter/eval.py#L611)), about −0.14 on the hero's 23 tags. The 67B's 65K→262K switch, with the same tokenizer and Paloma files, shows both: from step 155,999 ([65K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep8_bs1024_seq65536_sw2k_v4_2048_muon_cooldown_step141k)) to 156,000 ([262K run](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/moe_67b_a2b_d2560_ep1_rep1_ctx4_bs256_seq262144_ctxext_step156k)), `eval/paloma/macro_loss` rose 2.1774 → 2.2150 while the other 14 subsets moved +0.0004, and `eval/macro_loss` fell 2.0260 → 1.8607 (2.0379 without the zeros). Either fix is small: mask zero-token tags in the top-level macro as the group macros already do, or keep all 16 subsets by setting `GrugEvalConfig.max_seq_len` (#9890) to 65,536 for the 262K phase.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
🤖 **Weight merging the final hero checkpoints: −0.003 loss at 65K, saved as a resumable checkpoint**

Averaging the final 65K-phase checkpoints lowers loss by about 0.003 on every eval. On the ladder law L = 1.5 + 84.8·C^−0.09 that's worth roughly 7% more training compute, for free.

**Checkpoint:** `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-merge-hb-avg11/checkpoints/step-390251`

- **Weights:** an equal-weight average of 11 checkpoints: 385,500–390,000 every 500 steps, plus the final 390,251. Each weight tensor is rescaled to stay on the hyperball (details below).
- **Training state:** step 390,251, with that checkpoint's full optimizer state and QB betas. It has the hero's checkpoint layout, so it resumes directly with `initialize_from` or loads weights-only for evals and export.
- **`metadata.json`** records the sources, the weights, the merge space and where the training state came from.

All evals are dropless at 65,536 context with `qk_mult` 1.66. Each row is the change versus step 390,000.

| Merge | Clean Paloma | Uncheatable | All evals |
|---|---|---|---|
| step 390,000 (baseline) | 1.7515 | 1.4786 | 1.6953 |
| step 390,251 (final) | −0.0001 | −0.0003 | ±0.0000 |
| average of last 2 | −0.0012 | −0.0011 | −0.0013 |
| average of last 4 | −0.0020 | −0.0020 | −0.0021 |
| EMA, 0.5 per 500 steps (10 ckpts) | −0.0020 | −0.0019 | −0.0021 |
| EMA, 0.8 per 500 steps (10 ckpts) | −0.0028 | −0.0029 | −0.0029 |
| average of 10 (385,500–390,000) | −0.0028 | −0.0031 | −0.0030 |
| average of 10, hyperball | −0.0028 | −0.0031 | −0.0029 |
| **average of 11, hyperball (saved)** | **−0.0030** | **−0.0033** | **−0.0032** |

- **What matters:** how many checkpoints go in, and how evenly they're weighted. The wider and flatter the average, the bigger the gain, and it hadn't levelled off at 11.
- **Hyperball rescaling changes nothing:** the plain average already sits at 0.9995 of the sphere radius.
- **Step-to-step noise is small:** one more stretch of training (390,000 → 390,251) moves the loss by at most 0.0003, an order of magnitude less than the merge.
- **Every eval set improves,** all 23 of them.

**Process**

1. **Choosing eval sets:** the 4K re-evals of the 16K and 65K checkpoints showed which sets don't fall smoothly from step to step. "Clean Paloma" leaves out PTB (contaminated reads), WikiText-103, TwitterAAE and Gab, whose loss rose 7–12 times across those 23 checkpoints. It averages the other 12 sets. "Uncheatable" averages all 7 of its sets.
2. **Merging:** sources load one at a time into a float32 running sum of the fp32 weights. The hero keeps no separate master copy, so these are the master weights.
3. **Hyperball mode:** after averaging, each MuonH/AdamH tensor is rescaled to its sources' mean norm, over the same axes the optimizer holds fixed:
   - 2-D weights: the whole matrix is one ball.
   - Stacked weights: one ball per layer.
   - Routed experts: each layer's whole bank of all 384 experts is one ball (`ALL_EXPERTS`).

   Adam-trained leaves (embeddings, router, norm gains, attention gate) are plain averages.
4. **Saving:** the merged weights are combined with 390,251's step, optimizer state and QB betas, using a template built from the hero's own optimizer config. Before launching, I checked that template against the 390,251 manifest: all 56 optimizer-state arrays and 36 parameter arrays match in shape and dtype.
5. **Verification:** the job reloaded the saved checkpoint and checked the weights bit for bit and the optimizer state by per-leaf checksums. The eval numbers above for the saved row come from that reloaded copy.

Each variant ran as one job on one rack at production priority, logged to W&B in `marin_moe` as `hero-merge-*` (the saved one is `hero-merge-hb-avg11-save`).

**Code:** branch [`larry/hero-ckpt-merge-eval`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/larry/hero-ckpt-merge-eval) at [`dff14a5`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/dff14a54199eaf97a3719d0b6d64a99fb044d47f). The work is in `experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_checkpoint_eval.py`, using `--merge-source PATH WEIGHT` (repeatable), `--merge-space hyperball` and `--save-merged OUT STATE_FROM`; the CPU tests are in `test_checkpoint_eval.py`. The saved checkpoint was made with:

```
python -m experiments.grug.moe_hero_ep.launch_checkpoint_eval --run-id hero-merge-hb-avg11-save \
  --merge-source <ckpts>/step-385500 1 ... --merge-source <ckpts>/step-390000 1 --merge-source <ckpts>/step-390251 1 \
  --merge-qk-mult 1.66 --merge-space hyperball \
  --save-merged s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-merge-hb-avg11/checkpoints/step-390251 <ckpts>/step-390251 \
  --seq-len 65536 --version dev --run
```

where `<ckpts>` = `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/grug/hero-ctx65k-step372k/2026.08.19.2/checkpoints`.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
🤖 An agent literature survey for the Mochi post-training recipe found two Nemotron-sourced changes for train/inference mismatch in async MoE RL. Mochi RL already uses one of them (router replay). The other, an FP32 LM head, has not been tested by us. Nothing here was measured empirically on Mochi: this is a pointer for the RL team, not a result.

**What Nemotron reports**
- The [Nemotron 3.5 Super/Lightning technical report](https://research.nvidia.com/labs/nemotron/files/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-and-Lightning-Technical-Report.pdf) (RL section) says router replay plus an FP32 LM head "reduce the KL error between the training and inference engines by more than an order of magnitude". The two are reported together, so the report does not say how much each one contributes.
- Aside: the [HF MoE handbook](https://huggingface-moe-blogpost.hf.space/) says the NeMo-RL recipes for Nemotron 3 Super/Ultra freeze the router matrix in async RL and keep the load-balancing bias live, and that "whether replay pays off in reward is still contested". Router freezing is an alternative or a complement to replay.

**Where Mochi stands (from existing work, not new measurements)**
- Router replay: Mochi (Hero) RL already uses captured-route replay, and it passed the recorded 4K RL gate in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388. Its measured replay result is batch-order sensitivity of the gradient: 71.96% → 1.37% at PP48, with +5.3% scoring-plus-update time. That is not a serve-vs-trainer logprob gap, and the same issue notes that serving–trainer differences persist.
- Bit-identical numerics: the stack beginning with https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10634 was closed in favour of score centering with TIS (https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11066, open), with probes in https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10658 (open). The Mochi RL launcher is https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11321 (draft).
- FP32 LM head, serving side: the pinned vLLM fork (`0ac9dcb`) already supports it. `vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py` reads `--hf-overrides '{"head_dtype": "float32"}'` and accumulates the head GEMM into FP32. Its comment says this is "required for RL training-inference consistency". The Mochi serve config (`experiments/evaluation/mochi/model-mochi-sft-step400407.yaml`) does not set it, so served logits are BF16.
- FP32 LM head, trainer side: SkyRL's Megatron wrapper calls the model with `fp32_output=False` (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_model_wrapper.py`), so trainer logits are BF16 too. Matching vLLM would need a Megatron-side FP32 output projection, which is not checked here.
- Related Snowball evidence, not RL and not Mochi: in an Oct 25 Levanter-vs-vLLM scoring check on Snowball, silent MoE token drops and BF16 combine weights were each separate numerics boundaries. Fixing them one at a time cut the p99 per-token logprob gap from 3.96 to 0.60 nats.

**What we did not do:** no empirical study on Mochi of the FP32 head, router freezing, or replay versus no replay. The survey proposed a 1 h arm; it moves off our list and into this issue.

Done when: the RL team decides whether to test an FP32 LM head on both engines (vLLM `head_dtype` plus a Megatron FP32 output projection) on Mochi, measured as the serve-vs-trainer logprob or KL gap on fixed responses with replay on, and records the decision here. Router freezing is optional, as a separate arm.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

The draft [Mochi RL recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/75bf9fba6c8419070e87c9f97ddd0478148a27a9/experiments/post_training/mochi_rl/recipe.yaml#L78-L82) enables router replay but has no head-precision override. The [Megatron wrapper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/82cee32cfd5bd479aa0670ba1a92a9c0f96ec4bf/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_model_wrapper.py#L351-L360) passes `fp32_output=False`; [Megatron's implementation](https://github.com/NVIDIA/Megatron-LM/blob/7c0fac795b76180c26e363fa292c1ce2c025c4df/megatron/core/transformer/module.py#L593-L635) shows that changing this flag only casts outputs after the model forward. [#10388](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10388#issuecomment-6379516756) reports a remaining serving–trainer logprob gap with replay, but no Mochi FP32-head result. The evaluation YAML named above is absent from current `main`; #11321 is the active Mochi recipe.

**Relevant code**
- [Mochi generator config](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/75bf9fba6c8419070e87c9f97ddd0478148a27a9/experiments/post_training/mochi_rl/recipe.yaml#L126-L149) — serving precision insertion point.
- [Megatron wrapper](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/82cee32cfd5bd479aa0670ba1a92a9c0f96ec4bf/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/workers/megatron/megatron_model_wrapper.py#L351-L360) — learner forward path.
- [Pinned vLLM head](https://github.com/marin-community/vllm/blob/0ac9dcb157ee86ccb447bc717259159c41ad456a/vllm/model_executor/layers/logits_processor.py#L142-L177) — FP32 accumulation path.

# Proposed Fix

This needs a paired numerical experiment before a production change. If the RL team allocates the run, use one immutable Mochi checkpoint and fixed responses, routes, replay setting, weights, and scoring layout. Measure four arms: BF16 on both engines, FP32 serving only, FP32 learner only, and FP32 on both. Wire and verify vLLM `hf_overrides: {head_dtype: float32}` in #11321, and implement a genuine FP32-output Megatron head projection; verify its GEMM output precision and backward path rather than relying on `fp32_output=True`.

For each arm, report chosen-token logprob-gap RMS/p99/max, same-token probability-ratio outliers, scorer/serve throughput, and memory, with run IDs and source revisions. Compute full-distribution KL only if full-vocabulary logits are captured. Record the RL team's go/no-go decision against the measured parity gain and cost here; treat router freezing as a separate arm.

The `marin` Finelog hub repeatedly returned `log read failed: External error: snapshot read deadline exceeded` from `FetchLogs` on November 12. The SkyRL CatCount Iris job succeeded, but its nightly gate failed because it could not read the complete native log to check metrics. OPD and Grug passed in the same [Actions run](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/43268375464).

Reproduce:
1. Read the [CatCount run log artifact](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/actions/runs/43268375464/artifacts/13968636355). Streaming reads timed out repeatedly from 17:21 to 17:34 UTC. The job then reported `Job completed with state: succeeded` at 17:34:09 UTC.
2. Run `iris --cluster marin job logs /runner/skyrl-nightly-cat-count-h100-43268375464-1-a1 --no-tail --max-lines 60000`. The [gate script](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/e567c3c2d82f7cd26e8ce50d0fc4f81960cc7db3/infra/ci/run_skyrl_cat_count.sh#L26-L32) did this after job success and received the same deadline error at 17:34:21 UTC. A bounded `--max-lines 100 --substring WANDB_MIRROR` read still failed at 18:21 UTC.

Expected: `FetchLogs` serves the completed job's native log so the gate can check its metrics. The uploaded streaming artifact includes four training steps but not the complete metric record, so the gate result cannot be reconstructed from it.

The [same-day Finelog hub incident](https://marina.oa.dev/echo/wiki/970) tracks intermittent query latency. [Other succeeded canaries](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11263) also hit `FetchLogs` deadlines. The server-side cause of this exact read timeout remains unconfirmed. [Atlas preview 31](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/c9742a15-fb46-4d56-bc88-aa916351ebd3/v/31/) now shows a visible script-load error and a Reload page action that retains the selected source. issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
Large NCCL MIN/MAX reductions return incorrect values in the initialized SkyRL policy runtime and make strict replica verification reject matching weights.

Reproduce:
1. Initialize the production Ray policy workers on 64 GB200s in one NVLink domain, with PP2/CP4/EP4/DP8, NCCL 2.30.7 and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE=262144`. Retain the actual Megatron data-parallel groups including context parallelism: 32 ranks per pipeline stage.
2. Inside each worker, run this known-input check on its existing group before weight publication:

Pinned inputs: diagnostic revision `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033`, frozen configuration SHA256 `0d4ca250683aaa64d295c4137677709b00941ad8ff307055afdf7e5b63e5a2ce`, and the same adopted Snowball SFT export (input artifact version `2026.11.17.1`, identity suffix `81b4d4d5`). Task image: `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`, frozen `megatron production` bootstrap. The Linux runtime manifest pins PyTorch 2.14.1; the loaded PyTorch version was not independently captured in these receipts.

```python
import torch
import torch.distributed as dist
import megatron.core.parallel_state as mpu

group = mpu.get_data_parallel_group(with_context_parallel=True)
members = dist.get_process_group_ranks(group)
base = torch.arange(16_777_216, device="cuda", dtype=torch.int32) % 128
source = base + dist.get_rank()
low, high = source.clone(), source.clone()
dist.all_reduce(low, op=dist.ReduceOp.MIN, group=group)
dist.all_reduce(high, op=dist.ReduceOp.MAX, group=group)
assert torch.equal(low, base + min(members))
assert torch.equal(high, base + max(members))
```

Expected: exact integer MIN/MAX values on every member, with source bytes unchanged.

Observed: all 64 workers fail on 64 MiB arrays in their two 32-rank dense groups. Rank 0 has 11,620,913 wrong MIN elements and 11,652,720 wrong MAX elements. The same handles pass at 1,024 and 4,194,305 elements. The eight-rank expert groups pass all three sizes. Independent NumPy hashes confirm the results; all 128 failed output hashes differ from every possible rank-offset reference pattern, which excludes a simple wrong-member set as the explanation.

At the strict comparator boundary, all 117,568 live sender tensors retain their entry/exit hashes, data/storage pointers, offsets, strides and tensor IDs. Actual group names and members match the expected geometry. Replica hashes agree, source intervals do not overlap, and input bytes stay unchanged during the known-input reductions. The unchanged `compare_replicas` then reports 876,550,056–945,509,596 mismatched bytes per rank. Its current 16 MiB raw-byte chunks create 64 MiB int32 reduction buffers: [comparison code on main](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/3e8c7baa26a451b1f8c630bd6dc68a7135907a32/vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/weight_sync/expert_block/verify_weights.py#L91).

A separate eight-GPU control passes Ray/torchrun, masked/unmasked GPU visibility and `NCCL_BUFFSIZE` unset/262144. This report therefore reproduces the defect inside the initialized 64-worker runtime; an equivalent standalone 32-worker reproduction and the exact NCCL/PyTorch mechanism remain unproven.

Proposed mitigation, not implemented or GPU-qualified: bound raw-byte comparison chunks to 4 MiB so each int32 reduction is 16 MiB, while comparing every byte with the same strict MIN/MAX rule. Keep the failing 64 MiB case as a correctness regression and investigate the runtime cause separately.

Pinned analysis and all 516 raw-receipt SHA256 values: `s3://marin-us-east-08a/marin/experiments/nccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118/analysis-v1.json` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-08a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fnccl-minmax-32-rank-20261118%2Fanalysis-v1.json)). Diagnostic source revision: `767592680758e3bc47c5ecda385973c3199ca033` (local research commit, not yet published). No fix commit or further GPU iteration has been made.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
The shared grader scores a PASS from zero evidence when a task has no FAIL_TO_PASS and no PASS_TO_PASS ids and the parsed test log is empty.

`grade()` resolves a task when the parsed PASSED set is a subset of the expected set. With empty id lists the expected set is empty, so an empty parse is a vacuous subset and `resolved` is true. `test.sh` then writes reward 1. `test.sh` writes reward 0 when `resolved` is false.

Impact: the reward is noise. Two trials with identical empty evidence score differently. We saw this on one converted task row. Its grader scored 1.0 on the upstream image side and 0.0 on the repaired-base side from identical empty logs. The row cannot carry a meaningful fidelity verdict, so it is held out of admission.

Reproduce:
1. Build a task config with `"FAIL_TO_PASS": []` and `"PASS_TO_PASS": []`.
2. Run `grade(config, "")` on an empty log.
3. `grade()` returns `resolved: true`. `grade.py` exits 0. `test.sh` writes reward 1.
4. Run `grade(config, "PASSED tests/test_a.py::test_one\n")` on a log with one parsed test.
5. `grade()` returns `resolved: false` from the same empty id lists. `test.sh` writes reward 0.

Expected: a task with no test ids and an empty parsed log is UNSCORABLE. The grader must not resolve it. It must not score a pass. The verdict should say so in the log.

Fix (in review): `grade()` now marks the empty-ids-and-empty-log case as `unscorable`, forces `resolved` false, prints `UNSCORABLE`, and exits 1. `test.sh` then leaves reward 0. Tasks with test ids keep the old verdict logic. A behavior test covers the three cases.

Evidence:
- Repro row: `nvim-lua__plenary.nvim-251` (SWE-rebench V2.1 repair fidelity gate, sample manifest 200 rows).
- Upstream-image trial receipt: exit 0, `test_output.log` empty, elapsed 18 s, `verdict.json` = `{"detail": {"exit_code": 0}, "reward": 1.0, "status": "scored"}`.
- Repaired-base trial receipt: exit 0, `test_output.log` empty, `verdict.json` = `{"detail": {"exit_code": 0}, "reward": 0.0, "status": "scored"}` (the real run parsed tests, so the subset check failed).
- Row data: `FAIL_TO_PASS` is null. The grader had no ids to check on either side.

issues.author: karansag
issues.body:
## TL;DR

We scored how predictable each candidate teacher's traces are for our own Snowball student, using per-token negative log-likelihood (NLL) under a frozen checkpoint. Lower NLL means the traces are more predictable under that scorer, rendering and loss mask. Under the 10/05 SFT checkpoint, contributor traces (Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith, Qwen3.6-27B TMax) and the collaborator's Qwen3.5/3.6 teacher traces score 0.25–0.55 nats per loss token, while the GLM trace sets score 1.172–1.863 all-token and 1.180–1.866 text-only. The pre-SFT base parent gives a similar broad ordering, 0.085–0.158 nats higher, so much of the separation is already present before the 10/05 SFT. This is a likelihood measurement, not a quality measurement, and no matched-token teacher or closeness comparison has been run yet.

## Why we measure this

The Mochi post-training plan has to choose teachers for the SFT mix. If student closeness predicts how much a teacher's traces teach, we can rank candidate data with a cheap scoring pass instead of a full training arm. Three different kinds of evidence make that worth testing, and they do not all point the same way.

**Outside evidence, ablated.** OpenThoughts ablated the teacher model directly and found that the teacher's own benchmark rank did not predict the student's ranking: QwQ-32B produced stronger students than DeepSeek-R1 when it was selected as the code or math teacher, even though DeepSeek-R1 is the stronger model by benchmark average. The reported values are overall student averages after selecting that teacher for code and for math, not teacher scores ([arXiv 2506.04178](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04178), Section 4.6 and Table 8). OpenThoughts-Agent reports the same pattern for agentic traces: selecting GPT-5.3-Codex as the teacher gave lower Terminal-Bench 2.0 performance than selecting GLM-4.7-AWQ, despite GPT-5.3-Codex being the stronger model ([arXiv 2606.24855](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.24855), Section 3.5). Neither paper measures student closeness to the teacher traces. In these ablations, teacher strength was not the right ranking variable; neither identifies closeness as the substitute.

**Collaborator result, measured.** A collaborator's teacher study on a Snowball-family student (Antidoom-RLVR1-Step12, two epochs, batch 32, LR 1e-5) found that the strongest teacher could produce the weakest student. A later 500-task comparison matched length and solve rate and still favored the Qwen3.6-35B-A3B-trained student over the GLM-5.3-Flash-trained student; she reported GLM SFT loss about 3× higher before and after SFT, and that scaling the 35B traces did not appear to help much. This is paraphrased from the team's summary of her posts, which link the primary Discord messages: [Oct 24 post](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1355318637854199848/1563524283588677727), [Nov 9 follow-up](https://discord.com/channels/1354881461060243556/1355318637854199848/1569357141855314110). The released traces are public: [marianna13/rts-tmax-teacher-traces](https://huggingface.co/datasets/marianna13/rts-tmax-teacher-traces) at revision `bc3de8cb`, CC-BY-4.0, five teachers on the same two task pools, one attempt per task, every verified trial kept whether or not it was solved. This is a motivating observation, not a causal proof.

**Our measurement, this issue.** We scored our own student's NLL on those teacher traces and on our contributor rows. Our numbers put the GLM traces furthest from the student, the same direction as the collaborator's training outcome.

**Our own training comparison, measured but not matched.** Our agentic SFT shootout trained on GLM 5.3 traces and on contributor rows (Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith, Qwen3.6-27B TMax) on the same 1,432 tasks, parent and recipe. Every GLM arm scored below its parent on SWE-bench and TBLite, while the contributor rows beat the GLM LOW rows by SWE-bench +26 [+17, +36] points and TBLite +9 [+1, +17] points ([issue 10213 summary](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10213#issuecomment-6618401658)). The contributor tokens were also 1.27× larger, and the teachers and harness formats differed, so this is not an isolated teacher comparison. A collaborator's separate write-up reports 46.5% on SWE-bench Verified random-100 from a 12.8% starting checkpoint using Qwen3.8-27B CalibForge plus Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith traces, and 50.5% after RL ([blog post](https://lukedhlee.github.io/blog/2026/10/21/turning-snowball-into-a-coding-agent/)); we have not independently verified those values.

**How to read the contrast.** The two sets of experiments used different teachers and had different outcomes, which is consistent with the closeness hypothesis. It does not prove it, because other things also differ: the data and task pools, the student checkpoint (our shootout used Snowball v0 and v0.1; the collaborator's used the general-SFT 09-21 checkpoint), the recipe and dose (3 epochs at 1e-6, versus the collaborator's epochs followed by RL), the evaluation protocol (32k context, 1,800 s, one trial, versus 64k, a 3× timeout and three repeats), the harness the traces were recorded in, and stack fixes the collaborator applied for training precision and expert capacity that our arms predate.

**Where the evidence is weak.** The controlled teacher ablations are dense 7B–32B students (Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-8B/32B), not a 67B MoE and not a 535B MoE. The two Snowball comparisons involve near-versus-distant teachers but are not matched-token teacher ablations. Closeness could matter at 7B and not at our scale, or the reverse.

**Hypothesis.** A student may learn more per supervised token from traces it already finds likely, because it is imitating behavior closer to its own distribution. If this holds, the closeness score ranks candidate teachers and data for the Mochi SFT mix. If it fails, teacher and data selection must be decided by matched-token training outcomes, and the closeness score is only a diagnostic.

**What would falsify it.** A distant teacher winning at matched tokens and matched tasks, a near teacher losing, a closeness ranking that does not match the outcome ranking across several teachers, or low NLL explained by the student having already seen the rows rather than by the teacher's style.

**Baseline and RSR measurement.** This report gives the mean per-token NLL baseline. We scored these cells with Snowball using Rank-Surprisal Ratio (RSR), the mean target-token rank divided by the mean negative log-likelihood under the student. The paper proposes RSR to capture both alignment and informativeness and reports a mean absolute Spearman correlation of 0.86 with post-training reasoning performance across five students and trajectories from 11 teachers. [Paper abstract](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.14249v5) In a separate agentic study, Qwen3-8B scored assistant tokens with ranks capped at 100. Mean RSR recovered the published ordering of four teachers on a source-balanced OpenThoughts-Agent sample of 1,000 trajectories per teacher. Trajectory length, mean NLL, error-retry rate and tool-action ratio failed to recover that order in this sample. The separate data-selection test was inconclusive. [Issue 9348](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9348), following [issue 8533](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8533). The pooled-token RSR subsection below gives the Snowball 10/05 results and their limits.

## What we measured

Per-token NLL of one frozen student on candidate teacher traces, in nats per supervised loss token, token-weighted. "Text" excludes target tokens whose id is ≥128000 (chat-template specials), which are 0.2–1.5% of loss tokens. The per-trace mean is the unweighted mean of per-row means. Every value below is a mean over whole cells; the cells are not paired with each other except where an equal-task gap is stated explicitly.

Two reviewed datasets exist, and they are not the same rows or the same pass count:

- **Single pass, four cells (all loss tokens):** 8,540 rows in four cells, one pass, no training, zero missing rows. These four values are whole-cell, all-loss-token means. This is the run quoted in the issue 11535 status comment.
- **Three-pass campaign (text-only; 500 tasks per internal cell, 250 per collaborator split):** three internal 500-task cells (contributor, GLM v7 LOW, GLM v7 HIGH), ten collaborator cells (five teachers × two pools, 250 tasks each), and one 10/05-only contrib-full cell.

Cell names in plain words:

- **contrib:** our contributor rows on 500 shared tasks — Kimi-2.5 SWE-smith (250 tasks) plus Qwen3.6-27B TMax (250 tasks).
- **contrib-full:** every contributor plain row, 2,978 rows, one task each. It is not paired with any other cell. Its full-pool mean was 0.283 versus 0.294 for the sampled 500-task cell; that comparison alone does not establish sample representativeness.
- **glm-low / glm-high:** GLM 5.3 v7 traces at the LOW and HIGH reasoning-effort settings, on the same 500 tasks as contrib.
- **collaborator cells:** the released five-teacher trace sets on the collaborator's two task pools, RTS and TMax-legacy, 250 tasks per split, one attempt per task; summarization gives several rows per trial.

## How we measured

- **Scorer:** `experiments/post_training/teacher_nll/score.py` at commit `5e2ba6e9b87db5038211da796ef0e5779f2fe637` (SHA256 `45a84de6789f89fb173e190b2db937505c2008a0510964e97d35c91359640b3f`). Direct vLLM prompt-logprob scoring, TP1/DP8 with expert parallel, prefix caching off, 73,728 context, 7,168 batched tokens, 32 sequences, one completion token per prompt. The loss weight at position *i* scores token *i*+1, the trainer's convention; no masked token is converted into a target.
- **Students:** 10/05 SFT `open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05` at revision `8c76b22a`, and the pre-SFT parent `open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8` at revision `058ecaf2`. No distributed-loader flag; weights load from the Hub on the GPU host.
- **Single-pass cells:** the scorer reused the frozen token IDs and loss masks; no re-rendering, truncation or trajectory deduplication. Seven original SWE holdout rows were scored for completeness and remain ineligible for training.
- **Campaign cells:** rendered with the 10/05 tokenizer and chat template, byte-identical to `grug_sft/tokenizer/2026.09.18`, with `enable_thinking=True` passed explicitly. The collaborator's traces were re-rendered independently and matched 100/100.
- **Parity check against the trainer:** the 16 rows of a smoke step-0 batch scored 0.380693 under vLLM versus 0.380914 from the native trainer, a difference of −0.00022 nats against a 0.01 gate.
- **Passes:** the campaign cells are three full passes, each in a fresh engine process, with a pass spread of ≤0.0003 nats; the base parent is one pass. The single-pass cells are one pass under 10/05.
- **Intervals:** 95% bootstrap, 10,000 resamples over tasks, seed 20261113, rows clustered by (family, task). Paired gaps use the shared task set. Text-only means are reported without intervals; the all-token and base-text columns carry the campaign's own within-cell bootstrap.

### Pooled-token RSR, ranks capped at 100

Rank-Surprisal Ratio (RSR) is the mean target-token rank divided by the mean negative log-likelihood under the student; the paper interprets lower RSR as better informative alignment. We ran it with the same Snowball 10/05 student on the same 14 cells, in one pass over 9,943 rows in one fresh engine. The run reproduced the earlier mean NLL on every cell, largest difference 0.000131 nats per token. Each cell's value is the sum of capped ranks over loss tokens divided by the sum of NLL over those tokens, so longer scored rows carry more weight.

What this shows:

- The two measures disagree. The rank correlation between pooled-token RSR and mean NLL over the 14 cells is −0.125, so "closest teacher" depends on which measure is read.
- By mean NLL the collaborator's teachers order 122B, 9B, 35B-A3B, 27B, GLM (closest first) on both task pools. By pooled-token RSR the RTS order is 35B-A3B, 27B, 9B, 122B, GLM (best first), and the TMax order is 27B, 35B-A3B, 9B, GLM, 122B.
- GLM-5.3-Flash has the highest mean NLL on both pools, and the highest pooled-token RSR on RTS and the second-highest on TMax, behind Qwen3.5-122B.
- Our contributor rows have low mean NLL, but their pooled-token RSR values (4.317 and 4.390) fall inside the range of the four GLM cells (4.205–4.620).

Limits of this RSR measurement:

- **Aggregation.** Our column is a pooled-token ratio: the sum of capped ranks over loss tokens divided by the sum of NLL over those tokens, which weights longer scored rows more. The paper's formula in its appendix A.8 uses the ratio of sums of trajectory-level means. On our data, taking the ratio of summed row means gives a correlation of −0.108 with pooled mean NLL and puts Qwen3.5-9B lowest on both RTS and TMax. Row-to-trajectory equivalence is unverified.
- **The cap.** "Tokens over the cap" is the share of a cell's loss tokens whose rank exceeds 100, so the cap changed those terms. Without the cap of 100, several cells change a lot (Qwen3.5-122B RTS is 55.97 instead of 3.861).
- **Rank convention.** The rank is the serving engine's tie-inclusive rank: 1 plus tokens with a strictly higher logprob plus other tokens with an identical logprob. On the 16 parity rows, a strict comparison reduced the all-loss-token capped rank sum by 0.11% (141 of 128,420) and the text-only sum by 0.10%. This was measured on the parity rows only.
- **Logit dtype.** The logit dtype used for the ranks is unverified.
- **Scope.** One pass, one student, one serving build. No training-outcome inference is drawn.
