| MATH-500 | 10.05 final | 2000 | 95.9% | 1.0% | 0.7% | 0.3% | 0.2% [0.1, 0.5] |
| GPQA-Diamond | 10.05 final | 2374 | 67.2% | 23.7% | 22.4% | 1.3% | 1.4% [1.0, 2.0] |

Setup: The control is the `control` arm of the #11188 data-patch experiment: the historical 262K cold-start SFT recipe, run for 222 updates. Its evals are `sft11188-control-s100b-*` and `sft11188-control-s222-*` under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/evals/`. The control has no step-200 eval, so this comment reports step 222. The 10.05 final pools four eval campaigns that store vLLM's `finish_reason`: `20261017-021639`, `20261021-193028`, `20261023-*` and `20261024-014627`, plus GPQA from `20261022-004247`. All runs use temperature 0.7, 10 repeats for AIME24 and OlympiadBench, 3 for GPQA, and a context of about 73.7k tokens. GSM8K is excluded: its config disables thinking and does not ask for a box.

Definitions:
- No box: no `\boxed{` or `\fbox{` anywhere in the response. Matching a plain `\boxed` counts responses that only quote the prompt's "Mark your solution with \boxed".
- Truncated: `finish_reason == "length"` for the 10.05 runs. The control archives store no finish reason, so truncation is inferred: the re-tokenized response is within 300 tokens of the benchmark's ceiling, where outputs pile up (AIME24 72,898, OlympiadBench 69,952, MATH-500 72,534).
- Gave up: in the last 4,000 characters (or last 15%), a time-pressure, guess or stuck phrase ("given the time", "I'll guess", "I give up", "I'm stuck") followed within 300 characters by a commitment ("I'll assume", "I'll go with", "the intended answer is"). Reading 12 random matches plus earlier full reads gives 80–85% precision. Wider hedge words ("not sure", "I'll go with") are not usable. On AIME24 the responses containing them are still 90% correct.

Observations:
- Unboxed AIME24 and OlympiadBench responses are 96–100% truncated, and the grader scores almost none of them correct (0 of 385 on AIME24 for 10.05).
- When the model gives up, it is mostly wrong: 0–16% correct on OlympiadBench, 47% on GPQA (chance is 25%). Examples: "Given the time, I'll guess D. Many multiple choice questions have the answer D." and "Given the time, I'll assume the track is a semicircle of radius R = 1 m." Most cases are multi-part physics on OlympiadBench and stereochemistry on GPQA.
- Truncated responses usually keep reasoning until the cap without concluding. On AIME24 (10.05), 94% of 193 truncated responses never state the correct answer, and three problems (aime24-14, -26, -22) account for 55% of them. On OlympiadBench, a read of 21 truncated traces found 12 stuck or looping, often from the first 10–30% of the response. In 85 of 105 truncated multi-part physics responses, the model repeatedly re-derives the "context answers" given for earlier parts.
- The other arms do not move either rate. At matching steps, `cap32k`, `cap32k-giveup` and `utf-normalize` stay within ±2.5 points of the control on finished no-box and on gave up. `cap32k` truncates 4–5 points less on AIME24 and OlympiadBench (one seed, about two standard errors).

Gate: Incidence ≥5% holds only for truncation (AIME24, OlympiadBench, GPQA). Training documents matching truncation are nearly absent: 58 of 665,326 competitive-programming rows end in an unclosed code block. Give-up endings are about 1.3% of the weighted mix and unboxed endings about 0.04%. Per the issue, this stops at step 2 for give-up filtering. The measured failure is not stopping on hard problems, which points to reasoning-length or stopping behaviour as the next target.

Caveats: One seed per arm. Control truncation is inferred. "Final answer with no supporting derivation" is not measured: a proxy (the boxed value first appears at the very end) misfired on reformatted expressions and was dropped.

issues.author: gonzalobenegas
issues.body:
### What

PR #10984 adds the original [GenomeQA benchmark](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05774) to TaskCompendium. Models answer 5,200 binary-choice and multiple-choice questions across six biological subtasks, using the [pinned Hugging Face dataset](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa/tree/e655e415fa30681dddbaf4acc182bcbd8ac41943) and the authors’ fixed prompt, without tools or retrieval.

### Why

A model can describe a splice site in words. Can it also recognize one when given a DNA sequence? GenomeQA lets us test that distinction with sequence-based questions about regulatory elements, splice sites, species, histone marks, transcription-factor binding sites, and motifs. The six subtask scores show where a model can select the correct biological label from the sequence and where it struggles. That gives us a way to compare checkpoints and track which sequence tasks improve as training changes.

Hugging Face’s biology team used a modified multiple-choice version of GenomeQA to evaluate [Carbon-X](https://huggingface.co/HuggingFaceBio/Carbon-X). Its taxonomy task differs from the original, which limits direct score comparisons.

### Decisions for review

The first two rows are the priorities for review.

| Decision | Upstream behavior and Marin’s proposed approach | Question for reviewers |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **1. Reuse terms and ID policy eligibility** | The authors publish the [original questions on GitHub](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/tree/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/benchmark). We found no explicit reuse license for those questions, the [Hugging Face copy](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa), or the [runner prompt](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/run.py). The adapter fetches pinned assets and uses synthetic test fixtures. Questions and responses stay in controlled storage; public reports would contain aggregate scores. | Should GenomeQA be considered for Marin’s ID evaluation policy while reuse terms are unspecified, or should explicit permission be a prerequisite for consideration? If it remains a candidate, what permissions do we need to run it and publish aggregate scores? |
| **2. Thinking settings and output budget** | The [released runner](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/run.py) leaves the output limit to the provider. Our GenomeQA runs used 16,384 generated tokens per question, shared between reasoning and the final answer. We tested Gemma and Qwen with thinking off/on and GPT-OSS at low/medium effort. Gemma hit the cap on 12 of 5,200 questions with thinking off and 1,341 with it on. By comparison, [Marin’s SimpleQA Verified evaluation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11393) uses 2,048 tokens off and 16,384 on. | For routine GenomeQA evaluation, should we choose one reasoning setting per model or report paired settings? If paired, should the modes share a cap or have separate caps? Is 16,384 appropriate given Gemma’s truncation rate? |
| 3. Headline score | The [paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.05774) reports binary-choice and multiple-choice scores separately. Marin keeps both, shows each biological subtask’s score, and adds an overall mean. Within each subtask the two formats count equally. Each of the six subtasks then gets one-sixth of the overall score. | Should the equal-subtask mean be Marin’s headline score, alongside the six subtask results and the two paper-comparable format scores? |

### Validation

All 5,200 Hugging Face rows match the authors’ release on the evaluation fields. The runs used the fixed prompt and sampling settings from the released runner (temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95).

All six native runs are complete: **5,200/5,200 graded per run**. They use the same questions, prompt, sampling, and total output cap. GPT-OSS reasons at both settings: low/medium is not off/on. These are single-seed comparisons, not claims of statistical superiority.

| Biological subtask | Gemma off | Gemma on | Qwen off | Qwen on | GPT-OSS low | GPT-OSS medium |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Enhancer/promoter | 38.60% | 36.30% | 47.20% | 50.40% | 48.90% | 50.00% |
| Splice sites | 37.30% | 23.40% | 29.70% | 32.00% | 37.70% | 35.00% |
| Species classification | 47.10% | 34.90% | 50.00% | 50.20% | 49.90% | 49.40% |
| Histone marks | 40.70% | 31.70% | 40.40% | 38.80% | 39.70% | 40.20% |
| TF binding sites | 41.80% | 39.40% | 41.80% | 42.60% | 46.30% | 45.70% |
| Motifs | 59.00% | 69.00% | 57.00% | 59.50% | 60.00% | 60.00% |
| **Overall macro** | **44.08%** | **39.12%** | **44.35%** | **45.58%** | **47.08%** | **46.72%** |
| Truncations / 5,200 | 12 | 1341 | 318 | 393 | 34 | 42 |

Gemma thinking falls **4.97 points**, with 25.79% truncation; Qwen thinking rises **1.23 points**; GPT-OSS medium falls **0.37 points**. All non-length-stopped responses in these runs parsed successfully. All 2,140 length-stopped responses remain in the denominator. Of those, 353 had nonempty final text and none contained a parseable answer. Grading available final content at the cap changes none of the six scores. Truncations materially limit interpretation of Gemma’s thinking-on result.

- **Paper comparison.** Maverick scored 50.60% on all 5,200 questions versus 49.07% derived from the paper’s binary-choice and multiple-choice tables.
- **Replay.** We verified the prompts, generation settings, and weights for 31,200 saved responses. Replaying them through the corrected grader at `b706dbdc87` reproduced every native extracted answer and metric. All 26 grader/importer tests passed.
- **Current diagnostics (`2d24e8922a`).** The grader reports `unanswered` once per response and records the reason when extraction fails. Historical archives retain the earlier diagnostic fields. The length-stop recheck established that all six accuracy scores and extracted choices are preserved.
- **Blinded spot check.** A single Codex reviewer labeled 24 saved responses before seeing the references or grades. All 24 agreed on extraction and score: seven correct, eleven wrong, and six truncated. The sample included one truncation per run.

### Cost

**The six native runs consumed 30.03 H100-hours** including serving and recovery. Worker time sums the durations of started worker attempts. Elapsed time spans the first worker start to the last worker stop, including recovery gaps and excluding the initial queue wait.

| Scope | H100s per worker | Worker time (min) | Elapsed (min) | H100-hours |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Gemma off and on, including recovery | 2 | 399 | 5,310 | 13.29 |
| Qwen off | 4 | 91 | 91 | 6.04 |
| Qwen on | 4 | 118 | 118 | 7.86 |
| GPT-OSS low | 1 | 95 | 226 | 1.58 |
| GPT-OSS medium | 1 | 76 | 76 | 1.26 |

<details>
<summary>Model pins, usage, replay evidence, and recovery details</summary>

Current-main validation (2026-11-17, `5e07ba7498`): **23 focused tests and lint pass; all applicable CI checks are green**. The PR reuses main’s `final_only` implementation; its custom shared-code addition is removed. All six advisory lanes completed; fixes reuse the existing Parquet reader and centralize repeated constants. The compact grader and source-row dictionaries were retained because splitting this linear grading operation or wrapping boundary rows would add little value.

At `5e07ba7498`, the November 17 audit established: **all 31,200 saved answers across six runs match**, with zero source-row, prompt, generation-setting, extracted-answer, metric, or weight differences. All expected cell populations and latest graded attempts were verified. The upstream `final_only` change alters none of these results; no saved message combines a refusal field with nonempty content. Follow-up constant cleanup is semantically identical, and the shared Parquet reader preserves all 5,200 source hashes. The CPU-only audit succeeded within its one-hour cap, with **zero new model calls**.

Private EvalDash ingestion reproduces all six macros, all six subtask and twelve cell metrics, and full 5,200-item coverage. The macro remains continuous, with weighted uncertainty and no fabricated integer correct count. **A shared reporting gap remains:** `coverage.n_unanswered` is not populated by the native reader, although the saved `unanswered` metric is correct. No public records were ingested; this verifies backend reduction and measurement projection, not browser rendering.

Historical paper comparison: Maverick’s complete 5,200-question run scored **50.60%**, versus **49.07%** derived from the paper’s BCQ/MCQ table. Replaying it through TaskCompendium reproduced every per-item metric and all 120 grouped metrics with identical prompts. A separate two-question live native smoke also passed.

Review fixes in `b706dbdc87` reject `B1` and `B or (C)`, identify renamed pinned input files by digest, and independently test wrong answers and cell populations. All 26 grader/importer tests and changed-file lint passed. CI passed. A CPU-only replay of all 31,200 native final answers on the corrected grader found zero changes to extracted answers or metrics. Rechecking all 5,200 historical Maverick responses changed one histone MCQ from unparseable to a valid wrong answer (B, gold A). Its parse failures fall from six to five and the macro stays 50.60%.

**Blinded spot check at `b706dbdc87`.** A single Codex reviewer inspected 24 saved responses, four per run and 12 per format, and recorded the final choices before seeing the answer key or grader verdicts. All 24 extracted answers and grades agreed: seven correct, eleven wrong, and six length-truncated. Four truncations had empty final content and two had partial text; all six scored zero. Sampling deliberately included one truncation per run. This checks grading against the pinned answers, without estimating a population error rate or assessing the biological validity of the answer key.

Unlike the [merged SimpleQA Verified example (#11393)](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11393)’s 2,048/16,384 off/on allowances, these comparisons keep the output cap equal to avoid changing both thinking and budget.

The declaration now follows the [add-eval guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/8eca4ffc4b5bc9b63de1db08c3c77c8763e0b4f6/docs/tutorials/add-evaluation.md). Its curation source ID is `Eval:genomeqa`, its recipe name is `eval-genomeqa`, and its protocol benchmark key is `genomeqa`. The recipe pairs converter version `2026.11.18` with the grader hash. The publication and output-budget test passed using this declaration. The six archived model runs below used the earlier declaration.

All native inference used runtime `fe813e34c2a0d047f10a1604a12da35f162031cd`. Gemma: `google/gemma-4-26B-A4B-it` at `4d7ae4984b7db7de8f8457170b3f1a419ee76d52`, two H100s. Qwen: `Qwen/Qwen3.6-35B-A3B` at `995ad96eacd98c81ed38be0c5b274b04031597b0`, four H100s (TP2 × DP2). GPT-OSS: `openai/gpt-oss-20b` at `6cee5e81ee83917806bbde320786a8fb61efebee`, one H100. Compilation and CUDA graphs remained enabled. Template checks and saved request options verify the selected thinking/effort controls. Other settings retain checkpoint/server defaults; these are fixed GenomeQA-protocol runs, not each model’s full recommended sampling recipe.

| Run | Input tokens | Output tokens | BCQ macro | MCQ macro |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| gemma-off | 7,298,523 | 1,436,334 | 54.43% | 33.73% |
| gemma-on | 7,288,123 | 47,058,415 | 49.47% | 28.77% |
| qwen-off | 7,654,474 | 13,909,197 | 51.87% | 36.83% |
| qwen-on | 7,644,074 | 28,897,134 | 54.03% | 37.13% |
| gptoss-low | 7,812,272 | 8,041,128 | 53.77% | 40.40% |
| gptoss-medium | 7,812,272 | 8,005,514 | 54.73% | 38.70% |

Usage covers final graded attempts only; output includes reasoning and final answers without a separately measured split. Qwen thinking uses 2.08× output tokens; GPT-OSS medium uses 0.44% fewer than low. Failed-attempt usage is not included.

This is historical worker runtime, including serving overhead, not billing or a sum of authorization caps. Queue-only attempts have no start timestamp and contribute zero. Gemma’s paired/recovery workers span both modes, so their time is not falsely split. GPT-OSS low includes the preempted worker and successful recovery; its capacity-blocked recovery obtained no GPU. All inference workers are stopped. The subsequent audit is CPU-only and makes no model calls.

Native retries retained successful answers. Gemma’s final one-question recovery preserved all 5,199 prior responses; GPT-OSS low recovery preserved all 5,058. Qwen on recovered 28 first-pass infrastructure failures; GPT-OSS medium recovered 126 across two further native passes. Successful grades were not resampled. Earlier queue, connection, and preemption failures are operational history, not additional scored model failures.

Private audit evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/genomeqa/audit-merged-main-20261117/` · [Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fgenomeqa%2Faudit-merged-main-20261117%2F). Includes per-item hashes, aggregate audits, ingestion projections, worker timestamps, and the prior detailed issue record.

Native result roots: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/genomeqa/gemma-paired-fe813e34-20261112/` · [Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fgenomeqa%2Fgemma-paired-fe813e34-20261112%2F), and `s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/experiments/genomeqa/cohort-fe813e34-20261116/` · [Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Fmarin%2Fexperiments%2Fgenomeqa%2Fcohort-fe813e34-20261116%2F). Original questions/responses remain controlled.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Pinned assets, parser details, and historical parity</summary>

Data: [HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa](https://huggingface.co/datasets/HuggingFaceBio/genomeqa/tree/e655e415fa30681dddbaf4acc182bcbd8ac41943), revision `e655e415fa30681dddbaf4acc182bcbd8ac41943`; only `binary/train-00000-of-00001.parquet` and `mcq/train-00000-of-00001.parquet`. The `train` split is used for evaluation. Evaluation fields match the author release; metadata equivalence was not checked.

Binary SHA-256: `0ef4c3d33541980e3fded9a5b23a952296ce3c51cb0415b42c0299a61c21938a`; MCQ: `c1cbb51449eb8a5241890337c88dc1bc0a58974b8eb4cb8bc49f310b12faeb75`.

Prompt: authors’ [run.py](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/run.py), revision `7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d`. Parse the literal without executing upstream code. Prompt-development-set disjointness has not been established. The paper’s CC BY Figure 8 differs from the runner; it is not substituted. Code/data availability statements do not establish reuse terms for the assembled dataset or runner prompt.

For each subtask, average its BCQ and MCQ accuracies; overall is the mean of those six values. Reversing the two equal-weight averaging steps gives the same result. `genomeqa_macro` uses weight 5 for the 100-question motif cells and 1 for each 500-question cell; ordinary accuracy remains unweighted. Format macros follow the authors’ [aggregation](https://github.com/ai4nucleome/GenomeQA/blob/7ccc230e734fc11a365fd1963b593b5fd11e834d/collect_res.py).

Parsing selects final content, strips completed thinking blocks, isolates the last `### Answer` section, and accepts one valid option. Without a heading, an unambiguous explicit `Answer: X` is accepted. Conflicting options, incomplete thinking blocks, and missing answers score zero. The grader receives final text only. Validation reports count length and content-filter stops from archived model turns. An empty or unparseable final answer is recorded as unanswered regardless of the stop reason. Main’s shared `final_only` selector returns content without reasoning fallback or a benchmark-specific refusal-field override. The saved Gemma thinking-on run contains 1,321 empty final-content responses with nonempty reasoning; they remain zero-scored rather than extracting an answer from reasoning. Raw messages remain archived.

Maverick (2026-11-06, historical Evalchemy path): macro 50.60%, BCQ 57.43%, MCQ 43.77%, unweighted 47.46% (2,468/5,200); paper-derived macro 49.07%. Six parse failures, no truncations or separately classified refusals. Four failures were splice-site MCQ, one histone MCQ, one TFBS MCQ. Natural-language declarations such as “The answer is X” would recover one additional correct answer: macro 50.6167%. Those counterfactual scores were not adopted. Reported API cost was $3.08, conservative accounting bound $3.93, excluding CPU hosting and connectivity pilot.

The first complete motif-MCQ cell scored 64/100 versus the paper’s 65/100; its temporary integration code was retired after the full run. The initial native replay reproduced the six historical extraction failures. The November 17 replay at `b706dbdc87` left five: one histone MCQ yielded a valid wrong answer. Both versions scored 2,468/5,200 correct. The two-question native smoke used 1,982 input and 348 output tokens ($0.0010417 API cost); it validates execution, not performance. Its provider request included seed/thinking kwargs absent from the historical run, without proving provider enforcement.

</details>

### Remaining scope

- Track current CI and required approval on [PR #10984](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10984).
- Before public reporting: resolve sample-access controls and the shared unanswered-count metadata gap, then validate the browser presentation of six subtask scores. Additional scalar metrics alone do not create six dashboard columns.
- Official-policy admission remains a separate research decision. No further inference is required for this adapter’s validation.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖
# Research

GenomeQA needs a 5,200-item source, final-answer grading, a complete 12-cell macro reduction, and six primary dashboard scores. At this checkout, Evalchemy is a separate fork; Marin owns launch configuration and result ingestion. Marin currently lets model generation settings override an evaluation's token cap and generation arguments, so the agreed GenomeQA request cannot be assumed from its YAML alone. No open Marin PR implements GenomeQA; the related [LAB-Bench PR #10582](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10582) remains a separate draft.

**Relevant code**
- [external Evalchemy source](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/config/external/evalchemy/pyproject.toml#L10-L11) — fork ownership.
- [config_for()](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L76-L92) — model settings override evaluation settings.
- [EvalchemyResult](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/lib/marin/src/marin/evaluation/evalchemy/result.py#L79-L100) — task metric ingestion.
- [evaluation registry](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/evaluation/evals.py#L205-L234) — Marin registration.

# Proposed Fix

1. In `marin-community/evalchemy`, add one source for the pinned binary and MCQ files. Preserve question text, option order, composite IDs, and the authors' fixed prompt. Keep answer fields out of requests.
2. Add benchmark-scoped final-content selection before shared letter extraction. Record raw response, selected span, answer letter, finish reason, and distinct refusal, parse-failure, truncation, and transport-failure outcomes. Test conflicting markers and incidental letters in analysis.
3. Emit all 12 cell accuracies and denominators, six equally weighted subtask scores, BCQ/MCQ summaries, and the overall macro. Gate complete scores on all 5,200 graded items; expose partial coverage without silently changing denominators. Test unequal cell sizes and missing cells.
4. In Marin, pin the fork revision, add portable GenomeQA configuration and registry entries, and verify that the report and EvalDash expose the overall and six primary scores. Resolve generation-setting precedence and inspect captured provider requests for the 16,384-token total cap, sampling, and model-specific reasoning settings.
5. Reproduce the offline data and prompt checks. Once provider, effective limits, license/attribution, and cost bounds are settled, run only the agreed 100-item motif MCQ Maverick comparison and retain per-item evidence. Keep official evaluation-policy adoption separate.

This calls for a fork adapter PR followed by a Marin integration PR linked to #10981; it is larger than a single triage fix.

comments.body:
🤖 Audited the remaining implementation guidance against current main, `fec8b74093e9319893a04d8196e46af1b07f87c3`, and updated the issue:

- Current launches ingest FineStore artifacts and canonical benchmark metadata. Validation now covers that path through record construction and dashboard measurement; a legacy JSON fixture alone is insufficient. Six subtask columns need explicit reporting views rather than extra scalar metrics alone.
- Existing final-channel and thinking-marker helpers can be reused. The letter grader still stringifies responses, and the boxed-answer helper permits a reasoning fallback, so neither meets GenomeQA's extraction contract unchanged.

issues.author: asartran
issues.body:
The marin unit test `tests/rl/test_rl_launch_documents.py::test_rl_launch_documents_load_with_the_vendored_launcher` takes 37 s at the median (55 s at p90, 114 s max) across 306 CI runs from Nov 15-18, which makes it one of the two slowest test files in the marin unit suite. CI deals test files to four marin shards, and the shard holding this file is often the last to finish, so it sets how long many PRs wait.

Almost all of that time is the SkyRL-side check, not the environment build. Timed on a development machine at `main` with a warm SkyRL environment:

| Stage | Time |
|---|---|
| Render the 103 launch documents (`render_launch_census`) | 5.5 s |
| SkyRL launcher subprocess loading the 103 documents (`tests/rl/launch_document_loader.py`) | 42.6 s |
| Build SkyRL's CPU environment from an empty uv cache | 10.9 s (0.5 s warm) |

Each `launch_config.load_launch_config` call composes the full SkyRL training config through Hydra (`_compose_source_recipe` -> `compose_skyrl_config` -> `hydra.compose`), with most of the time in OmegaConf deep copies, so the check costs about 0.4 s per document. It grows with every new launch document.

Done when:
- the test's CI time no longer grows with the number of launch documents, or stays under about 10 s on a GitHub `ubuntu-latest` runner, while still checking that every launch document loads with the vendored launcher (for example in the nightly slow job if not on every PR).

The test renders every launch document, then the loader calls `load_launch_config` once per document. Source recipes enter `_compose_source_recipe`, which composes a full SkyRL config for each call; 103 documents therefore add roughly 43 seconds to the PR unit shard. The scheduled `slow` job already runs tests marked `slow`.

**Relevant code**
- [`test_rl_launch_documents.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/rl/test_rl_launch_documents.py#L18) — full census test
- [`launch_document_loader.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/tests/rl/launch_document_loader.py#L27) — per-document load

Split the test so PR shards render and check the full document census, while the nightly slow job loads every document with the vendored launcher. This removes the repeated Hydra composition from PR unit shards and preserves the full load check each night.

issues.author: penfever
issues.body:
## TL;DR

In progress. Base Micro210 row measured (pooled 0.1333 / mean-of-benchmark-means 0.1596; 438/440 slots scored — BFCL UID 232 and BixBench UID 89 unscored in verifier preparation). This issue tests Deletion Tuning ([arXiv 2611.10866](https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10866)) on the Snowball 262K long-context-extension (LCE) base: 3-4 Deletion Tuning variants are trained and measured under the same policy, with paired deltas against the base.

## Description

Deletion Tuning post-trains a model only by zeroing a small set of pretrained weights. Each gate-projection weight `W` gets a trainable logit `G`. Training uses the soft mask `W * sigmoid(alpha * G)`, and `alpha` increases linearly (for example from 1e2 to 1e3 for SFT, 1e3 to 1e4 for GRPO). Evaluation and rollouts use the hard mask `W * 1[G > 0]`. Gates start from Wanda scores (`|W| * ||x||`); `eta = 1/2048` selects the low-Wanda delete group at initialization (the noisy logit init then deletes about 0.18% of the targeted gate weights). The regularizer is `-lambda * ||W_masked||^2`, with `lambda = 1e-5`. The paper reports that deleting fewer than 0.05% of all weights matches full fine-tuning under GRPO, SFT and on-policy distillation, up to Qwen3-30B-A3B (gate projection of all 128 experts masked, router frozen). It also reports that prior-task accuracy stays within about 1 point of the base.

The base model is [open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/snowball-67b-a2b-base-262k-qk175-skew8/tree/step-157000) (#8977, item 5), the base of the current long loops. The evaluation is Micro210 (#10804, #10933) at the same pins, seeds and task/attempt IDs for every row.

## Hypothesis or Goal

On a 67B-A2B MoE, a learned deletion mask on expert gate projections recovers most of the Micro210 gain of full fine-tuning from the same data and budget, with less forgetting and a mask artifact that is much smaller than a checkpoint.

## Plan

1. ~~Measure the base under Micro210~~ **DONE** (2026-11-18, run `2026.11.18.3`): pooled 0.1333, mean-of-benchmark-means 0.1596, native equal-20 0.1596, 438/440 slots scored (BFCL UID 232, BixBench UID 89 unscored in verifier preparation).
2. Implement Deletion Tuning in the Snowball training path: a gate logit per masked weight, the `alpha` ramp, Wanda initialization from a calibration sample, and a hard-mask export that writes a standard checkpoint (deleted weights set to zero) plus the mask artifact.
3. Train and measure these variants under Micro210:
   - **V1 SFT, paper scope:** mask the gate projection of every routed expert; learn it with SFT on a fixed sample of the Exp3 SFT mix (#11658), with the paper's SFT hyperparameters.
   - **V2 RL, paper scope:** the same mask scope, learned with GRPO on the Exp3 RL curriculum, with the paper's GRPO hyperparameters (the paper's main regime).
   - **V3 wider scope:** mask gate, up and down projections of routed and shared experts, in the V1 regime. The paper does not test this.
   - **V4 controls:** a Wanda-only mask and a random mask, each at the sparsity that V1 learned, with no training. The paper does not report a random-mask control.
4. For each variant, report the Micro210 score with uncertainty, the paired deltas against the base, the learned sparsity, the mask size, and the GPU-hours. Where a full fine-tuning row on the same data exists, compare against it.

## Status

Base row measured and durable (`s3://marin-us-east-02a/marin/users/benfeuer/snowball-deletion-tuning/micro210-base/2026.11.18.3/` with checksums; also on [#11337](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337#issuecomment-6988511341)). Core masking module + tiny-MoE tests on `benfeuer/snowball-deletion-tuning`; the production SFT path corrected to Levanter (`exp3_sft_spec` → Levanter Snowball model + shared SFT launcher) with the integration plan API-verified; V2 targets Megatron/SkyRL (design verified against megatron-core 0.18.0). The V1 entry is resolved and validated on `benfeuer/snowball-deletion-tuning-run`: the Exp3 production SFT recipe retargeted at the Deletion Tuning main, 75 updates on the V5 mix as the Exp3 run consumed it, AdamW 5e-4 constant on the gate logits only; the production dry-run resolved at 256 H100 / 75 steps / ~5.03B positions (nothing submitted), 17 behavior tests pass and a CPU smoke ran the DT main end to end; the hard-mask export is the next landed item before submission. Logbook: [marin-logbooks#63](https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/63) (branch `codex/63-snowball-deletion-tuning`; index PR cold-read SATISFIED).

## Links

* Paper: https://arxiv.org/abs/2611.10866
* Logbook: https://github.com/marin-community/marin-logbooks/issues/63
* W&B Report: (to add)

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-18: initial-deletion-fraction correction (eta = 1/2048 selects the delete group; ~0.18% of gate weights start deleted) — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6983705526).
- 2026-11-18: training path = Exp3 SFT runtime for V1/V3, Megatron/SkyRL for V2 — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6984380965).
- 2026-11-18: SFT-path implementation deviations recorded (V3 down-projection Wanda proxy, subsampled delete threshold, packed-uint8 mask artifact) — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6984567000).
- 2026-11-18: **CORRECTION** — the production SFT path is Levanter (SnowballConfig + shared SFT launcher), not sft_runtime; supersedes the earlier path comment — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6986444207).
- 2026-11-18: V2 learner path = Megatron (the vendored SkyRL dispatcher supports only `strategy: megatron`) — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6984946982).
- 2026-11-18: base-row number correction (438/440 scored; pooled 0.1333 = 58.3848/438) — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6988314930) and this correction.

- 2026-11-18: V1 entry resolved, dry-run verified, and validated (data = the Exp3 V5 release as the Exp3 run consumed it, seed 0; 75 updates = 10 percent of 746 rounded, batch 256, context 262,144; Wanda calibration on the first 64 training batches; AdamW constant lr 5e-4, weight decay 0, on the gate logits only; the Exp3 initial-eval-match gate dropped because the Deletion init deliberately perturbs the masked weights; 5 h deadline and 1280 H100-h guard over a ~969 H100-h point estimate; 17 behavior tests and a CPU smoke through the pod entrypoint, catching seven bugs in the never-executed Deletion code) — [comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11663#issuecomment-6994821567).

## Conclusion

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

Effort: low (issue, linked PRs, code, and paper; 2026-11-18). [PR #11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) contains Snowball SFT, asynchronous RLOO-N, and a Micro210 runtime, but remains open. Its reported evaluation is for a trained model, covers 200 tasks and 440 attempts after excluding Tau3, and has one attempt unscored; it does not provide a 210-task/450-attempt base row. [PR #11658](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11658) pins the Exp3 V5 SFT mix but is also open, while [#10933](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10933) tracks the missing general Micro210 launcher on `main`. The [paper](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.10866v1) trains gate logits with a soft mask, uses a hard mask for evaluation and rollouts, and reports about 0.18% of targeted gate weights deleted at initialization under its Gaussian Wanda prior, despite `eta=1/2048`.

Relevant code: [routed expert weights and HF export](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/benfeuer/long-loop-prototype/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/model.py#L1558), [SFT loss](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/benfeuer/long-loop-prototype/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L924), [Micro210 selection](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/benfeuer/long-loop-prototype/experiments/post_training/long_loop/evaluation.py#L42). No open PR specifically implements Deletion Tuning.

# Plan

1. Freeze the comparison contract: exact Snowball base revision, Micro210 dataset/runtime pins, seed, task and attempt IDs, score aggregation, and a separate held-out retention panel. Resolve Tau3 and the missing scored attempt before calling a row “Micro210”; if the common cohort is 200 tasks/440 attempts, label it as a subset and use it for every row. Run or identify the matching base row first.
2. Add a Deletion Tuning mode to the Snowball post-training path after the overlapping code lands: freeze base weights and router, train only mask logits with an explicit routed-gate scope for V1/V2 and routed-plus-shared gate/up/down scope for V3, calibrate Wanda scores on a pinned 2,048-prompt sample, apply the paper’s SFT and GRPO alpha schedules and regularizer, and use hard masks for evaluation and rollouts. Export both a compressed mask and a standard checkpoint with deleted weights zeroed. Validate optimizer filtering, multi-device expert sharding, restart, soft/hard agreement, and export/serve parity on a small configuration before a 67B run.
3. Pin a fixed Exp3 SFT sample and RL curriculum. Run V1 first, then V2, V3, and the Wanda/random controls at V1’s learned sparsity. The existing Snowball RL recipe is RLOO-N; V2 needs an actual GRPO objective to test the paper’s regime, or an explicit “RLOO-N adaptation” label. Keep initial checkpoint, data, steps, and evaluation policy matched to any full-fine-tuning comparator.
4. Publish per-attempt results and paired uncertainty clustered by task ID, plus Micro210 and retention scores, targeted and whole-model sparsity, compressed mask bytes, and GPU-hours. Compare with full fine-tuning only where its data and budget match; otherwise report the missing comparator.

This spans training, rollout, export, and evaluation paths and requires GPU experiments, so it is a staged research task rather than a small issue-fix PR.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

Full Harbor-trial evaluation tasks lose their `task.toml`-declared verifier and agent deadlines during task preparation. A session default of 300 seconds replaces the declared verifier timeout. The trial runtime then injects the row limit as Harbor's `verifier.override_timeout_sec`. Harbor applies the override instead of the task value. Trials whose verifiers need more than 300 seconds fail with `VerifierTimeoutError`.

## Where the 300 seconds come from

- `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/dataset/harbor.py`, `lower_harbor_task`: the `HARBOR_TRIAL_SESSION` branch returned `rollout_spec(task, session)`. It did not read the `task.toml` `[verifier] timeout_sec` or `[agent] timeout_sec` fields. The caller's session supplied all limits.
- The canonical full-trial session config sets `verifier_timeout: 300` (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/config/task_session_config/default.yaml`).
- The trial runtime (`vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/skyrl_train/rollouts/agent_runtime.py`, `original_harness`) sets `verifier.override_timeout_sec = lowered.limits.verifier_timeout` and `agent.override_timeout_sec = lowered.limits.total_turn_timeout`. Harbor resolves the override first (`vendor/harbor/src/harbor/trial/trial.py`, `_compute_verifier_timeout_sec`), so the task's own declaration never applies.
- The published Micro210 policy dataset (`open-athena/Marin-Micro-Eval-210` at `4564ed081c316bc3231ae5c3a53a46b39248c819`) ships the same flat limits for all 210 rows: `verifier_timeout` 300.0, `total_turn_timeout` 1800.0. Its release builder hard-coded one limit set for every row and did not read task.toml. That builder is archived off-main. Prepared rows pass through the trainer unchanged, so the 300 s value reaches the runtime.

This is a hard-coded default. The preparation code does not apply a cap and does not read task.toml.

## Evidence

Exp3 Micro210 (step-20 seal, 440 attempts, 5 infrastructure absences):

- `tb2-recovery/terminal-bench/mcmc-sampling-stan` repetitions 1 and 2: task.toml declares `[verifier] timeout_sec = 1800.0`. Trial receipts show `verifier.override_timeout_sec = 300.0` and `Verifier execution timed out after 300.0 seconds`.
- `tb2-recovery/terminal-bench/large-scale-text-editing` repetitions 0 and 1: task.toml declares 1200.0. Same 300 s override. Repetition 2 finished inside 300 s and scored, which shows the cap sits at the edge of the verifier's real runtime.
- `ot-tblite-recovery/pgn-chess-repair-puzzles` repetition 2: a different failure mode. The task declares no build timeout, so Harbor's 600 s default applied to a build-at-start Dockerfile under concurrent sandbox builds. Receipt timings: repetitions 0 and 1 built their sandboxes in 102.2 s and 100.2 s; repetition 2 hit `EnvironmentStartTimeoutError` after exactly 600.0 s.

Agent deadlines have the same problem: the row limit 1800.0 replaces task-declared agent timeouts. 32 of the 70 Harbor tasks in Micro210 declare more than 1800 s (10 tau3-pi and 10 bixbench-pi at 3600 s, 10 swebench-verified at 3000 s, 2 ot-tblite tasks at 3600 s).

## Tasks affected

48 of the 70 Harbor tasks in the Micro210 selection declare a verifier timeout above 300 s. The declared value was truncated to 300 s for every one of them:

| Declared verifier timeout | Tasks |
|---|---|
| 7200 s | tb2 terminal-bench/sam-cell-seg |
| 3600 s | ot-tblite pdf-table-parsing, pgn-chess-repair-puzzles |
| 3000 s | all 10 swebench-verified tasks |
| 1800 s | tb2 terminal-bench/dna-assembly, feal-linear-cryptanalysis, mcmc-sampling-stan, rstan-to-pystan |
| 1200 s | tb2 terminal-bench/large-scale-text-editing |
| 900 s | all 10 ds-1000-local; ot-tblite acl-permissions-inheritance, build-system-task-ordering, multi-labeller, python-api-rate-limit, schedule-vacation; tb2 merge-diff-arc-agi-task, raman-fitting, vulnerable-secret |
| 600 s | ot-tblite ekf-localization; tb2 modernize-scientific-stack; all 10 bixbench-pi tasks |

Environment build/start timeouts are not affected: the row limits carry no build field, and Harbor honors the task declaration or its 600 s default.

## Earlier runs

The same absence pattern appears in the #11337 recipe rows, because each run consumed the same frozen rows:

- Round 2 (437/440): three infra-unscored TB2 attempts, UIDs 225/268/269, `VerifierTimeoutError` — mcmc-sampling-stan rep 2 and sam-cell-seg reps 1 and 2 (declared 7200 s).
- Round 1 (439/440): the one unscored slot was UID399 = tb2 dna-assembly rep 0 (declared 1800 s).
- SFT-746 eval-only row (420/440): 19 unknown outcomes with the reason "Harbor trial has no verifier score". They include tb2 UIDs 135/224/225/268/269/312/357, ot-tblite UIDs 227/314/315/360, swebench UIDs 306/350, ds-1000 UIDs 186/274, and bixbench UIDs 1/265/353.
- 10/05 baseline: run 2 lost 6 TB2 attempts and the RNO control lost 2; run 1 scored 440/440 because its verifiers completed inside 300 s.

The failures cluster on rows whose models produce plausible solutions. A weak model fails the tests fast, so the verifier stays under 300 s. A stronger model triggers the verifier's expensive path, which exceeds 300 s.

## Verifier wall time on a correct solution

Measured with the pinned task images and the oracle solutions:

- `large-scale-text-editing`: the verifier finished in 117 s wall with reward 1 in a 1-CPU, 2 GB container that matches task.toml. The run includes apt and uv setup, 1M-row CSV regeneration, the vim run, and the comparison. The 300 s override sits near the verifier's real runtime, so network setup variance decides the outcome.
- `mcmc-sampling-stan`: the verifier's own tests re-run the full 4-chain, 100,000-iteration MCMC twice, with internal pytest timeouts of 2000 s and 6000 s. The author therefore expects up to roughly two hours of verifier work. A local measurement of the full path (RStan build plus two verifier re-runs) is in progress. The trial receipts already show both failed repetitions ran into the 300 s cap mid-verifier.
- The pinned `mcmc-sampling-stan` image ships R 4.3.3 without cmake and without gfortran. The oracle solution installs gfortran but not cmake, and RcppParallel (a StanHeaders dependency) fails without cmake. The oracle solution cannot install RStan on the pinned image as-is; mcmc-sampling-stan repetition 0's verifier finished in 3.3 s with reward 0 for this reason.

## Fix

Bind the task-declared agent and verifier deadlines into the prepared row limits in the `HARBOR_TRIAL_SESSION` branch of `lower_harbor_task`, like the shellbox branch already does. A task.toml with verifier timeout 1800 s then produces a prepared `verifier_timeout` of 1800 s. A silent `[verifier]` section produces Harbor's own 600 s default. A silent `[agent]` section leaves no task-declared agent deadline, and the deployment settings govern it.

The prepared `attempt_timeout` also grows to cover the declared phases: `max(session attempt_timeout, build_timeout_sec + agent + verifier + cleanup)`. Harbor cancels the whole trial when the attempt expires, so a row that promises a 7200 s verifier under a 2460 s attempt deadline would still go unscored. Behavior tests: `vendor/skyrl/skyrl-train/tests/cpu/test_harbor_task_lowering.py`.

## Not in scope

- No new canonical policy revision was published and no evaluations were rerun. The frozen Micro210 rows and the recorded scores stay as they are. Rebaseline decisions belong to the experiment owners.
- The pgn-chess-repair-puzzles sandbox-start timeout needs a separate decision (prebuilt image pin, a declared build timeout, or a retry on `EnvironmentStartTimeoutError`).

Part of #11686.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Legacy Grug SFT runs under `experiments/post_training/long_loop` (PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120), head `c6676c91ef`) force the step-1 restore check to a permanent checkpoint, save `keep` milestones permanently, and can write the final step twice when it is also a `keep` milestone. Across 17 dated runs on 2026-11-18 under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/`, this produced 43 native checkpoint prefixes totaling 24,360,070,312,426 bytes (24.36 TB), including 33 prefixes (17,887,983,830,450 bytes, 17.89 TB) in the dated non-one-hour inventory and 10 prefixes (6,472,086,481,976 bytes, 6.47 TB) in the one-hour pair. A manual cleanup deleted 27 intermediate prefixes (16,984 inventoried objects, 11,704,773,554,338 bytes, 11.70 TB of inventoried objects deleted; billed quota relief was not measured).

Most of the mechanism already exists in Levanter and Marin. PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) added `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints`, PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) applied final-only permanent retention with rolling temporary checkpoints to `SFTSpec`, and PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) fixed forced final re-saves on `main`. Long-loop legacy Grug SFT needs four changes:

1. Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper and retain `wait_until_finished()` in `sft_runtime/train.py`, and bring in PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) from `main`.
2. For an unlisted step-1 restore gate, explicitly request a temporary save through the checkpointer, run the non-forced save path, wait for commit, then load from the actual temporary destination. Preserve a named permanent step-1 milestone. The gate copy counts toward rolling retention and can be pruned after enough newer temporary commits or on a permanent commit.
3. Default `sft-smoke.yaml` and long-loop Grug SFT recipes to rolling temporary checkpoints (`keep: null`, time-based `save_interval`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2`) plus explicit named permanent steps (`[{"every": s, "until": s}, ...]`) for export and eval milestones.
4. Remove and verify absence of `metadata.json` before deleting payload objects in `Checkpointer._do_rm_checkpoint` so subsequent discovery skips the prefix; abort payload removal if marker removal fails.

## Prior work

| Item | State | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| PR [#4457](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/4457) / Issue [#4456](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4456) | Merged / Closed | Sets default `keep` for `default_train`, `default_sft`, and `default_dpo` to empty so only rolling temporary checkpoints and the final permanent checkpoint are kept. |
| PR [#4387](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/4387) / PR [#5066](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5066) / Issue [#4386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/4386) | Merged / Closed | Adds `temporary_base_path` to `CheckpointerConfig` and routes temporary checkpoints to region-local TTL temp buckets while keeping forced and step-policy saves permanent under `base_path`. |
| PR [#5945](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5945) | Merged | Sets Grug launchers to `keep=None` (final permanent checkpoint plus temporary recovery saves). |
| PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) | Merged | Adds `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` to `Checkpointer` and `CheckpointerConfig`, pruning older temporary checkpoints on commit while deleting all temporary checkpoints when a permanent checkpoint commits. |
| Issue [#5386](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/5386) | Open | Tracks resume corruption paired with sparse permanent checkpoints and single-temporary retention losing 8k steps. |
| PR [#9427](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9427) | Merged | Adds on-demand permanent checkpoint requests and lowers hero temporary checkpoint TTL from 14 days to 3 days. |
| PR [#10498](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10498) / Issue [#8290](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/8290) | Merged / Closed | Bounds SkyRL RL recovery checkpoints to 2 by default via `SkyRLRetentionPolicy`, protecting pending HF exports and selected best checkpoints. Long-loop RL already uses this in `experiments/post_training/long_loop/rl.py:62` (`retained: 3` in `specs/rl.yaml:4`). |
| Issue [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453) | Open | Documents TensorStore chunk-layout failures when resuming into a root that still contains uncommitted partial checkpoint directories. |
| PR [#10774](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10774) | Merged | Commits the completed step on SIGTERM preemption before exit in Grug trainers. |
| PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) | Merged | Sets `SFTSpec.checkpointer` to `save_interval=30m`, `keep=None`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints=1` in `experiments/sft/launcher.py:601-605`, routing recovery saves to Marin's 14-day TTL scratch prefix. |
| PR [#11217](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11217) | Merged | Sets hero SFT (`experiments/grug/moe_hero_ep/launch_hero_sft.py`) to save permanent checkpoints every 500 steps alongside hourly temporary checkpoints. |
| PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) / Issue [#11534](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11534) | Merged / Open | Makes `Checkpointer.on_step(..., force=True)` wait for and reuse a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step instead of rewriting `step-N/`. Merged to `main` on 2026-11-17 (`bc25c57f14`), absent from PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) (`c6676c91ef`). |

## Current behavior in long-loop SFT

All line citations below refer to PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) at `c6676c91ef` unless noted as `main` (`ea1257ca8d`).

Long-loop SFT has two launch paths in `experiments/post_training/long_loop/spec_pipeline.py:122-133`:

1. Shared `SFTSpec` path (`shared_sft.py:105-122`): inherits `SFTSpec.checkpointer` from `experiments/sft/launcher.py:601-605` (PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782)): 30-minute rolling temporary checkpoint (`keep_last_temporary_checkpoints=1`), `keep=None` (permanent final checkpoint only), temporary root resolved via `apply_output_path` (`lib/marin/src/marin/training/training.py:243`).
2. Legacy Grug path (`sft.py:40-85`, `sft-smoke.yaml`, `sft_runtime/train.py`), used by the 2026-11-18 Snowball ablations and the live eight-hour arms:
   - **Paths (`sft.py:53-56`)**: sets `base_path = <output>/checkpoints` and `temporary_base_path = <output>/temporary-checkpoints`. Sets `load_checkpoint = False` and `load_checkpoint_path = []`, which disables own-root resume (`experiments/grug/checkpointing.py:162-163`; an empty list also overrides `TrainerConfig.checkpoint_search_paths` at `lib/levanter/src/levanter/trainer.py:968` so auto-resume requires `load_checkpoint_path = None`).
   - **Default schedule (`sft-smoke.yaml:8059,8073-8089`)**: enables `save_checkpoints: true`, `keep: [{every: 15}]`, `save_interval: 30m`, `delete_old_temp_checkpoints: true`, `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2`. Every 15th step is permanent (`is_temporary: false`) under `<output>/checkpoints/step-N`.
   - **First-step restore gate (`sft_runtime/train.py:204-217,1526-1530`)**: when `first_checkpoint_restore_step` is set (set to `1` in all 17 runs on 2026-11-18 and in the three eight-hour configs), `restore_first_checkpoint` calls `checkpointer.on_step(tree=state, step=step, force=True)` at `train.py:208` and reloads from `checkpointer.base_path` at `train.py:212`. Because `force=True` sets `my_save_permanent_ckpt = True` (`lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py:622-623`), `step-1` is written as a permanent checkpoint in `checkpoints/step-1` and is not pruned.
   - **Per-step checkpointer call (`sft_runtime/train.py:1542`)**: calls `checkpointer.on_step(tree=state, step=current_step)`. In `Checkpointer.on_step` (`checkpoint.py:628-633`), `step % current_every == 0` takes precedence over `save_interval` and saves a permanent checkpoint under `base_path`; time-policy saves go to `temporary_base_path` with `is_temporary=True` (`checkpoint.py:652-655`).
   - **What is deleted (`checkpoint.py:659-665,718-740,768-779`)**: after a temporary checkpoint commits, rank 0 prunes older temporary checkpoints beyond `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` via a background `fs.rm(plain_path, recursive=True)` thread. After any permanent checkpoint commits, rank 0 calls `_prune_temporary_checkpoints(0)` to delete all tracked temporary checkpoints. This pruning path only removes temporary checkpoints. The frozen inventories quantify permanent checkpoint prefixes; the cited base-start and eight-hour configs disable time-based saves, while the one-hour configs allow them at `1h`. The inventories do not establish an absence of temporary writes across all runs.
   - **Why the final save is doubled (`train.py:1542,1570-1571`, `checkpoint.py:609`)**: when the final step matches `keep`, the periodic call (`train.py:1542`) already writes it. The later forced call (`train.py:1570`) on the pinned legacy source can rewrite it because PR [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) lacks PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) (`main` `checkpoint.py:618-621`) and line 609 (`if step == self._last_save_step and not force: return`) does not return when `force=True`. The observed doubled finals are consistent with a second OCDBT generation in the same `step-N/` directory. Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper (`checkpoint.py:756-761`) and retain `wait_until_finished()`. PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) independently makes the forced path on `main` reuse a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step. Neither guard prevents a rewrite across a new process or resume.
   - **Other retention hooks**: `BestValidationCheckpoint` (`sft_runtime/validation_checkpoint.py:89-92`) deletes older parameter-only validation checkpoints under `eval.best_checkpoint_path` when enabled. `archive.py:100-142` (`checkpoint_cleanup`) only runs in post-archive cleanup after verified HF publication.

## 2026-11-18 storage evidence and projected savings

At 2026-11-19 01:22:06Z, shared `cw-us-east-02a` STANDARD storage reported 971,569,804,211,080 bytes used of 1,000,555,581,276,160 bytes quota (28.99 TB headroom, zone/storage-class level; receipt `048e21ad`). Across 17 dated long-loop training runs under `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/` (excluding six post-hoc BF16 downcast roots), three frozen inventories account for 43 native checkpoint prefixes:

| Cohort (frozen snapshot) | Runs | Prefixes | Actual bytes | Superseded intermediate bytes (exact) | Failed step-1-only bytes (exact) | Doubled-final excess (est.) | Single-gen retained incl. failed-run step 1 (est.) |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dated non-one-hour inventory (`7a10d9c8`, 15 runs) | 15 | 33 | 17,887,983,830,450 (17.89 TB) | 6,988,863,920,962 (6.99 TB, 18 prefixes) | 401,190,894,951 (0.40 TB, 1 prefix) | 5,113,836,902,455 (5.11 TB, 13 finals) | 5,785,283,007,033 (5.79 TB) |
| One-hour FP32 pair (control + treatment) | 2 | 10 | 6,472,086,481,976 (6.47 TB) | 4,314,718,738,425 (4.31 TB, 8 prefixes) | 0 | 1,078,690,430,031 (1.08 TB, 2 finals) | 1,078,677,313,520 (1.08 TB) |
| Combined 2026-11-18 training cohort | 17 | 43 | 24,360,070,312,426 (24.36 TB) | 11,303,582,659,387 (11.30 TB, 26 prefixes) | 401,190,894,951 (0.40 TB, 1 prefix) | 6,192,527,332,486 (6.19 TB, 15 finals) | 6,863,960,320,553 (6.86 TB) |

Evidence fingerprints: 33-prefix inventory `7a10d9c8`, 27-prefix cleanup inventory `10f82be8`, one-hour step-15/60 inventory `ac410e45`, cleanup delete result `111df195`, quota snapshot `048e21ad`, byte-accounting artifact `daf14dfa`.

Notes on measurements and estimates:
- Measured single-save sizes on 67B Snowball: E12 FP32 runs (`params=float32`) are 539.34 GB (doubled final 1,078.68 GB, ratio 2.000); base-start BF16 runs are 401.19 GB (doubled final 802.39 GB, ratio 2.000); E12 BF16 runs are 270.33 GB (doubled final 540.66 GB, ratio 2.000). The one non-doubled completed final (`carried-replay-v9-eager` step 2, where `2 % 15 != 0`) was 270.33 GB (ratio 1.000 vs step 1).
- The 27-prefix manual delete (16,984 inventoried objects deleted, 11,704,773,554,338 bytes, 11.70 TB; billed quota relief not measured) equals the 26 superseded intermediate prefixes across the 16 completed runs (11,303,582,659,387 bytes: 16 `step-1` = 6.46 TB, 4 base-start `step-15` = 1.60 TB, 6 one-hour `step-15/30/45` = 3.24 TB) plus the 1 `step-1` prefix from the failed `base-start-20261118/control` run (401,190,894,951 bytes).
- For a doubled final we use the same run's step-1 size as a single-generation proxy. The inventories do not isolate bytes by generation.
- At a successful final commit and after pruning, the proposed policy would avoid retaining about 17.50 TB across this cohort (12.10 TB on the 33-prefix subset), assuming the listed intermediates are all dispensable. This is post-prune retained footprint, not cumulative writes or billed relief. The 0.40 TB failed-run save is included in the retained estimate until lifecycle cleanup.
- For the three live eight-hour FP32 arms (config sets `first_checkpoint_restore_step=1`, `save_interval=null`, `keep=[{every: 120, until: 240}, {every: 480, until: null}]` on a source without PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552)), estimated native checkpoint storage after successful completion is 5 single-save equivalents per arm (step 1 + step 120 + step 240 + 2x step 480, about 2.70 TB per arm, 8.09 TB across three arms), excluding exports and temporary overlap. This estimate counts the forced step-1 save separately from the earlier 6.47 TB planning figure (4 saves per arm). With a temporary step-1 save and single final write, estimated post-prune native checkpoint storage drops to steps 120, 240, and 480 (3 x 539.34 GB, about 1.62 TB per arm, 4.85 TB across three arms), avoiding about 1.08 TB per arm (3.24 TB total).

## Proposed rolling-checkpoint policy

Existing PRs cover most of the design: PR [#5983](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/5983) provides rolling temporary retention (`keep_last_temporary_checkpoints`), PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782) provides the `SFTSpec` default, and PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) fixes the forced final double-save on `main`. No existing PR wires these rules into the legacy Grug long-loop path or makes deletion metadata-first.

Proposed behavior for long-loop Grug SFT:

1. **Named permanent steps for export and eval**:
   - Declare milestone steps explicitly (for example `[120, 240, 480]`) and encode them for `CheckpointerConfig.keep` as `[{"every": s, "until": s} for s in sorted(set(steps))]`. Because `Checkpointer._get_current_step_save_interval` (`checkpoint.py:745`) selects the first interval with `until >= step`, for strictly increasing positive steps `s_1 < ... < s_k`, each interval `(every=s_i, until=s_i)` matches `step == s_i` and no step in `(s_{i-1}, s_i)`. No Levanter schema change is needed to represent arbitrary named steps.
   - Default `sft-smoke.yaml` and runs without named milestones to `keep: null` (final permanent checkpoint only).
2. **Rolling temporary recovery checkpoints**:
   - Set `save_interval: 30m` (or `60m` for multi-hour runs), `delete_old_temp_checkpoints: true`, and `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints: 2` for multi-hour runs (`1` for short runs where losing one interval is acceptable).
   - Route `temporary_base_path` to a same-region short-TTL prefix (for example `tmp/ttl=3d/...` matching PR [#9427](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/9427), or `<output>/temporary-checkpoints` when `<output>` is already under a short TTL). Never route across regions.
   - For resumable runs, set `load_checkpoint: null` and `load_checkpoint_path: null` so `TrainerConfig.checkpoint_search_paths` searches both `base_path` and `temporary_base_path`.
3. **Temporary first-step restore gate**:
   - For an unlisted step-1 restore gate, explicitly request a temporary save through the checkpointer (`request_checkpoint(CheckpointRetention.TEMPORARY)`), run the non-forced `on_step` path, wait for commit, then load from the actual temporary destination (`temporary_base_path or base_path`). Preserve a named permanent step-1 milestone. The gate copy counts toward rolling retention and can be pruned after enough newer temporary commits or on a permanent commit.
4. **Single final permanent write**:
   - Use the existing `save_final_checkpoint` helper and retain `wait_until_finished()` at `sft_runtime/train.py:1570-1571`, and bring in PR [#11552](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11552) from `main` so the forced path also reuses a pending or committed permanent save from the same checkpointer and step.

## Risks and mitigations

| Risk | Mechanism | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| Resume while a delete is in progress or crashed mid-delete | `Checkpointer._do_rm_checkpoint` (`checkpoint.py:768-779`) runs `fs.rm(plain_path, recursive=True)` on a background thread. Recursive removal may delete data objects before the metadata marker. If a process dies mid-delete, `metadata.json` can remain while payload objects are missing. Resume fallback (`experiments/grug/checkpointing.py:184`) only catches `FileNotFoundError`, so a TensorStore read failure aborts resume. | Remove and verify absence of `metadata.json` before deleting payload objects so subsequent discovery (`checkpoint.py:1249-1250`, `checkpointing.py:86-88`) skips the prefix. Abort payload removal if marker removal fails. This does not protect a reader that already selected the checkpoint. Keep writes and deletes to a reused step prefix serialized. |
| Selection file naming a rolled or deleted step | External scripts or mismatched `selected.json` files can point to an intermediate step that was later pruned (seen on 2026-11-18 when two historical one-hour `selected.json` files pointed to `step-15`). | Keep temporary checkpoints strictly in `temporary-checkpoints/` with `is_temporary: true` and permanent milestones in `checkpoints/` with `is_temporary: false`. Preserve and enforce the `is_temporary is False` guard in `sft.py:75,95` and `shared_sft.py:142` across all export, eval, and selection writers so no selection file can bind a temporary checkpoint. Declare export/eval steps in `keep` upfront. |
| Uncommitted partial checkpoint directories on resume | Issue [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453): a crash mid-save leaves partial TensorStore files without `metadata.json`; re-saving that step after resume can fail with a chunk-layout mismatch. | Rolling retention does not prevent this. Keep `temporary_base_path` on a short TTL and track [#10453](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/10453) separately (or clean uncommitted dirs above the restored step on resume). |
| Transient peak storage above `N` checkpoints | Commit-before-prune holds `N` retained copies while writing the next save. One in-flight save can temporarily add a third 539 GB copy (about 1.62 TB for two retained copies plus one write), before permanent milestones and any delete backlog. Async deletion can lag or fail, so this is not a hard peak bound. | Size storage headroom gates for `N + 1` temporary saves plus planned permanent milestones and delete-backlog margin, or set `N = 1` when headroom is tight. |
| Failed runs leaving orphaned temporary checkpoints | If a run dies before committing a permanent checkpoint and is not resumed, `_prune_temporary_checkpoints` never runs again. | Place `temporary_base_path` under a same-region short TTL prefix (`tmp/ttl=3d/` or `tmp/ttl=14d/`) so orphaned temporary checkpoints expire automatically. |

## Open decisions

1. Default `keep_last_temporary_checkpoints` for multi-hour long-loop SFT runs: `2` (one extra retained copy of about 539 GB in FP32) or `1` (matches `SFTSpec` default in PR [#10782](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/10782)).
2. Keep `first_checkpoint_restore_step = 1` as a temporary save on every run, or restrict it to smoke/qualification runs.
3. Land the `metadata.json`-first deletion fix in `lib/levanter/src/levanter/checkpoint.py` on `main` separately from the legacy long-loop change against the prototype branch (`benfeuer/long-loop-prototype`).

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

On eval-r2, three 15-update G20-fp32 continuations at 2e-5 scored higher than the single BF16-policy G20r2 comparator: 293, 291 and 284 exact matches of 855, against 214 for the comparator and 224 for the 10/05 start. At 5e-6 the same policy scored 221 of 855 against 231 for its BF16 twin. All served weights are BF16; the FP32 runs are served through a verified round-to-nearest-even downcast of the FP32 endpoint. Micro210 on the FP32 export has not run yet.

## Question and why it matters for the Mochi post-train

Does a short SFT continuation at 2e-5 keep more of each update when the optimizer holds FP32 parameters, FP32 gradients and FP32 optimizer state, rather than the BF16-only policy our arms have used?

The reason to ask is the size of one update relative to BF16 resolution. At 2e-5 a typical per-element move over a short continuation can be smaller than one BF16 code step. A BF16-only policy rounds parameters to BF16 after every update, so part of each update may be discarded before it can accumulate. This motivates comparing the two precision bundles under a matched recipe.

The sealed Mochi source recipe keeps FP32 parameters on device. These Snowball screens inform the next recipe comparison, and transfer to a live Mochi run remains untested.

## What the FP32 policy bundle means

"FP32 policy" here means: FP32 parameters, FP32 gradients into the optimizer, and FP32 optimizer state during training. The mixed-precision policy sets compute and output to BF16. The served weights are BF16, produced by a verified downcast.

The training setting enables pinned-host FP32 master parameters and changes parameter, gradient and optimizer-state dtypes together. The original G5 and G20 comparisons use the same grown E12 data and order as their BF16 comparators, with the same grouping, learning rate and update count. The data-seed-1 arm changes the general sample and order. Because the bundle changes parameters, gradients and optimizer state together, a difference between the two policies is not attributable to any one of those three.

## The zero-learning-rate observation

A same-data 15-update run at learning rate zero on the BF16 path still changed weights. On one expert bank of 21,810,380,800 BF16 values, 1,779,049,111 values changed (8.156892%), and every change was exactly one BF16 code step. At starting magnitude ≥ 1e-3, a population of 19,996,770,120 values, the zero-rate run and the matched 5e-6 run changed the same 1,627,374,248 positions to identical bits. In the smaller population of 1,813,610,680 values, the zero-rate run changed 151,674,863 and the 5e-6 run changed 201,668,362. The symmetric zero-rate versus 5e-6 final-bit disagreement was 53,561,310 values, 0.2456% of the bank, all below starting magnitude 1e-3. The eight plain-Adam leaves and the AdamH output projection stayed bit-identical to the start.

The reviewed reading of that observation is that the observed changes can occur at zero learning rate on this BF16 GPU path. It does not isolate renormalisation as the cause, it does not show that all remaining differences are learning, and it covers one group with one run per condition at endpoints only; attention, shared-expert and 2e-5 extensions were not part of that review.

## Route from an FP32 checkpoint to served BF16 weights

Training ends with FP32 parameters, and serving needs BF16 weights. The initial HF export jobs for both FP32 endpoints were OOMKilled with no retries. The G5 logs place its failure in late parity work. The reviewed split route is below:

1. **Params-only BF16 downcast.** A worker streams FP32 native parameter chunks directly to BF16, checks integer round-to-nearest-even against each write and read-back, rejects nonfinite values, and excludes optimizer slots and the pending quantisation betas. The audit for the 2e-5 run covers 27 parameters and 67,078,882,816 elements, with zero round-to-nearest-even mismatches and zero values below 1.18e-38.
2. **Independent verifier.** A separate job casts the run-specific FP32 endpoint with its own round-to-nearest-even implementation and compares: 22,747,545,600 checked values across eight parameter matrices, zero cast-bit mismatches, and all 16 magnitude-bin changed counts matching the prior FP32 scan. The producer covers all 27 leaves; this bitwise check covers eight matrices, not the entire model.
3. **Standard BF16 export** with the original FP32 optimizer-slot provenance guard. The export audit found 0 changed values, 0 signed-zero flips and 0 nonfinite values between the downcast checkpoint and the exported tensors, across 11 groups and all 67,078,882,816 elements.

The served weights are that BF16 cast. FP32 changes below a BF16 rounding boundary are invisible to serving metrics. Shard payload hashes in the export manifest are producer assertions unless independently rehashed; the receipt review of the storage copy is not a full independent payload rehash.

The same route and the identical independent check were used for the 5e-6 run, the same-seed repeat and the data-seed-1 run, each against its own endpoint and count reference.

## Results: eval-r2 edit-call

eval-r2 is 171 synthetic Pi edit prompts over 11 tasks; the table pools seeds 1 to 5 (855 grades per run). Each continuation used 15 updates on 64 H100. The 10/05 row is the starting checkpoint. All rows are served as BF16 weights, and for the FP32 rows those weights are the verified downcast. "Exact" counts a reply whose applied edit matches the target file exactly after stripping line-end spaces and tabs.

| Run | Seed 0 (of 171) | Greedy (of 171) | Seeds 1–5 (of 171) | Pooled exact (task bootstrap, descriptive) | Strict pooled | BF16-visible change vs the 10/05 BF16 start |
|---|---:|---:|---|---:|---:|---|
| FP32 policy, 5e-6 (G5-fp32) | 49 | 66 | 44 / 43 / 44 / 50 / 40 | 221/855 = .258 (.192–.303) | 720 | 835,259,286 of 67,078,882,816 values, 1.2452%; 20,312 of 20,392 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5 (G20-fp32) | 60 | 79 | 58 / 50 / 56 / 72 / 57 | 293/855 = .343 (.280–.406) | 788 | 3,330,528,658 values, 4.9651%; 20,313 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5, same seed and data order | 61 | 82 | 63 / 52 / 57 / 64 / 55 | 291/855 = .340 (.277–.403) | 780 | 3,327,404,185 values, 4.9604%; 20,313 tensors |
| FP32 policy, 2e-5, different general sample and order | 66 | 80 | 61 / 51 / 54 / 64 / 54 | 284/855 = .332 (.273–.396) | 775 | 3,275,384,396 values, 4.8829%; 20,314 tensors |
| BF16 policy, 5e-6 (G5r2) | 49 | 60 | 49 / 44 / 44 / 51 / 43 | 231/855 = .270 | — | baseline policy |
| BF16 policy, 2e-5 (G20r2) | 53 | 63 | 40 / 46 / 44 / 45 / 39 | 214/855 = .250 | — | baseline policy |
| 10/05 start | 50 | 59 | 47 / 44 / 45 / 48 / 40 | 224/855 = .262 | — | reference |

The change column is an endpoint-versus-start count of the BF16 export against the pinned 10/05 BF16 mirror: the sum of changed values over 67,078,882,816 compared elements. It counts BF16-visible changes, not raw FP32 changes, and differences between runs are differences of baseline-relative counts rather than a direct comparison of the exports.

- At 2e-5, FP32 against its BF16 twin: +79/855 (+9.24 points). Against 10/05: +69/855 (+8.07 points). The two largest task gains account for 31 of 79 and 30 of 69.
- The same-seed repeat and the data-seed-1 run are +77 and +70 of 855 against the BF16 twin (+9.01 and +8.19 points). Each is higher on 10 of 11 tasks and tied on one. Against the original FP32 run they are −2 and −9 of 855; the data-seed-1 run is also −7 against the repeat and +60 against 10/05.
- At 5e-6, FP32 against its BF16 twin: −10/855 (−1.17 points), descriptive, one trained checkpoint per policy at 5e-6.
- Across the three observed G20-fp32 exports the pooled scores were 293, 291 and 284 of 855, each above the 214/855 G20r2 result.
- The CPU data-path audit for the data-seed-1 run found zero shared full-example fingerprints among its 439 general rows, and confirmed the same 41 edit-call packs at the same positions and the same model seed. Multi-host loader execution was unverified.

## Limits

- These are eval-r2 edit-call scores from one checkpoint per training run and BF16 serving weights. Micro210 is the planned broader check on the original export.
- The FP32 policy changed parameter, gradient and optimizer-state dtypes together, so no single dtype is isolated.
- The three G20-fp32 runs at 2e-5 used the same model seed.
- Exact added-row task and file overlap was zero. Exposure through the general mix, including the data-seed-1 run's new general sample, remains unverified, as does task and TMax exposure inherited from the base data.
- The 10/05 seed-0 and greedy results came from an earlier serve. Its pooled seeds 1–5 came from a separate noise-only serve. The G20 and G5 seed-0, greedy and pooled results share a serve within each export. Each checkpoint was served once under its listed setup. The 2e-5 FP32-policy arm has three training runs; the BF16-policy comparator has one.
- The zero-rate observation is endpoint-only, one group, one run per condition.
- Export manifest shard hashes are producer assertions unless independently rehashed.

## What runs next

- The 60-update FP32 pair was cleared at 20:52:44 UTC on 2026-11-18 and both jobs were submitted at 20:53 UTC. The control is general-only; the treatment replaces 164 of 1,920 packed rows with 41 E12-B packs and 123 TMax packs. The schedule holds 2e-5 through update 4,275, including all 60 updates. At 45 seconds per update the fast-path estimate is about 45 minutes of training-step time per arm, with first-step and other overhead extra.
- Micro210 is planned on the original G20-fp32 BF16 export.

## 1. TL;DR

- **BF16 stored-parameter finding:** 26 finished ablation runs and 4 short diagnostics trained with `params=bfloat16` and `master_param_mode=device` ([BF16 inventory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021)); [draft PR 11717](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11717) enforces FP32 stored parameters.
- **Status at the 04:49Z update on November 19:** `control`, `single`, and `Warm A` were training. Slow `repeat` was cancelled (`04:46:32Z` readback: killed); `repeat-r2` did not launch. `Warm B` was still queued at the latest placement readback (`0/8`). `Warm A control` was cleared under the new rule: continuations from 10/05 carry optimizer state and use the cooled-down LR; fresh state is reserved for starts from the pretrained base.

## 2. Data

| Set | Construction and size | Loss mask and supervised targets |
|---|---|---|
| **General packs** | Rows sampled from the replay of the 10/05 mix, in a fixed order within each frozen row schedule (`262,144` positions/pack; 1,927 text-format components including agentic sources; full 10/05 mix is `79.65%` SFT + `20.35%` pretraining replay; `data_seed=1` changes the general sample and order). | Full-text causal loss (from config, trainer source, and CPU row audit; no prompt mask; S3 general cache weights were not re-read directly). Planned eight-hour control CPU row-proof count: `3,779,290,292` targets over `15,360` packs (`93.86%` of positions, ~`246k`/pack). |
| **E12-B** | Programmatic exercises from TMax train-split code bodies with one to four corrupted regions, with one Pi 0.87 nested `edit` call as the target (`5,536` exercises / `724` tasks / `41` packs; `5,536/5,536` exact Pi 0.87.0 pure-edit matches; `0` overlap with `eval-r1`/`eval-r2` tasks). | **Final edit call only:** `2,176,018` targets over `10,579,547` real positions (`20.6%` of real positions; `20.25%` of `41 × 262,144` padded positions; mean `53,074`/pack). |
| **TMax** | Successful Qwen3.6-27B mini-swe-agent traces from `allenai/tmax-sft` (`9d6ab747`, thinking split). Full train source pool: `4,647` traces / `909` tasks / `129` packs (`900` of those `4,647` source-pool traces were already in 10/05; `507` / `101` held out). Selected for one-hour and eight-hour arms: packs `0–122` (`123` packs, `4,512` traces; packs `123–128` excluded). | **Full-trace causal loss:** within each trace, each position has weight `1` except the final EOS position, which has weight `0`. The weight at position `k` supervises token `k+1`, so this mask excludes the transition to the next trace. Across selected packs `0–122`: `31,605,382` targets of `31,609,894` non-pad positions (`98.02%` of padded positions; mean `256,954`/pack): assistant `47.5%` (`15.01M`), tool outputs `33.4%` (`10.57M`), user `13.9%` (`4.39M`), system + tool schemas `3.9%` (`1.23M`), role headers `1.3%` (`0.41M`). Matches general packs' full-text loss except each TMax trace excludes its transition across final EOS. (Measured on rendered traces and cache audit; independent technical read in progress.) |

For `Warm A` and queued `Warm B`, `7.25%` is the repeat-schedule projection, not consumed data.

## 3. Scale against 10/05 SFT

Formula: Levanter `lm_flops_per_token` (non-causal full-span attention convention) for Snowball (`hidden=2560`, `intermediate=1280`, `shared=2560`, `layers=26`, `heads=20`, `kv_heads=5`, `vocab=128,256`, `256` experts, top-4, `sliding_window=2048`, `7` full-attention layers per `_long_layer_schedule(26, 4)` — layers 3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 25 — matching the 10/05 W&B analytic value `23,911,178,240` forward FLOPs/token). Training FLOPs = `3 × 23,911,178,240 × positions` (`7.173353e10` FLOPs/position; `6.02e17` FLOPs per 32-pack update).

| **10/05 SFT** (step `157,000 → 161,750`) | `4,750` | `256` | `318.77B` (`318,767,104,000`) | `2.29e22` | `100%` |
