## 4. Recipe facts per run family

All 11-17 to 11-19 arms below use `seq=262,144`, `bs=32`, Mochi grouping (`grug_moe_muonh_v1`, `global_grad_norm=1.0`, `weight_decay=0.0`, special-token LR `√32 × LR`), and BF16 compute/output.

| **Carried BF16** (`C-replay r3`, `C-e12`) | 10/05 native `step-161750` | Carried | `5e-6` constant | BF16 | `15` |

## 5. Results so far

**Edit-call (`eval-r2`, 5-seed pooled, `855` replies/arm):**
- **Carried BF16 step-15:** `C-e12` `.263` (within-serve seeds `41–50/171`) versus `C-replay r3` `.271` (`43–53/171`) and `10/05` `.262` (`40–48/171`; all BF16-parameter continuations marked in [BF16 inventory](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6999152021)).
- **15-update BF16 vs FP32 (`G5`/`G20`):** full table in [issue 11687 body](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687) (`G20-fp32` `293 / 291 / 284` of `855` vs `G20r2` BF16 `214/855` and `10/05` `224/855`; `G5-fp32` `221/855` vs `G5r2` BF16 `231/855`).
- **One-hour FP32 pair:** full table in [one-hour edit-call comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6996439113) (treatment `337/855` = `.394` vs control `222/855` = `.260`, `+13.45` pp, higher on all 11 tasks).

**Micro210 (pooled mean over scored attempts of `440` suite / `100` agent assignments; bounds set excluded trials to `0` or `1`):**

| Arm (runs) | Agent (scored/100; excl) | Agent bounds | Suite (scored/440; excl) | Suite bounds |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **1h FP32 treatment** (`44652` / `44653`) | `15.57%` (`97`; `3`) / `14.42%` (`95`; `5`), avg `14.99%` | `15.10–18.10%` / `13.70–18.70%` | `38.79%` (`437`; `3`) / `40.14%` (`435`; `5`), avg `39.47%` | `38.52–39.21%` / `39.69–40.82%` |

**Held-out retention loss (one-hour FP32, updates 15 / 30 / 45 / 60):** treatment `0.495105 / 0.494793 / 0.495092 / 0.495328` versus control `0.494975 / 0.494503 / 0.494595 / 0.494820` (within `0.00051` nats at every check; [one-hour edit-call comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6996439113)).

**Earlier `2e-5` BF16 runs are confounded:** the earlier E12 pilot control and treatment ([issue 11536](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536)) scored below 10/05 on Micro210. In the TMax comparison ([issue 11539](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11539)), both continuations scored below their parent on BFCL ×5 under both evaluated serve stacks. These continuations used fresh optimizer state, BF16 stored parameters, and LR `2e-5`, so the results cannot assign the drops to any one of those factors. Earlier pretrained-base screens ([issue 11537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11537), C150/O150) also used BF16 stored parameters at `2e-5` with fresh state from the pretrained base (so their gaps to 10/05 are not drops from their initializer) and need an FP32 redo.

(2) Treatment arms bundle E12-B and TMax together, so their individual contributions are not separated, and TMax uses full-trace loss rather than assistant-only loss. (5) Harness parity between the four one-hour Micro210 runs (`44652`, `44653`, `44658`, `44659`) and the earlier `10/05` parent runs (`44627–44628`) was not rechecked. (6) Nine known broader-suite import failures remain unresolved and outside the 20-source Micro210 results; they are not counted as passing.

spillover_issues.title: [post-training] FP32 policy versus BF16 for short SFT continuations at 2e-5

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

Ablations on Snowball (the 10/05 SFT model) to choose SFT and RL settings for the Mochi 535B post-training run. Each experiment has a 1 h version and an 8 h version. Most backlog items have not run yet; current results are under Status.

## Description

Snowball is a smaller Grug MoE with the same post-training stack as Mochi. Each experiment changes one setting of the SFT or RL recipe (data, optimizer, loss mask, precision, tool format, RL task choice) and compares it against a matched control. The arms are read out with Micro210, BFCL ×5 and a retention panel. Experiments that look useful are then checked on Mochi.

Issue 11177 made the long loop runnable from the 10/05 SFT. Issue 11337 tracks run-ready Snowball recipes and Micro eval scores. Issue 11531 tracks Snowball long-loop SFT on TPU v4.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Find which recipe settings change Snowball's agentic and tool-use scores enough to carry into Mochi's next SFT/RL stage.

## Sub-issues

Each result is posted on its own issue:
- Snowball long-loop SFT on TPU v4: issue 11531
- Malformed JSON in nested Pi edit calls: issue 11536
- SFT optimizer, Muon-H vs Adam (C150 vs O150): issue 11537
- TMax data, with vs without: issue 11539
- RL samples per prompt: issue 11594
- Mochi BFCL ×5 versus Snowball models: issue 11538

## Status

- **Tool-call format:** see the sub-issue. Malformed nested `edit` calls end more than half of Snowball's SWE trials. An SFT slice of valid nested edits (E12) is trained but not yet read out.
- **SFT optimizer (C150 vs O150):** BFCL ×5 favours Muon-H (30.24% vs 24.55–24.72%, one run each); Micro210 pending. See issue 11537.
- **TMax pair:** held-out TMax loss falls sharply; BFCL ×5 falls vs control. Micro210 pending. See issue 11539.
- **Mochi BFCL ×5 (Pi agent, 123 tasks):** 450/615 record score under the configured retry rule; 449 first-attempt wins, one first-attempt reward unavailable after a timeout.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

- 2026-11-16: Flat edit tool ruled out for reported benchmarks and the default harness. The fix for malformed edits goes on the model side (SFT data).
- 2026-11-16: The SFT training data's tool calls were audited: 452 of 47.4M assistant call spans failed a JSON check. No data repair.

## Conclusion

comments.body:
🤖 The C150, O150 and TMax SFT arms have trained but still need Micro210 readouts. The E12 one-hour arms also await readout; [#11536](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536) tracks their nested-edit hypothesis. The two published [long-loop recipes](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337) changed training recipes and have different scoring coverage, so their aggregate scores do not isolate an ablation effect.

Plan:
1. For each SFT or RL setting, pin a control and one-setting treatment at the one-hour and eight-hour budgets. Match the starting checkpoint, source and data revisions outside the tested change, task IDs, seeds, Pi harness, and eval policy. Preserve the consumed configs and checkpoint revisions.
2. Finish the pending C150/O150/TMax and E12 one-hour Micro210 readouts first. Compare matching task IDs and report scored/unscored counts, per-benchmark and aggregate deltas, BFCL ×5, and the retention panel. Include malformed nested-edit rates for E12. Use [#11536's gate](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11536): at least a 50% rate reduction against its control with no Micro210 or retention loss.
3. Advance arms with a positive paired agentic/tool-use result and no retention regression to matched eight-hour controls. Repeat the same panels, report uncertainty and incomplete coverage, and record null or adverse results. Check surviving settings on Mochi before selecting its SFT/RL recipe.
4. Keep an arm table here with the changed setting, control and treatment pins, both budget readouts, BFCL and retention results, and the carry/drop decision. Add each run-ready recipe, exact data mix, Micro policy, immutable checkpoint, and archive receipts to [#11337](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11337).

## Metric definitions

Equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native per-source avg_score fields. Those fields include excluded assignments in their denominators. Available-only columns omit excluded scores and therefore use different denominators.

Task-equivalent differences are n × (arm mean − parent run 1 mean), summed over sources. Here n counts assignments, not necessarily distinct task identities. Fractional graders produce fractional task-equivalents, not additional integer wins. No individual task outcomes have been paired.

BFCL /10 is the native score mass for the ten-assignment Micro slice. C150 has five known score units, nine scored assignments and one unknown outcome: its assigned score bounds are 5–6 /10. The regional parent has seven known score units over nine scored assignments plus one unknown: assigned bounds 7–8 /10. This slice is not the earlier 123-task ×5 BFCL evaluation.

The parent repeat has seven unknown outcomes: one BixBench and six TB2. The first parent reports 440/440 scored and zero excluded. Both have complete native aggregate dumps; the repeat does not have complete scored outcomes. The two runs use the same configured seed and recipe, not independent training seeds or proven matched random streams.

## Evidence boundaries

All 14 scored rows have reviewed native aggregates and terminal resource accounting. For the earlier seven rows, individual source files were metadata-listed, not independently checked for exact assigned-UID membership, raw exceptions or file hashes. Each current TMax and cw-rno2a dump has 21 streamed and hashed files, 440 unique expected UID strings, and all 20 source means/counts/exclusions reconciled under the frozen UID-source mapping. That reduced extraction does not independently prove the actual source-file-to-UID/task join. Produced suite artifacts match the 440-row reference bytes and order where checked; that does not attest live runtime consumption. Native completion, archive membership and trace capture are separate evidence.

Requested H100-hours are physical-attempt resource envelopes, not utilization, invoices or Pod/provider-release timing. Native success is not broad-suite green or evidence that the unresolved import failures are harmless.

The two parent judge workers and brokers each had only A0. Their final preemption_count of one accompanies terminal KILLED cleanup after the policy child finished; no native restart gap was found. This does not prove continuous HTTP health or explain the repeat's seven exclusions. The bound vllm_server.py is identical between those runs; a different file in the current checkout is not a run-to-run source change or a deployed-byte readback.

## Historical TMax results

The old RNO control run used eight slots and three-hour child caps. It reported 438/440 scored, two excluded, native equal-20 45.065889%, available equal-20 45.101604% and pooled available 38.591730%. The old TMax arm failed and yielded a conservative recovered subset of 437/440: available macro 52.39%, pooled 44.99%, three unknown. There was no complete native aggregate for that arm. Neither result fills a current-harness row. The superseded failed parent recovery is not used here.

The two current TMax runs bind the original cw-us-east-02a exports without copying: arm 134,181,708,393 B; control 134,181,708,404 B. Both have 87 HF objects and 39 weight shards. Fresh metadata and header checks are not a new full tensor-payload parity audit.

Both current roots and policy children succeeded, each with seven terminal jobs and seven A0 attempts. The arm has one BixBench exclusion; control has one TB2 exclusion. Both remain unknown. Available-only weighting changes BixBench 1/10 to 1/9 in the arm and TB2 2/30 to 2/29 in control. Their task-difference bounds refer to these unknown scores, not confidence intervals or matched task outcomes.

The same startup config-parse diagnostic appeared in both completed parent logs and TMax; later scoring superseded the early zero-ready snapshot. Its cause and harmlessness are not established. Terminal accounting does not establish both GPU Pods absent or provider release.

## RL training, exports and native closure

Both RL training arms reached saved step-10 native checkpoints, but their training roots failed during teardown. Both HF exports are structurally verified in cw-rno2a. The two Micro210 repetitions per export and regional parent all have successful roots and policies, seven terminal jobs and seven observed A0 attempts per evaluation. Judge workers and brokers were KILLED after policy completion. No retry or continuous-health inference follows from the one-attempt observations. W&B in-run metrics and teacher-closeness NLL are not Micro210.

Accepted failure/preemption/job-wide retry limits are explicit: root 0/0/0; policy 0/1000/0; judge 1/10/1; broker 0/1000/0; prepare-model 1/100/0; prepare_micro and verify_ready_inputs each 0/100/0. Limits are not counts of observed retries. Timeout waits are per wait, not total-completion guarantees; native TIMEOUT bypasses ordinary requeue.

All 39 same-named shard hashes recorded in the two export manifests differ between the RL exports and from the parent's retained verified shard hashes. The two RL exports have identical byte totals and index layout; that does not make them the same model. These are exporter-recorded digests, not new independent full-payload rehashes or evidence of learned improvement.

For all five cw-rno2a runs, actual CPU, judge and broker task images were b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974, matching cw-us-east-02a. Their policy task images matched the pinned 13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8 request. Equal image digests do not establish imported module bytes, model load, service health or platform equivalence. All five produced suite objects match the 440-row reference bytes; that does not prove live runtime consumption or assigned-UID coverage.

The harness selects the separately pinned tools tokenizer and template, not the export's embedded template. CPU runtime-configuration proofs reproduce the same render fixture for the parent and both RL exports. Their BOS/EOS defaults agree; the export generation-config difference is a transformers_version field. Actual GPU runtime identity remains a separate observation.

## Unscored contributor

Contributor SFT is not run and the full run is not planned. Only a two-update smoke existed. Its historical step-2 checkpoint and export are absent at the current read, so there are no scorable weights. The export was recorded at the handoff path on 11-13 with 39 safetensors; who removed it and when are unknown. No new contributor training, export or evaluation has been authorized.

## Publication status

Both current TMax rows and all five cw-rno2a rows have reviewed native aggregates and terminal resource accounting. No causal optimizer/SFT/RL finding, calibrated significance or equivalence claim follows from this table.

🤖 ## Finding: the long-loop SFT ablations used a different optimizer grouping from 10/05 and Mochi

Found on 2026-11-17 while preparing an arm that restores the 10/05 optimizer state: the saved state did not fit the optimizer that the long-loop SFT code builds.

## What differs

| Parameter family | 10/05 (saved optimizer state, logged config) | Mochi SFT (sealed source, hero-EP optimizer) | Long-loop SFT ablations (bound source) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Stacked expert `w_gate` / `w_up` / `w_down` (4-D) | MuonH | MuonH | **Adam** |
| Stacked `rms_attn` / `rms_mlp` scales (2-D) | Adam | Adam | **MuonH** |
| Shared expert weights (3-D) | MuonH | MuonH | MuonH |
| Gradient clipping | none | not compared | **1.0** (E12 config) |

## Cause

The long-loop `sft.py` imports the generic `experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py`. Its MuonH rule accepts only 2-D and 3-D weights and has no rule that sends RMSNorm scales to Adam. With stacked blocks the 4-D expert weights fall through to Adam and the 2-D stacked norm scales go to MuonH. The June TPU optimizer implementation that the 10/05 model card links to, which is consistent with that run's saved optimizer slots and logged config, and the hero-EP optimizer in the sealed Mochi source both handle the stacked case explicitly (RMSNorm scales to Adam, 2-D to 4-D weights to MuonH). The generic file at `main` commit `18ae01ee42` is byte-identical to the one the ablations used.

## Runs affected

- **Affected (bound source and published consumed configs; worker import bytes not separately attested):** the E12 all-weights and general-only arms, the TMax arm and its control, C150, and the low-learning-rate replay rerun of 2026-11-17.
- **Related code, swapped families not trained:** the E12 attention-and-head-only arm freezes the expert and norm families, so the swap does not act on it.
- **Not affected:** Mochi SFT through step 400,407 (from its sealed source, not a fresh worker attestation); O150 (plain Adam by design); the RL arms (Megatron AdamW).

## What this does and does not show

- The E12 all-weights and general-only arms and the TMax arm and control used this grouping in their bound source. None is a matched test of the 10/05 optimizer set-up.
- It is a candidate cause of that drop. It is **not** shown to be the cause; no run with the corrected grouping has been evaluated yet.
- The 10/05 grouping is established from its logged optimizer config (`rmsnorm_to_adam=true`, no clipping) and its saved optimizer slots. The exact commit that run was launched from is not recorded in its W&B run.

## Next

1. A replay-only arm on 10/05 (15 updates, fresh optimizer state, learning rate 5e-6) with the 10/05 grouping and no clipping. The grouping change labels all 27 parameter leaves of the model the same way as the 10/05 optimizer state.
2. The same arm with the uncorrected grouping finished training on 2026-11-17 and is being evaluated; the pair gives the comparison.
3. A fix for the generic optimizer, or a switch of the long-loop SFT code to the hero-EP optimizer, follows as a PR.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## Summary

On the 64-H100 Long Loop layout with XLA autotune level 0, EAGER CUDA module loading has not eliminated the intermittent first-step stall. On source `5cbfba9f`, both fresh-state expert-MuonH runs without a host rebind (G5 and G20) stalled on their first stock call; they were submitted 60 ms apart and shared fabric. In the recorded EAGER/autotune-0 BF16 cohort with host rebind, six first stock calls completed (v9, C-replay r3, C-e12, G5r2, G20r2 and G0r2) and one stalled (G0). These observations do not isolate a rebind effect or estimate failure rates.

Three C150 base-start treatment arms, with routed experts on Adam, each completed 150 updates with EAGER and no rebind. The plain control is outside that count. This is a different optimizer path and does not establish that EAGER fixes the expert-MuonH stall. The runtime mechanism remains unknown. See [the draft launch change](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11647).

## Distinct observations

- **First-step stall:** G5 and G20 stalled with EAGER and no rebind on the `5cbfba9f` expert-MuonH path. G0 also stalled after its host rebind, with EAGER and autotune level 0.
- **NCCL initialization:** In a task-0 capture, five G20-FP32 r2 worker main threads were waiting in `NcclCollectives::CreateCommunicatorsWithCancel` during clique initialization. A matching relaunch completed. This is a separate observed signature; its cause and any connection to the first-step stall remain unresolved.
- **Slow steps:** Earlier BF16 runs showed approximately 115–132 seconds per step, and G5-FP32 showed approximately 120–134 seconds per step after step 1. Faster observations were approximately 39–52 seconds per step. Whether these observations share a cause is unknown.

## Earlier observations

Earlier LAZY runs stalled or ran slowly. An earlier EAGER/autotune-0 fresh-state H run without a host round trip completed its first two stock calls in 58.2 and 49.1 seconds and logged a first loss of 0.6393635273. Carried-state v9, C-replay r3 and C-e12 also completed their first EAGER/autotune-0 stock calls. An older EAGER run with autotune level 4 on a different graph stalled in `cuModuleLoadData`.

## Symptom

The Long Loop Grug MoE SFT loop can stall in its first compiled train step on eight hosts with eight H100s each. All 64 GPUs stayed busy, but the step did not complete. Among the Long Loop runs examined, the stall has been observed only in graphs with expert weights in MuonH. The stalled loop is on the Long Loop branch, not main. A related first-update stall on a different layout is tracked in [the Snowball optimizer issue](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440); a common cause is not established.

## Observed setup and expected behavior

Run the Long Loop SFT graph from commit `917055e33f44ddb3b5e1a927eab0793e7a9f4501` with replica=1, data=8, expert=1 and context=8 across eight H100 hosts, with expert matrices in MuonH. The first train step should finish and subsequent steps should run without a host round trip. Two runs stalled before completing that step.

A successful diagnostic retained the compiled executable reference while it snapshotted the entire train state to host memory, deleted its device arrays, and restored the state before the first call. Its first three steps took 80.7, 49.0 and 41.1 seconds. In a separate paired diagnostic, a direct compiled call and the subsequent stock call took 52.5 and 46.1 seconds; the latter followed a direct execution and a host state reconstruction.

## Evidence and limits

Isolated expert momentum, projection and Newton–Schulz probes completed. In the paired diagnostic, StableHLO and optimized HLO were byte-identical and all 76 input leaf metadata entries matched; the stock call made no rank-zero compiler requests. Disabling the persistent executable cache did not prevent the stall, and the successful reconstruction run used autotune level zero. Its pre-reconstruction buffer inventory found no shared buffer start addresses and no pending shards on all 64 ranks. The cancelled stalled attempts did not retain those buffer inventories, so this does not establish their buffer state.

The cause is unknown. Whether the same mechanism also explains the observed slow steps remains open. The highest observed per-task sample was 146.2 GiB against a 640 GiB allocation. The snapshot peak was not measured.

The v7a2 rank-zero runtime inventory reports JAX, jaxlib, jax-cuda13-plugin and jax-cuda13-pjrt 0.11.1 and CUDA runtime 13.0.96. The source declares `jax[cuda13]==0.11.0` in its root dependency set; the installed rank-zero inventory is the runtime observation. All eight task image pull events identify `ghcr.io/marin-community/iris-task@sha256:b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`.

Evidence is stored in 02a temporary prefixes and expires after 30 days:

- Reconstruction run: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118/fresh/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-prelude-v7a2-20261118%2Ffresh%2F)).
- Paired HLO evidence: `s3://marin-us-east-02a/tmp/ttl=30d/long-loop-436/e12/h-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118/fresh/evidence/` ([Filer](https://filer.marina.oa.dev/#s3%3A%2F%2Fmarin-us-east-02a%2Ftmp%2Fttl%3D30d%2Flong-loop-436%2Fe12%2Fh-muon-dispatch-v6-20261118%2Ffresh%2Fevidence%2F)).

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖

# Research

The published Long Loop `train_step` compiles gradient accumulation and `optimizer.update` into one donated-state call, so the stalled step does not identify the blocked operation. The successful host-state reconstruction and direct-call diagnostic narrow the conditions but do not establish a buffer aliasing cause; the cancelled stalls have no buffer inventories. The cited source commit `917055e` is not available in the repository, and open PRs #11639 and #11640 change expert MuonH grouping and configuration while explicitly leaving this stall unresolved.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L1037-L1077`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c6676c91efe773f251d455f97c59e060b49faf1b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L1037-L1077) — gradients and optimizer share one JIT call.
- [`optimizer.py#L96-L123`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/44323775503ca44a2e8ef345bdcd45a6f0b5ba1e/experiments/grug/moe/optimizer.py#L96-L123) — generic MuonH update path.
- [PR #11639](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11639) — stacked-expert backend and grouping change.
- [Issue #11440](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11440) — related XLA stall; common cause unproven.

# Proposed Fix

1. Preserve the exact `917055e` diagnostic source, launch configuration, runtime inventory, first-step input metadata, and compact HLO artifacts before the 30-day evidence prefixes expire. Pin the image and the optimizer mask used by each run; the public prototype branch is not an exact reproduction of that commit.
2. Run bounded, fresh 64-GPU repeats of the direct first call and host-state reconstruction from the same initialized state and batch. On each stall, collect all-rank host stacks, two time-separated NCCL RAS counter snapshots, GPU process state, and pre-call buffer inventories. Compare those with completed attempts; current inventories cover only a successful run.
3. With the same state and sharding, place explicit completion boundaries after gradient computation and after the MuonH update. Compare expert-MuonH and expert-Adam controls, then reduce the blocked phase to a smaller JAX/PJRT replay if it persists. Treat split-step success as a diagnostic because splitting changes the compiled graph.
4. Patch only the isolated cause. Qualify the result with repeated 64-GPU first steps, at least three finite updates per run, unchanged optimizer numerics, and no host-state reconstruction before or between steps. Keep #11639/#11640 separate unless a matched control implicates their changes.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body: 🤖 One untested explanation is how long the trainer holds a Python reference to the compiled executable returned by the stock step-zero precompile. H and v5b discarded that return immediately and stalled. v7a2 held it through the host state round trip and cleared it immediately before the stock call. v6b made zero rank-zero compiler requests on its observed stock call, which followed a direct execution and state reconstruction. H, v5b and v7a2 had no compiler-request instrumentation. The planned two-step test keeps the AOT return until just before H's first stock call, leaves the original state in place, and counts dispatch-time compiler and cache requests. This checks whether the first step completes without a state round trip in the instrumented run. If it does, a matched run with the same instrumentation and no retained reference would help isolate the effect of retention.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body: 🤖 The first-step loss in the completed direct-dispatch and rebind observations, including F v8 and Hb, was 0.6393635273. Original F read back as 0.6393433809, and the earlier E12 r2 run as 0.6393431425. The two original-run values are close without being identical. V6b’s two successful H lowerings had byte-identical optimized HLO. There is no optimized-HLO capture from the stalled H call or from the original F call, so this does not establish program identity across the slow and fast runs. One untested explanation is a runtime kernel or library path that differs with allocator state or scratch availability. The nearest W&B sample for each of H, v5b, v7a2 and Hb covered eight devices, was within 3.1 seconds of step-1 entry, and showed about 60.9–61.0 GiB per device. Those snapshots measure coarse device residency. They do not expose live allocator blocks, fragmentation or scratch availability. The retained v6b optimized HLO lists 65 cuBLASLt matmul sites with explicit algorithm IDs and 32 MiB workspace in the backend configuration and result tuple, alongside CUTLASS and other custom calls. V9 will record per-device memory and local allocator stats at the first stock call while counting compiler requests.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body: 🤖 C-replay r2 completed the strict 72-leaf carried checkpoint restore, 36 moment audits and the full-state host round trip, including pinned-host optimizer leaves. The trainer held the Python reference to its AOT executable through rebind and cleared it before stock dispatch, as v7a2 did. Step 1 began at 05:14:52 UTC and was still incomplete when the job was cancelled at about 05:23 UTC. The two task captures include 16 worker main threads. Fourteen were under CustomKernelThunk and cuLaunchKernelEx, the same frame chain sampled in H and v5b. Two were under CublasLtMatmulThunk and cublasLtMatmul, with cuKernelSetAttribute above them. These captures contain no thunk ID or kernel name that binds the same operation across runs. Fresh-state runs completed after the same kind of round trip. In C-replay r2, step 1 remained incomplete at cancellation despite the round trip. The carried moments, restore path and optimizer implementation differ from Hb, so this comparison leaves the cause open.

comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 A two-update carried-state replay with CUDA confirmed in EAGER mode on all 64 ranks completed the first stock train call in 78.814 s and the second in 49.111 s. The first loss was 0.6393635273, matching the logged oracle. C-replay r2, the LAZY comparison, completed the same carried restore, moment audit and full state rebind, then reached the first stock call and was cancelled with that call incomplete. Both used explicit XLA autotune level 0. The EAGER diagnostic kept the underlying source and training inputs, adding observation around the stock call and running on a separately scheduled gang.

🤖 Two fresh-state runs on November 18, G5 and G20, stalled on the first training call despite CUDA module loading being EAGER and XLA autotune level 0, confirmed on all 64 ranks in each run. Both used the same grown repair mix and 4-D MuonH/SYRK path as C-e12, with fresh optimizer state and the first-step host rebind disabled. Their learning rates were 5e-6 and 2e-5. comments.author: karansag
comments.body:
🤖 In the observed intervals, the eight-hour FP32 runs on 64 H100s in cw-us-east-02a fell into fast and slow groups. Repair rows were not required for slow updates: Warm A was slow on both observed zero-repair updates, while single stayed fast on the observed repair-bearing updates. This weighs against repair rows directly accounting for the gap. It leaves the schedule, batch-content interactions and run-level causes open.

| Run | Repair-row schedule | Planned repair rows per update (mean) | Steady step time (start-to-end timestamp interval) |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| control | none | 0 | median 45.9 s (203 updates) |
| single | 164 rows once over the run | 0.34 | median 45.6 s (171 updates) |
| repeat (cancelled) | 164 rows in every 1,920-row block | 2.7 | about 126 s/update at the 62-update readback |
| Warm A | same as repeat | 2.7 | median 124.6 s (53 updates) |
| Warm B | same as repeat | 2.7 | 132.7 s and 122.9 s (updates 2–3) |

Steady times exclude the first update. Times are start-to-end intervals from the rank-0 `train_step` timing journal.

Within single, steps that carry repair rows run at control speed:

| single, repair rows in the update | Updates | Median | Mean |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 0 | 127 | 45.4 s | 45.7 s |
| 1 | 40 | 46.4 s | 46.3 s |
| 2 or more | 4 | 45.4 s | 46.4 s |

Shifting the row-to-update join by one update either way gives the same qualitative result.

Within Warm A, the two updates with no repair rows (24 and 25) took 125.0 s and 133.5 s. The other 51 updates took a median of 124.6 s.

Checks so far:
- **Warm B timing.** Warm B's first recorded `train_step` timestamp interval was 763.5 s, after a separately logged 24.6 s first-step compile. Updates 2–3 took 132.7 s and 122.9 s.
- **Configuration.** All five were configured for 32 packed rows per update, 262,144 positions per row and 480 updates. The Warm arms restore state, and Warm A uses a different LR schedule. Actual batch input dtypes, shapes and shardings were not compared in the retained timing logs.
- **Placement snapshot.** The four live runs ran on the same fabric and machine type. No common host or NVLink domain was observed, and some racks overlap between fast and slow runs. This does not rule out host effects.
- **Compile times.** Warm A's first-step compile took 32.5 s and single's took 13.4 s. The logs record no executable fingerprint.

The next distinguishing step is to log the executable fingerprint and the input shardings and dtypes at step 1, for one fast and one slow run.

spillover_issues.author: penfever
spillover_issues.body:
Verifyit declares `requires-python = ">=3.11"` (`lib/verifyit/pyproject.toml`), and its runtime imports `enum.StrEnum` (`lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/grade.py:15`, `spec.py:17`, and four grade modes) and `tomllib` (`spec.py:15`, `modes/grade_json_schema.py:15`). The task-curation grading harness runs the staged runtime through the grader machine's own `python3` (`taskcompendium.runtime.grading._verifyit_reward`), so every grader machine below Python 3.11 fails grading with an import error instead of a verdict.

Task-curation workspace tasks whose source environment lowers onto a Python 3.10 base hit this at rollout: the Daytona census validates the machines, setup completes, and then the verifier returns `infra_error`:

```
File "/tests/.taskcompendium-runtime/verifyit/grade.py", line 15, in <module>
    from enum import StrEnum
ImportError: cannot import name 'StrEnum' from 'enum' (/usr/local/lib/python3.10/enum.py)
```

This affects the DCAgent python-tests family, where 7 of 10 sources lower onto `python:3.10-slim` bases (curriculum-easy, pymethods2test and its large cut, unitsyn-python and its large cut, e2egit and its large cut); their workspace-image graders run the image's Python 3.10.

Reproduce:
1. Convert a real `DCAgent__exp_rpt_curriculum-easy` row through `convert_python_tests` (the grader environment inherits the workspace image).
2. Grade an empty submission with `grade_empty_in_sandbox` against a Docker machine created from `RegistryImage(grader.docker_image)`.
3. Observe `infra_error` with the `StrEnum` import error above; on Python 3.11+ bases the same path returns `graded` with reward 0.0.

Expected: verifyit's runtime runs and returns a verdict on the grader machines the catalog's declared environments produce, including Python 3.10 workspace images, or the catalog refuses to declare a grader machine whose interpreter cannot run the runtime.

Evidence: end-to-end run over real TaskTrove rows on 2026-11-19 (multifile python:3.11 and stack-pytest/nl2bash ubuntu:24.04 graders return graded verdicts; the 3.10 cases stop at the import).

🤖 ## Research

`_verifyit_reward` launches the grader machine's `python3`, while Verifyit declares Python ≥3.11 and imports `StrEnum` and `tomllib`. That explains the reported Python 3.10 import failure. On current `main`, the DCAgent converter gets a separate grader environment from its conversion context, and the catalog declares `GRADER_PACKAGES` on a Python 3.12 base; the reported `/tests/.taskcompendium-runtime` path is absent from this checkout. No open PR references #11721.

1. Reproduce with a pinned affected row and record the resolved `grader.environment`, grader image digest, `python3 --version`, and runtime staging path. Compare them with the catalog's Python 3.12 grader image to locate where the workspace image became the grader image.
2. Correct that environment selection so Python-tests tasks keep their Python 3.10 workspace but grade in the declared Python 3.12 grader image. Add a qualification check that rejects a resolved grader interpreter below Verifyit's supported floor before admitting tasks.

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
## TL;DR

What is Mochi similar to? We measure the Mochi SFT model (535B-A23B, step 400407) against open-weight models three ways: Mochi's per-token NLL on each model's traces, each model's NLL on Mochi's generations, and agreement of next actions. A small set of Mochi traces on train-side agent tasks is also generated as a candidate teacher set. No results yet.

## Description

Parent: [issue 11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535). Companion measurements: [issue 11674](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11674) (Snowball student NLL closeness to teacher traces) and [issue 11673](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11673) (does closeness predict SFT outcome).

- **(a) Mochi as scorer.**
  - Mochi scores a pilot sample from each of the 14 trace cells in issue 11674, then the full cells if feasible.
  - The existing 10/05 token IDs and loss masks are the reference inputs. We will pin the shared tokenizer and template and verify token-ID and scored-position parity on the scoring route before publishing side-by-side results.
  - Reported per cell: mean NLL (all loss tokens and text-only), pooled-token RSR with ranks capped at 100, and the share of loss tokens above the rank cap.
  - The 14-cell comparator is the one-pass pooled-token RSR subsection of issue 11674.
- **(b) Mochi as teacher.**
  - Mochi continues teacher traces at seeded assistant-turn positions.
  - Snowball 10/05 scores the original teacher turn and Mochi's turn at the same position, paired.
  - Each comparator with prompt logprobs scores the same rendered assistant content, conditioned on the same preceding history, using its own tokenizer. We report nats per UTF-8 byte of the scored content, document token-boundary handling, and use the original teacher turn and the comparator's own continuation as within-scorer references.
- **(c) Behaviour.**
  - At the same cut positions and with the same tool schema, compare the next-action type and tool name, then compare a prespecified named argument for supported tools.
  - Report coverage and counts for no-call, invalid and unknown outcomes.
  - Compare BFCL ×5 per-task outcomes only where task, harness and repeat accounting permit a matched comparison.
- **Agent traces.** Select train-side TMax terminal and/or SWE-smith tasks. Identify and pin the original recording harness before calling the traces harness-matched. Keep verifier-confirmed successes as a candidate set for separate review.

Candidate models (availability and routing to be verified): Qwen3.6-27B, Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Qwen3.5-9B, Qwen3.5-122B-A10B, Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, GLM 5.3, Kimi-K2.5, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, MiniMax-M2.5, gpt-oss-120b.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Find which open-weight models' traces and behaviour are closest to Mochi, and whether Mochi is a near or far teacher for Snowball, as inputs to choosing teachers and data for the Mochi post-training mix.

## What this cannot show

- Likelihood and agreement are not quality.
- They do not show what training on a trace set would do; issue 11673 tests that.
- Low NLL can reflect prior exposure.
- Per-byte NLL across tokenizers is directional likelihood only. Tokenization and serve conventions differ materially between models.
- For likelihood scoring, we plan three fresh scoring passes on the same rows and report the within-setup spread. Generation and behaviour repeat counts are reported separately.

## Data rule

- The scoring and continuation prompt sets are measurements and do not become training data. They are excluded from the candidate trace set.
- Agent runs use train-side tasks only, bound to the frozen eval and TMax holdout deny lists before any run.

## Links

* Logbook:
* W&B Report:
* Important updates:

## Decision Log

## Conclusion

spillover_issues.title: [post-training] What is Mochi similar to? NLL and behaviour against open-weight models

spillover_issues.author: karansag
spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Literature review and three proposed one-hour Snowball SFT experiments testing external Mochi soft targets (Beyer et al., arXiv:2106.05237) and full-vocabulary self-anchoring (Ambient SFT, arXiv:2611.23229).**

## TL;DR

- **Paper identification:** We did not find an exact-title match for *"Language Models are Patient Teachers"* in the sources searched. The closest distillation paper is **[Beyer et al. (2021 / CVPR 2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2106.05237), *"Knowledge distillation: A good teacher is patient and consistent"***, bridged to truncated LLM teacher logprobs by **[Busbridge et al. (2025), Appendix G.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.08606#A7.SS4)** (*"Distillation Scaling Laws"*). (Sun et al., 2019, `arXiv:1908.09355`, uses "patient" for intermediate-layer BERT distillation, which requires white-box hidden-state access.)
- **Complementarity:** Beyer et al. study external-teacher function matching; our cached-target proposal uses $T=1$. **[Ambient SFT (arXiv:2611.23229)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23229)** uses full-vocabulary $T=2.5$ KL to a frozen starting scorer (without Hinton's $T^2$ factor). They target different parts of our SFT problem and need different teacher setups.
- **Proposals (none run yet):** Three one-hour FP32 Snowball experiment designs (`60` updates = `0.1579%` of 10/05 SFT) testing (1) Mochi top-20 + residual-tail KL vs hard-label Mochi traces, (2) prefill-only Mochi soft targets on unpacked general replay with zero synthetic data, and (3) full-vocabulary Ambient SFT self-anchoring with a proposed per-source mask.

## Parent, scope, and context

Parent: [issue 11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535). Background SFT results: [issue 11687 SFT summary](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-7000153313) and [one-hour edit-call comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-6996439113).

**Scope for all three proposals:** Train-side only; nothing has been run yet for these designs. Each proposal requires verified held-out separation across generation, scoring, and training, plus a fixed one-hour decision rule before scaling to eight hours. Lower held-out teacher NLL measures imitation of the teacher; edit-call, BFCL, Micro210, and general retention are separate outcomes. Experiments 1 and 2 test transferring Mochi's existing capabilities into Snowball as a proxy for soft vs hard distillation; diagnosing Mochi's own weaknesses is tracked separately under [issue 11535](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11535).

In the one-hour FP32 pair (`60` updates, fresh state, LR `2e-5`), hard-label `E12-B + TMax` scored `337/855` (`.394`) on `eval-r2` versus `222/855` (`.260`) for its matched general-only control (`+13.45` pp, higher on all 11 tasks). On Micro210 (two repeats of one BF16 export per arm), treatment averaged `39.47%` suite and `14.99%` agent versus `41.59%` suite and `20.00%` agent for control: suite difference `−2.13` pp (missing-outcome bounds `−2.96` to `−1.25` pp; control repeat spread `3.06` pp) and agent difference `−5.01` pp (missing-outcome bounds `−8.45` to `−0.95` pp; control repeat spread `6.32` pp).

Current infrastructure facts and input-parity gates:
- **Shared Mochi probe:** A shared Mochi serve with an unpinned build accepted `k=20` on the probe. The observed response included the actual token in addition to the top-20 when it was outside that set.
- **Tokenizer and template parity:** Mochi and Snowball 10/05 share the same pinned/configured `128,256`-token tokenizer and chat template; request-level token-ID parity against the unpinned serve still requires verification before scoring.
- **Checked student MoE routing:** The checked Snowball SFT student path runs with `expert_axis_size = 1` (local `sonic` MoE kernel, dropless with `0` dropped assignments). Dropless local routing applies to the checked student path and says nothing about teacher input identity.
- **Unpack/repack gate:** Snowball packs multiple documents into `262,144`-token rows isolated by `segment_ids`, whereas a single-prompt completions request attends across the full prompt. Any cached-logprob distillation must unpack rows into single conversations before Mochi scoring, repack with matching `segment_ids`, and gate on identical prefix token IDs, boundary masks, position semantics, and target-token offsets, reporting coverage for any unalignable documents.

## Paper review: Beyer et al. (2106.05237) beside Ambient SFT (2611.23229)

[Beyer et al. (2021 / CVPR 2022)](https://arxiv.org/html/2106.05237) study image classification distillation as **function matching** from a stronger external teacher, testing consistent views, mixup, long schedules, and a temperature sweep (reaching `82.82%` ImageNet top-1 with ResNet-50 from a BiT teacher at `9,600` epochs). Four takeaways and our adaptations connect to Snowball SFT:

1. **Consistent inputs:** In Beyer et al., student and teacher must see the exact same input view. Applying that principle here means gating distillation on the unpack/repack alignment check above rather than relying on tokenizer configuration or student-side dropless routing alone.
2. **Soft targets vs narrow hard labels (our hypothesis for agent transfer):** Beyer et al. showed that matching a strong teacher's soft targets transferred well across broad vision inputs; whether the same carries over to broad agent-capability transfer in LLMs is our hypothesis to test. By contrast, programmatic one-hot `E12-B` edits target a narrow synthetic fixture, and `TMax` (`allenai/tmax-sft`, Qwen3.6-27B traces) comes from a different teacher checkpoint; Snowball's use of those traces applies full-trace CE over all roles (supervised target shares in the selected `123` packs: `47.5%` assistant, `33.4%` tool outputs, `13.9%` user prompts, `3.9%` system/schemas, `1.3%` role headers).
3. **Patience vs our short budgets:** Beyer et al. found benefits from long vision-distillation schedules and reported their best ImageNet result at `9,600` epochs. Our one-hour run is `60` updates (`0.1579%` of 10/05 SFT) and an eight-hour run is `480` updates (`1.2632%` of 10/05). One-hour runs are directional screens, not tests of the patient ceiling.
4. **Top-$k$ truncation bridge:** [Busbridge et al. (2025), Appendix G.4](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.08606#A7.SS4) report that mixing top-$k$ distillation with ground-truth CE at `k=128`, `lambda=0.7` reached validation loss within `0.01` nats of full distillation in their setup. That result motivates mixing CE with truncated KL, but it did not test our `k=20`, residual-tail, teacher-generated-label objective.

[Ambient SFT (arXiv:2611.23229)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23229) uses a frozen pretrained scorer at `T=2.5` (full vocabulary, omitting Hinton's $T^2$ factor) in its instruction-tuning recipe; anchoring continuation SFT to frozen `10/05` is our adaptation. Ambient SFT Appendix D.5 raises temperatures for poorly fit sources; turning the regularizer ON/OFF per source is our proposed change, and the paper does not establish a Snowball new-skill tax.

| Dimension | [Beyer et al. (`2106.05237`)](https://arxiv.org/html/2106.05237) + [Busbridge App. G.4 (`2502.08606`)](https://arxiv.org/html/2502.08606#A7.SS4) | [Ambient SFT (`2611.23229`)](https://arxiv.org/html/2611.23229) (our `10/05` adaptation) |
|---|---|---|
| **Teacher** | Stronger external model (Mochi) | Frozen starting checkpoint (Snowball `10/05`) |
| **Temperature & vocab** | $T=1$, explicit top-20 + actual token + residual tail bin | $T=2.5$ (no Hinton $T^2$ factor), full `128,256` vocabulary |
| **Hypothesis for Snowball** | Test whether soft targets transfer Mochi behavior better than narrow synthetic/hard labels | Test whether full-vocab tail anchoring reduces forgetting during short continuation SFT |
| **Fits Mochi `k=20` endpoint?** | **Yes at $T=1$ with CE mix + residual tail bin** (actual Mochi top-20 mass coverage to be measured on a pilot sample) | **No — requires full vocabulary in-trainer:** $T=2.5$ spreads mass past rank 20, breaking the tail anchor |

## Proposed one-hour Snowball experiments

All three proposals share a **one-hour scale**: `60 × 32 × 262,144 = 503,316,480` scheduled positions per arm (`0.1579%` of 10/05 SFT, FP32 stored parameters). Under the continuation rule from `10/05`, carried FP32 optimizer state at cooled-down LR `5.094738e-6` is the default. Using a `10`-update linear warmup to `2e-5` instead requires its own decision and must be paired with a newly matched same-schedule control.

### Experiment 1: Mochi soft targets (top-20 + tail KL + CE) vs hard-label Mochi traces

- **One-hour version:** Replace the `164` added packs with `~164` packs of Mochi-generated coding/agent traces (`T=0.7`, assistant-only loss mask), mixed with general replay in identical examples, order, and masks across two matched `60`-update FP32 arms:
  - **Arm 1A (hard labels):** `L_total = L_CE` averaged over all supervised tokens in the batch (general replay + Mochi assistant tokens).
  - **Arm 1B (soft targets):** `L_total = ce_weight * L_CE + kl_weight * L_KL` at **$T=1$ only** (e.g., `ce_weight = 0.5`, `kl_weight = 0.5`), where `L_CE` keeps the exact same full-batch supervised target set and denominator as Arm 1A (general replay CE remains active with identical masks) and `L_KL` is the weighted mean of coarse-grained forward KL over KL-selected Mochi assistant tokens (normalized by actual valid KL weight mass, with zero contribution on empty selections). For each KL token, validate and deduplicate full-softmax logprobs and mass closure over `{top-20} ∪ {actual token}`, compute the exact non-explicit tail bucket within numerical tolerance using zero-mass limits, and reject invalid rows with coverage reported. Unmodified probability vectors coarsened into explicit singleton bins plus the remainder give a KL lower bound; the tail bin represents omitted mass, not its internal distribution (and cached top-20 logprobs are never rescaled to $T \neq 1$). Log `||grad_KL|| / ||grad_CE||` so step-size scaling is visible.
  - **Comparators:** Newly matched general-only CE control on the same continuation schedule and checkpoint. Existing `E12-B + TMax` runs used fresh state and a different data/mask recipe, so retain them as context only; `1A` vs `1B` estimates the matched objective contrast on identical examples, order, and masks, while comparing `1A` to historical `E12-B + TMax` cannot isolate the teacher/data effect.
- **What it would show:** Compares the mixed CE-plus-soft-target objective with vanilla CE (`1B` vs `1A`) on identical Mochi traces and masks, measured separately on held-out Mochi NLL (imitation), edit-call, BFCL, Micro210, and general retention. With the illustrative `0.5` CE coefficient, the comparison also changes CE scaling (to test adding KL at fixed CE scaling, set `ce_weight = 1.0` in both arms).
- **What it needs:**
  - *Data:* `~164` packs of Mochi traces plus cached top-20 `(token_id, logprob)` entries (`164 × 262,144 = 42,991,616` positions). Assuming `6` bytes/pair (`int32` ID + 2-byte logprob), dense storage across `20–21` slots is `5.16–5.42 GB` before framing/compression overhead; assistant-only storage depends on the measured assistant span share. Measure pilot top-20 mass coverage and alignment coverage before full collection.
  - *Trainer change:* Chunked gather-based `{top-k} ∪ {actual} + tail` KL kernel behind the same trainer interface as Experiment 3 (avoiding `[B, S, V]` logit materialization), with per-source mask and `||grad_KL|| / ||grad_CE||` watch metric; measure actual HBM delta before scaling.
  - *Serve:* Shared Mochi serve (subject to request-level tokenizer/offset parity check; no new GPU serve).
- **Main risk:** (1) Top-20 truncation misses tail mass on high-entropy reasoning tokens (mitigated by CE mix, exact complement tail bin, and a pilot check of top-20 mass closure). (2) Patience and SNR: `60` updates at `5.094738e-6` may be too short to separate `1B` from `1A` on two-repeat Micro210; gate scaling on a fixed one-hour rule across held-out Mochi NLL, edit-call, BFCL, and retention.

### Experiment 2: Mochi soft targets on unpacked general replay only (zero synthetic data)

- **One-hour version:** Train for `60` updates on the same `1,920` general replay packs as the matched general-only CE control — zero `E12-B`, zero Qwen `TMax`, zero new trace generation. Unpack up to `164` agentic/coding general packs (or a smaller assistant-filtered subset bounded by a pilot throughput/payload check) into single conversations, score with Mochi `prompt_logprobs(k=20)` (prefill-only), verify the unpack/repack parity gate and report unalignable-document coverage, and train with `L_total = ce_weight * L_CE + kl_weight * L_KL` at $T=1$. Ordinary `L_CE` keeps identical targets across both arms (including non-assistant spans in general replay) normalized by the full-batch supervised denominator; `L_KL` applies only to validated parsed assistant spans on the scored packs, normalized by actual valid KL weight mass.
- **What it would show:** Compares the mixed CE-plus-soft-target objective with vanilla CE on identical unpacked general replay without constructing synthetic data, testing our broad-transfer hypothesis across held-out Mochi NLL, edit-call, BFCL, Micro210, and general retention. If `ce_weight < 1.0`, the comparison also changes CE scaling (to test adding KL at fixed CE scaling, set `ce_weight = 1.0` in both arms).
- **What it needs:**
  - *Data:* Unpacked single-conversation prefill scoring (`k=20`) on the shared Mochi serve, repacking with `segment_ids`, alignment verification, and chat-template assistant span masks. Run a pilot throughput and payload-size measurement first on the shared proxy (`164` packs = `42,991,616` positions before assistant filtering) to size the one-hour scored slice.
  - *Trainer change:* Reuses the exact same `cached_topk_kl` trainer path as Experiment 1.
  - *Serve:* Shared Mochi serve only (prefill-only).
- **Main risk:** (1) Replay coverage: the sampled screen-1 general replay audit saw no declared native Pi nested edits, and that audit does not establish their prevalence or what the experiment can fix. (2) Shared-proxy throughput and payload volume for `k=20` prefill scoring, bounded by the pilot measurement.

### Experiment 3: Full-vocabulary Ambient SFT self-anchor (`2611.23229`) with per-source mask

- **One-hour version:** At the default cooled-down LR (`5.094738e-6`), compare matched `60`-update FP32 CE and CE-plus-TM arms from `10/05` on the same fixed mixture (`E12-B + TMax` or Experiment 1 Mochi traces) using the same frozen starting scorer (`10/05`) and token lineage. If the higher-LR schedule (`10`-update linear warmup to `2e-5`, subject to its own decision) is approved, compare CE and CE-plus-TM at that same schedule and include a newly matched `60`-update cooled-down-LR CE arm on the exact same mixture and checkpoint. (The `480`-update `Warm A` run is context only, not the matched lower-LR comparator.) Existing one-hour configs use `gradient_accumulation_steps = 4`; run temperature matching on a fixed quarter of accumulation slots (e.g., `1` of `4` microbatches, or freeze a new accumulation split common to all compared arms). Optimize `L_total = L_CE(all microbatches) + (1/3) * L_TM` at `T=2.5` (no Hinton $T^2$ factor), where `L_TM` is the weighted mean over selected eligible general-replay targets normalized by actual weight mass (with zero contribution on empty selections), with the proposed per-source mask ON for general replay and OFF for new-skill rows. The `1/3` coefficient is the proposed scalar on that restricted mean; it is not an exact effective equivalence to Ambient SFT's per-microbatch CE-or-TM switch.
- **What it would show:** Tests whether full-vocabulary `T=2.5` anchoring to frozen `10/05` improves the edit-call / BFCL / Micro210 / retention trade-off relative to matched vanilla CE at the same schedule (and, under the optional higher-LR comparison, relative to the newly matched `60`-update cooled-down-LR CE comparator; context from the historical one-hour pair: Micro210 agent difference `−5.01` pp, missing-outcome bounds `−8.45` to `−0.95` pp, control repeat spread `6.32` pp).
- **What it needs:**
  - *Data:* The existing `E12-B + TMax` option needs no new data generation or Mochi calls. The alternative uses the already collected Experiment 1 traces.
  - *Trainer change:* Unified temperature-matching PR (frozen BF16 `10/05` teacher on `pinned_host` streaming layer-by-layer, chunked full-vocabulary KL scan, per-source mask, `||grad_TM|| / ||grad_CE||` watch metric). At one teacher forward per four equal microbatch slices, ideal additional teacher work is about `25%` of one full student forward, or about `8.3%` of nominal forward+backward training FLOPs under a `3×` convention, before host-transfer, remat, and LM-head costs; actual HBM delta and step time are unmeasured and must be measured before claiming a cost.
  - *Serve:* None (the frozen teacher is evaluated in-trainer on the remote job).
- **Main risk:** (1) Masked-LR illusion: under the optional higher-LR comparison, TM must beat the newly matched `60`-update cooled-down-LR CE comparator on the new-skill vs retention frontier, not only unregularized `2e-5`. (2) MoE routing drift: smooth output KL may not prevent discrete top-4 expert flips across `256` experts.

## Recommended order

1. **First:** Experiment 3 (zero new data once the unified trainer PR lands and HBM/step-time overhead is measured) alongside a small pilot throughput, payload, and alignment check for Experiment 2 (unpacked `k=20` scoring and top-20 mass closure on the shared Mochi serve).
2. **Second:** Experiment 1 (`1A` vs `1B` on matched Mochi traces) once Mochi trace collection reaches `~164` packs, advancing only arms that clear the fixed one-hour decision rule to an eight-hour+ schedule.

🤖

# Research

Issue #11724 spans three experiment designs and a new trainer loss. The open long-loop trainer computes weighted cross entropy with a full-batch denominator; it has no teacher loss or per-source teacher mask. The FP32 60-update comparison in [#11687](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/11687#issuecomment-7000153313) improved edit-call by 13.45 pp but averaged 5.01 pp lower on Micro210 agent, so that result cannot establish a teacher-loss benefit. [#11717](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11717) is changing stored-parameter precision in the same trainer; the new objectives should use its FP32 policy.

**Relevant code**
- [`train.py#L923-L970`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c6676c91efe773f251d455f97c59e060b49faf1b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/train.py#L923-L970) — CE and accumulation denominator.
- [`model.py#L1414-L1475`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/c6676c91efe773f251d455f97c59e060b49faf1b/experiments/post_training/long_loop/sft_runtime/model.py#L1414-L1475) — current fused next-token loss.
- [#11120](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/11120) — owning long-loop implementation PR.

# Proposed Fix

1. **Pin the comparison.** After #11120 and #11717 settle, record the exact 10/05 checkpoint, carried FP32 optimizer state, cooled-down LR (`5.094738e-6`), 60-update row order, source masks, and held-out IDs in an immutable run manifest. Verify generation, teacher scoring, training, and evaluation sets are disjoint. A higher-LR screen needs its own matched CE control.
2. **Pilot the Mochi input path.** Unpack a bounded sample of general replay conversations and score with `prompt_logprobs(k=20)`. Admit a document only when request token IDs, target offsets, assistant spans, segment boundaries, and repacked positions match exactly. Check duplicate IDs and probability-mass closure over top-20 plus actual token and residual tail; publish rejected-document coverage, top-20 mass, request throughput, and payload size before collecting full targets.
3. **Build and measure temperature matching first.** Add a frozen 10/05 scorer and chunked full-vocabulary KL at `T=2.5`, with CE on all existing targets and KL on eligible general-replay targets only (`1/3` coefficient, one of four accumulation slices). Compare the chunked loss and gradients with a small dense reference, including empty masks and packed boundaries. Measure HBM and step time on the actual Snowball shape before scheduling the full pair.
4. **Run matched 60-update CE and CE-plus-TM arms.** Keep checkpoint, optimizer, LR, examples, order, and CE masks identical. Publish the decision thresholds and missing-outcome rule before launch. Read out held-out teacher NLL, edit-call, BFCL, Micro210, and general retention; advance to 480 updates only if the predeclared rule passes, with repeat variance reported.
5. **Then test external soft targets.** Reuse the validated scorer and add a separate `T=1` top-20-plus-tail KL path. Keep CE weight at `1.0` in both arms so the objective contrast isolates added KL. Run matched hard-label versus soft-target Mochi traces (Experiment 1), then scored general replay versus its CE control (Experiment 2), subject to the pilot's coverage and throughput. Report KL/CE gradient-norm ratio and valid-target coverage for each run.

The first implementation PR should cover the temperature-matching loss and its reference tests; the Mochi scoring and cached-target path can follow as separate changes. No teacher-target experiment has run yet.

spillover_issues.author: mcwitt
spillover_issues.body:
`levanter.grug._moe` marks the whole package private in its `__init__.py` ("Private Grug MoE backend implementations"), and then prefixes names inside it with an underscore as well. Thirty-seven of those names are imported by a module other than the one that defines them, so the marker says module-private about names that are never used module-privately.

`_zero_inactive_grouped_rows` is the clearest case. It is defined in `_moe/common.py` and used five times in `_moe/sonic_cute.py`, and never in the module that defines it.

The names span thirteen modules:

```
sharding.py                          9    ep_deepep.py                        1
ep_common.py                         9    ep_fixed_all_to_all.py              1
common.py                            6    ep_fixed_pooled_wave_all_to_all.py  1
sonic_cute.py                        4    ep_ragged_all_to_all.py             1
cudnn_wgrad_cute.py                  1    ep_ring.py                          1
local.py                             1    scatter.py                          1
sonic.py                             1
```

Some cross a distribution boundary, not just a module one. `lib/marin/src/marin/testing/moe/ragged_ep.py` imports `_clip_receiver_group_sizes`, `_EXPERT_CHUNKS`, `_quack_grouped_gemm_available`, and `_select_expert_mlp` from levanter, and `tests/test_grug_variant_contracts.py` imports `_compact_grug_mesh_shape`. A leading underscore is the only signal Python has for "do not import this", and marin imports them anyway.

The prefix also costs the thing it was meant to buy. Because everything is underscored, the package cannot distinguish a helper genuinely local to one module from one that is part of the package's internal interface. `_moe/sharding.py` and `_moe/ep_common.py` are effectively shared libraries for the backends, and nothing in the naming says so.

Dropping the prefix from names that cross module boundaries inside `_moe/` leaves the package private via its path, which is where privacy is already enforced. It is mechanical: every importer is in this repository, there are no dynamic lookups by name, and the compatibility rule in `AGENTS.md` says to update call sites rather than keep aliases. It is wide, though, which is why it does not belong inside a feature PR — #8549 added six such names by following the surrounding style, and the reviewer noticed the style rather than the change.

Raised in review on #8549: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8549#discussion_r3876485352

Done when:

- Names in `levanter.grug._moe` that are imported by another module no longer carry a leading underscore, and names used only within their defining module still do.
- Importers are updated in place, in `lib/levanter`, `lib/marin`, `tests/`, and `experiments/`, with no compatibility aliases.
- `uv run --no-project infra/ci/run_tests.py` passes, and `./infra/pre-commit.py --all-files` is clean.

## TL;DR

[PR #8651](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651) replaces Polars inside Zephyr's shuffle with DataFusion, keeps Zephyr's external spill files on region-local GCS, and exposes DataFusion SQL for columnar map and reducer stages.

Against current main/Polars, the 13 SQL-migrated Datakit stages used 29.39% less CPU, 21.38% less summed stage time, and 49.93% less peak shard memory. Across all 16 shuffle-affected stages, including fuzzy verification's unchanged Python reducer, CPU fell 26.82%. Region-local output validators matched exactly.

## Description

The SQL API mirrors the efficiency boundaries established by [#8154](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8154) and [#8256](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8256):

- `Dataset.sql(...)` runs batch-local map queries against an `input` view.
- `Dataset.group_by(..., reducer=sql(...))` runs a query over the complete target shard after Zephyr's external merge.
- Scalar SQL functions provide expression-based routing keys without serializing DataFusion objects into a plan.

Datakit normalization, fuzzy graph construction, all connected-component iterations, and final fuzzy-attribute materialization use these paths. Fuzzy verification still uses the generic DataFusion shuffle with its existing Python reducer. Download, MinHash, memory-store loading, consolidation, tokenization, and cache-probe work do not execute the new SQL path.

DataFusion native disk spill stays disabled. Zephyr continues to write bounded sorted Parquet chunks and external merge runs to the stage filesystem, which is GCS on Iris. Eight target-shard ranges bound each DataFusion sort while preserving one selected file per mapper flush at reduce time.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Remove Zephyr's Polars dependency and use DataFusion for shuffle sorting, reading, and columnar map/reduce computation without changing semantic output, moving external spill off GCS, or retaining the original DataFusion memory and CPU regressions.

## Status

The implementation is complete on PR #8651, rebased on control commit `dc584e765d` with treatment head `fbddc9de28`.

The affected repository selection passed 1,529 tests with three skips and five expected failures. Ruff, Black, license checks, Pyrefly, documentation checks, and all remaining changed-file checks passed.

| Shuffle only · Fuzzy verification · `stage2-Reduce` | 0.53 GB | 0.72 GB | +36.50% |

The SQL-migrated stages processed the same 558,478,005 logical items; all shuffle-affected stages matched at 559,057,070. Byte telemetry is not comparable because the treatment counts Arrow buffer bytes while the control counts its row-oriented representation.

The [control validator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-validate-20260828-control-v2) and [treatment validator](https://iris.oa.dev/#/job/%2Floom%2Fzephyr-sql-validate-20260828-treatment-v2) each found 9,672,101 downloaded rows, 9,268,156 normalized rows, 532,777 fuzzy cluster members with 246,814 representatives, 45,970 verified duplicates, and 9,222,186 consolidated and tokenized rows.

Measured CPU across the full ferry fell 9.04%, and summed stage time fell 4.09%. Root wall time rose 5.01% because unaffected runtime was noisier: tokenization elapsed rose from 333.92 to 474.38 seconds with CPU essentially unchanged at +0.69%, followed by a longer cache-probe scheduling delay. Unaffected-stage CPU was flat at -0.30%.

## Earlier evidence

The range-only DataFusion A/B, before the SQL path, used 5.25% more CPU than Polars across the 16 shuffle-affected stages while lowering peak shard memory 43.28%. That isolated Python row materialization and reducer callbacks as the remaining actionable cost.

A control-only Polars target-range sweep showed that the memory mechanism is engine-independent:

| Polars target ranges | Writer time | Change |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (baseline) | 2.600 s | - |
| 2 | 2.649 s | +1.92% |
| 4 | 2.770 s | +6.55% |
| 8 | 3.319 s | +27.69% |

| Polars target ranges | Peak RSS | Change |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 (baseline) | 1.434 GB | - |
| 2 | 1.256 GB | -12.40% |
| 4 | 1.080 GB | -24.70% |
| 8 | 0.988 GB | -31.07% |

An earlier pre-optimization Nemotron A/B raised affected-stage CPU 39.99% and peak memory from 7.88 to 13.42 GB. That run identified the original whole-buffer DataFusion `SortExec` problem and does not represent the current range-partitioned SQL treatment.

## Links

- Implementation and review: [PR #8651](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651)
- Per-stage A/B and historical detail: [sticky PR comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8651#issuecomment-5403476301)
- Root-cause and benchmark investigation: [Echo record](https://echo.oa.dev/wiki/267)

## Decision Log

- DataFusion native disk spill stays disabled so its internal sorter remains in memory.
- Zephyr's explicit sorted chunks and external merge intermediates remain on the stage filesystem and therefore use region-local GCS on Iris.
- DataFusion uses eight target-shard ranges because two exhausted the sorter and four retained materially more memory.
- SQL is exposed as a serializable Zephyr plan object instead of exposing DataFusion runtime objects.
- Datakit uses SQL only where the transformation is columnar; fuzzy verification retains Python callbacks for full-text comparison and side effects.

## Conclusion

The Python implementation removes the DataFusion memory and CPU regressions without modifying DataFusion. On the matched Datakit ferry, SQL-migrated DataFusion stages were faster than current-main Polars while using half the peak shard memory, and persisted outputs matched exactly.

spillover_issues.author: dlwh
spillover_issues.body:
## Description

Evaluate whether June 67B context-extension checkpoints use retained MRCR conversation context when scoring the same final assistant response. The paired evaluator compares `full_context` with `query_only`, scores response-body tokens, and stratifies deterministic bootstrap intervals by needle count and evidence distance.

## Task

An MRCR source document contains two worked examples, a long multi-turn conversation with 2, 4, or 8 relevant facts ("needles"), and a final query. `desired_msg_index` identifies a user request in that conversation; its matching answer is the immediately following assistant message.

Each source row produces two documents with the same final query and gold response:

```text
full_context: two worked examples + target conversation + final query -> gold response
query_only:   two worked examples + final query                       -> gold response
```

The primary two-shot prompt supplies the benchmark's 10-character answer prefix. The evaluator scores only the remaining gold assistant response body. The worked examples, retained conversation, final query, supplied prefix, and EOS are context and receive zero loss. Each condition occupies one unsliced, unpacked sequence.

The paired comparison asks whether retaining the target conversation improves the likelihood of the identical response. Results report `query_only - full_context` NLL and BPB gain, with response-token micro and per-example macro aggregation, sliced by needle count and evidence distance.

### Difference from standard MRCR

Standard OpenAI MRCR gives the model the complete conversation, samples a response, requires the nonce prefix in that response, and grades the generated text with a `SequenceMatcher` similarity score. This experiment instead teacher-forces the gold response and measures its token likelihood twice: once with the target conversation and once without it. The supplied prefix is not scored. The resulting paired NLL/BPB gain is a diagnostic of context use, not an official MRCR generation score, and should not be compared directly with published MRCR scores.

## Hypothesis or Goal

Context gain (`query_only - full_context`) should move from non-positive before extension to positive after 64K/262K adaptation. Fixed qk=1.57 comparisons isolate checkpoint adaptation; qk=1.75 is the deployable final arm.

### Links

- [OpenAI MRCR dataset and task description](https://huggingface.co/datasets/openai/mrcr/tree/f4c69fae7cf81f7ca26b9fee34b392a50f6b8a1d)
- [Research logbook](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/babf963076/.agents/logbooks/paired-mrcr-base-eval.md)
- [Implementation snapshot](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/63027b4e72)
- [Final qk1.57 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk157-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)
- [Final qk1.75 W&B](https://wandb.ai/marin-community/marin_moe/runs/mrcr-67b-step157000-qk175-cap262144-two_shot-v464cp8ep4)

## Results

Context gain is `query_only - full_context`, so positive NLL or BPB gain is beneficial.

| Checkpoint | qk | NLL gain (95% CI) | BPB gain |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| step 141000, pre-extension (8K) | 1.57 | -0.19453 [-0.21900, -0.16930] | -0.05789 |
| step 156000, 64K source | 1.57 | +0.40387 [+0.36399, +0.44537] | +0.12019 |
| step 157000, 262K extension | 1.57 | +1.18860 [+1.14205, +1.23597] | +0.35371 |
| step 157000, deployable arm | 1.75 | +1.26855 [+1.22432, +1.31342] | +0.37751 |

Each checkpoint used the same 299 paired source examples: 598 full-context/query-only condition sequences. Across four checkpoints, this is 1,196 paired checkpoint-example comparisons and 2,392 condition sequences.

Confidence is exploratory because each checkpoint received one evaluation pass over this dataset. One-shot/no-prefix and the full matrix remain untested.

comments.author: dlwh
comments.body:
🤖 Added a four-condition oracle-normalized measurement before rerunning the 299-example 262K slice.

The conditions form a 2×2 comparison: needles absent/present and distractors absent/present. `needle_only` retains all repeated target-request turns so the ordinal retrieval problem is preserved; `distractor_only` retains the complementary conversation turns. All four conditions score the same response-body tokens.

The headline recovery ratio is `(distractor_only NLL - full_context NLL) / (query_only NLL - needle_only NLL)`, computed as a token-micro ratio of aggregate paired contrasts. A 10,000-sample bootstrap resamples the same four-condition source tuples within needle-count and evidence-distance strata.

The ratio is identifiable only when the isolated-needle gain is at least 0.10 nats/token, its bootstrap lower bound is positive, at least 99% of bootstrap denominators are positive, and no denominator is zero. Before seeing results, the “good enough” gate is a recovery-ratio 95% lower bound of at least 0.80 plus a positive lower bound for distracted needle gain. Needle-count slices must each have positive distracted needle gain; distance slices are descriptive.

Implementation: https://github.com/marin-community/marin/commit/5c32364665

Next: run the pre-extension checkpoint as a memory/artifact probe on `v4-64-cp8-ep4`, then run the remaining three checkpoints if it succeeds.
