spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
Marin's Pulumi IaC has no single organizing convention: `infra/pulumi` splits into one GCP stack and four separate CoreWeave cluster stacks, `infra/buckets` spans GCS, CoreWeave object storage, and Cloudflare R2 in one stack, and Cloudflare DNS records are declared inline in three unrelated deploy stacks (`infra/grafana`, `infra/loom`, the CoreWeave federation stack) plus `infra/buckets`. Where a new resource belongs isn't predictable from any rule.

Evaluate consolidating to one stack per provider — GCP, CoreWeave, Cloudflare — with GitHub unchanged, since it's already provider-scoped.

**Prior research**

Full writeup, phase-by-phase migration plan, and `--target` mechanics: https://claude.ai/code/artifact/28f800f1-835e-479a-924c-596a10924138

The target model:
- **gcp** — absorbs `infra/pulumi`'s `marin` stack (federation-egress static IPs, GCLB/IAP, the `marin`/`marin-dev` Iris controllers' own VM-based provisioning, the project-wide IAM registry), the GCS slice of `infra/buckets`, and `infra/cloudsql`.
- **coreweave** — the four existing cluster stacks (NodePools, RBAC, Kueue, Traefik/cert-manager) merged into one, plus the CoreWeave object-storage slice of `infra/buckets`.
- **cloudflare** (new) — every DNS record (the federation CNAME, and each deploy stack's own record) plus R2, each record built from a `StackReference` into its owning stack rather than declared inline.
- `infra/ducky` and `infra/xprof` deploy through `iac.iris.service.IrisService`, a `local.Command` that shells to the Iris CLI rather than a `pulumi_gcp` resource — they don't own any GCP-provider resources and stay independent regardless of this change.

Benefits found: a single GCP stack makes authoritative GCP resources (e.g. a fully-owned IAM binding) safe to adopt, since GCP enforces authority per role/field and one stack means exactly one process ever computes a given role's complete membership — today's non-authoritative `*IAMMember` grants exist partly to avoid needing that guarantee across stacks. `infra/permissions` was already retired into the `marin` stack's `iac.gcp.iam.GcpIam` (#7576), so the same consolidation pattern has worked once before at smaller scale.

`pulumi up --target <urn> --target-dependents` lets one already-decided change land safely across a consolidated stack's resources — canary a CoreWeave config change cluster by cluster, or force one Cloud Run image bump without touching a sibling service. It doesn't reduce Pulumi's state lock, which is always stack-wide regardless of target scope, and the full program still evaluates and declares every resource on every run (a resource that's live but undeclared this run reads as "delete it," so a program can't skip building part of the graph to go faster).

That lock scope is why folding the GCP-hosted service deploys (Grafana, Echo, Evaldash, Loom) into the `gcp` stack is a separate, harder call than the rest of this. `.github/workflows/ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` already auto-deploys Grafana, Echo, Evaldash, Ducky, and Xprof on every push to `main`, each against its own stack in its own `concurrency` group, so unrelated services deploy in parallel today with zero contention. Merging Grafana/Echo/Evaldash into one `gcp` stack means their independent, path-filtered, automated merges start queuing behind whichever one landed first, even when the two PRs touch disjoint resources — `--target` doesn't fix this, since the lock isn't scoped by target. Recovering today's parallelism would need `ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` and `scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py` rebuilt to resolve per-service URN target sets and either accept serialized deploys or build an explicit queue.

Given that cost, this consolidation is staged: land the GCP substrate, CoreWeave, and Cloudflare consolidation first (no CI-automation conflict, since none of that is part of the automated rollout pipeline); leave folding the Cloud Run/VM deploys into `gcp` as an explicit follow-up decision rather than a default consequence of adopting the convention.

Open question — fold Grafana/Echo/Evaldash/Loom into the `gcp` stack:
- For: one audit surface for the account's entire Cloud Run/VM/IAM footprint; one credential story.
- Against: trades five parallel, low-friction automated deploys for one shared lock; requires new CI automation (per-service target-set resolution, a queue or accepted serialization) before it's safe; reverses `infra/pulumi.md`'s stated reason Grafana got its own project — its own image and deployment lifecycle.

Done when: a decision is made on the GCP/CoreWeave/Cloudflare consolidation and, separately, on whether to pursue folding the GCP-hosted service deploys in. If the first is accepted, file follow-up issues for each stack's migration.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 **Analysis — design decision, no PR.** Definition of done here is "a decision is made" on a fleet-wide IaC convention; that's a human architecture call, not an agent-implementable change. I verified the issue's structural claims against the tree and found one thing worse than stated. Below is decision-ready grounding.

# Research

The claims hold. Current layout, verified:

- **1 GCP + 4 CoreWeave stacks** share `infra/pulumi` (project `marin-iac`): [`Pulumi.marin.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/Pulumi.marin.yaml) plus `Pulumi.cw-rno2a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-east-02a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-east-08a.yaml`, `Pulumi.cw-us-west-04a.yaml`.
- **`infra/buckets` is one cross-provider stack** — GCS + CoreWeave S3 + Cloudflare R2 providers all instantiated in [`buckets/__main__.py#L23-L39`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/buckets/__main__.py#L23-L39).
- **DNS is scattered across 6 sites, not 4** (correction to the issue): `infra/grafana` ([`__main__.py#L190`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/grafana/__main__.py#L190)), **`infra/echo` ([`__main__.py#L257`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/echo/__main__.py#L257))**, **`infra/evaldash` ([`__main__.py#L121`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/evaldash/__main__.py#L121))**, `infra/loom` ([`infrastructure.py#L620`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/loom/infrastructure.py#L620)), the CoreWeave federation CNAME ([`iac/coreweave/dns.py#L37`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/coreweave/dns.py#L37)), and R2 in `infra/buckets`. The issue named only grafana/loom/federation/buckets; echo and evaldash also declare `cloudflare.DnsRecord` inline. Cloudflare is the most fragmented provider — strengthens the consolidation case.
- **`ducky`/`xprof` own no GCP-provider resources** — both build `iac.iris.service.IrisService`, a `command.local.Command` shelling to the Iris CLI ([`iac/iris/service.py#L25-L26`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py#L25-L26)). Correctly excluded from the `gcp` target.
- **Parallel-deploy cost is real.** [`ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/.github/workflows/ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml) matrix-deploys ducky/echo/evaldash/grafana/xprof on push to `main`, each in `concurrency: group: pulumi-rollout-${{ matrix.name }}` (L88-90), driven by [`scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/scripts/ci/pulumi_rollouts.py). Folding these into one `gcp` stack serializes them behind one stack lock.
- **Precedent works.** `infra/permissions` is retired into `iac.gcp.iam.GcpIam` (#7576); [`permissions/__main__.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/permissions/__main__.py) now raises rather than deploying.

# Recommendation

Adopt the staged split the issue proposes; it is sound and the risky part is correctly isolated.

**Do now (low-risk, no CI-automation conflict):** consolidate to `gcp` (substrate) + `coreweave` (4 clusters merged) + new `cloudflare` (all 6 DNS sites + R2, each built from a `StackReference` into its owning stack). None of these are in the automated rollout pipeline, so no lock contention is introduced. File one follow-up migration issue per stack.

**Defer (needs a separate decision + CI rework):** folding the Cloud Run/VM service deploys (grafana/echo/evaldash/loom) into `gcp`. As the issue notes, `--target` does not scope the state lock, so this trades 5 parallel path-filtered auto-deploys for one serialized lock and requires rebuilding `ops-pulumi-rollout.yaml` + `pulumi_rollouts.py` to resolve per-service URN target sets first. Recommend **not** doing this now — the audit-surface/credential-story benefit doesn't outweigh reversing the documented reason ([`pulumi.md#L39-L49`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi.md#L39-L49)) each service got its own lifecycle.

**Coordinate with in-flight work first** — these touch the same GCP-stack IAM surface and should land before the `gcp` consolidation to avoid rebasing churn: #8455/#8458 (authoritative + centralized app IAM grants), #8459/#8462 (remove retired permissions stack). The authoritative-IAM goal in #8455 is in fact the strongest single argument *for* one `gcp` stack (one process computes each role's full membership), so sequence it deliberately.

Needs a maintainer decision on the two questions above before migration issues are filed. Handing off — no code change to make here.

spillover_issues.author: rjpower
spillover_issues.body:
Some potential improvements we noticed during the hero run rollout.

scatter aggregation:
  - can you run a scatter aggregation step alongside the mappers? for each N map shards finished, read them in and reshuffle/merge the outputs by reduce shard. the inputs should be pre-sorted by target shard, so in theory this can be done with low-memory. this should reduce read traffic by a factor of ~N, and potentially eliminates the external sort we currently do entirely

datafusion as a loading api:
  - supports parquet reading & query push down
  - seems robust from our experience with finelog
  - trivializes a "lite" sql select only API
  - would be nice for library sharing across projects

mapper auto-tuning:
  - choose the number of mappers for the user based on heuristics or dynamically based on observations
  - we have many pipelines that run 10x too slow just because they have fewer mappers than needed
  - combine this with the scatter aggregation to avoid map/reduce shard blowup

better partial recovery:
  - allow recovering a partially complete run
  - for example the zephyr coordinator might write a state record once a minute recording all of the shard state
  - check for this when booting up and reuse it if the ids match

kv-store work scattering:
  - the kv store actors can be used in the some situations to split up imbalanced workloads
  - push the work to the kv store via compute functions


CC @ravwojdyla @muchanem

spillover_issues.author: wmoss
spillover_issues.body:
Iris controller restarts today are driven entirely by `iris cluster controller restart` (see `lib/iris/OPS.md`, `.agents/skills/restart-iris/`) — GCE clusters restart via SSH + `docker restart`, CoreWeave clusters via the Kubernetes API — not by Pulumi. This is an investigation, not a commitment to migrate: the restart flow has safety properties that a naive Pulumi resource-replace would break if not carried over deliberately.

Specifically: the controller keeps local SQLite state plus periodic GCS checkpoints, and restart takes a pre-restart checkpoint and writes a rollout record (image + matching checkpoint ref) so a failed health check can roll back atomically. DB migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so restoring an old controller image without its paired pre-migration checkpoint breaks. Any Pulumi-driven approach needs to preserve this checkpoint-before-restart / paired-rollback behavior, e.g. by keeping restart-with-rollback as a wrapped CLI step (similar to how `iac.iris.service` wraps a CLI today) rather than modeling the controller as a plain replaceable resource.

comments.author: claude[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation, not a bug fix — no PR. Analysis below; handing off to a human for the migrate/don't-migrate call.

# Research

Confirmed the issue body against the code. `iris cluster controller restart` is a CLI-side choreography around a mechanical platform restart; the safety lives in the CLI, not in the platform primitive.

Forward deploy in [`cli/cluster.py:controller_restart` L1117-1215](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117-L1215): pre-deploy checkpoint (L1180) → build fresh images (L1182) → write `PENDING` rollout record (L1187) → `restart_controller` (L1199) → on health-check failure `_auto_rollback` to previous image + its pre-deploy checkpoint (L1202) → write `COMMITTED` (L1206). `--rollback` (L1148) reverts to the recorded previous image + checkpoint.

The rollout record is a small state machine in GCS remote state, not in any deploy tool's state; the restarted controller consumes `ROLLBACK_REQUESTED` once on boot and self-clears. Migrations are forward-only and some are destructive, so an old image must boot on its paired pre-migration checkpoint — this is why image and checkpoint are recorded as a pair.

**Relevant code**
- [`cli/cluster.py#L1117`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1117) - restart/rollback choreography (checkpoint, record, restart, auto-rollback)
- [`controller/rollout.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/rollout.py) - `RolloutPhase`/`RolloutRecord`, read/write in GCS remote state
- [`platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/vm_lifecycle.py#L409) / [`k8s/controller.py#L517`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/platforms/k8s/controller.py#L517) - mechanical restart primitives (no safety logic)
- [`controller/migrations/`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/tree/main/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/migrations) - forward-only, sometimes destructive
- [`iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py#L156-L164) - existing CLI-wrap template to reuse

# Proposed approach

Do **not** model the controller as a plain replaceable Pulumi resource. A resource-replace would tear down and recreate around the restart, bypassing the checkpoint/rollout-record choreography and losing atomic rollback on a bad deploy.

Instead reuse the pattern already in [`iac/iris/service.py`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/main/infra/pulumi/src/iac/iris/service.py) (and the sibling finelog migration in #7571): wrap `iris cluster controller restart` in a `command.local.Command` component whose `create`/`update` verb runs the restart CLI and whose `delete` is a no-op (or `stop`, deliberately). Key the resource on the controller image tag plus a code hash so a change triggers `update` = restart-with-rollback; a failed health check propagates as a Command error, and the CLI has already auto-rolled-back. The rollout record stays in GCS remote state so `--rollback` keeps working out-of-band from Pulumi state.

Open questions for the human owner:
- Is the goal declarative *drift correction* (Pulumi restarts when image drifts) or just *inventory* (record the controller in the stack without owning restarts)? The wrapper above gives the former; only the latter avoids Pulumi ever triggering a restart.
- How should a Pulumi `up` that fails its health check and auto-rolls-back report to the operator — hard resource failure, or success-with-warning after rollback?
- Interaction with the manual `restart-iris` skill / direct CLI runs: Pulumi must treat an out-of-band restart as convergent, not as drift to undo.

Scope is a new Pulumi component plus wiring — multi-file design work, so leaving implementation to a human per the migration effort in #7571/#7262.

comments.author: loom-oa-dev[bot]
comments.body:
🤖 Investigation result: move Iris controller operations under the shared deploy interface, with Pulumi invoking the existing migration-aware restart transaction. Do not make the controller VM or Kubernetes Deployment a plain replaceable Pulumi resource.

Effort: medium, 2026-08-24. I stopped after the current code, linked PRs, Echo history, and Pulumi documentation converged on the same boundary.

### Current Marin context

The new work changes the operator interface, but not Iris's state-safety requirement:

- [#8537](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/8537) provides one command tree for Pulumi applications. The executable merged there is `marin-deploy`, so the exact spelling today is `uv run marin-deploy ...`; adding a `deploy` script alias is independent of this design.
- [`controller restart`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cli/cluster.py#L1263-L1532) resolves secrets, checkpoints the live controller, builds and pins images, writes `PENDING`, restarts in place, health-checks, and commits or restores the previous image plus checkpoint. The controller [consumes the rollback request once](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/iris/src/iris/cluster/controller/main.py#L51-L85).
- Pulumi [does not automatically roll back a failed update](https://www.pulumi.com/docs/support/faq/infrastructure/#automatic-rollbacks). Finelog therefore captures the active revision outside Pulumi, runs `pulumi up`, restores on failure, and refreshes state ([#7690](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/pull/7690), [current implementation](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/1936313ac7da5e1c4f08c0a1634e24cf66f4e772/lib/finelog/src/finelog/deploy/_k8s.py#L390-L471)). Iris needs that recovery boundary and its additional checkpoint pairing.

### Recommended first migration

1. Add a separate `infra/iris` application project with one stack per controller cluster. This follows the repository rule that application deploy lifecycles stay outside the static `infra/pulumi` substrate project.
2. Add an Iris controller component backed by `command.local.Command`. Its `create` and `update` verbs run the existing `iris cluster controller restart`; removal has no stop/delete verb. Inputs include the cluster, reviewed config hash, working-tree hash, and an explicit deploy generation for a forced same-tree restart. Pulumi's command provider runs `update` when inputs/triggers change instead of replacing the resource ([provider contract](https://www.pulumi.com/registry/packages/command/api-docs/local/command/)).
3. Add service-specific commands:

   ```text
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster>
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollout <cluster> --force
   uv run marin-deploy iris rollback <cluster>
   ```

   `rollback` must call the existing `--rollback` path and use the GCS rollout record. Pulumi history is not a substitute for the recorded image/checkpoint pair. The rollout record remains the recovery source of truth; Pulumi records which reviewed tree/config triggered the transaction.
4. Keep the existing fleet gates: clean/current tree preflight, one cluster at a time, baseline snapshot, five-minute verification, and smoke job. Do not add Iris to the parallel path-triggered deployment matrix in the first change. That matrix cannot currently stop the fleet at the first failed cluster, and GCE restarts also require per-user SSH access.

This stage gives Iris the shared `marin-deploy` UX and Pulumi update/audit surface while preserving the current transaction even when an operator runs `pulumi up` directly.

### Native-resource follow-up

A later CoreWeave-only stage can adopt the non-secret runtime objects into an application stack: ConfigMap, protected PVC, Recreate Deployment, Service, PDB, node-agent DaemonSet, LocalQueue, and priority classes. It should proceed only after the deploy driver is split into prepare/activate/finalize/rollback operations and these conditions are tested:

- no workload mutation before a fresh checkpoint and `PENDING` record;
- every activation or health failure restores the recorded image and checkpoint, waits for `ROLLED_BACK`, then refreshes Pulumi state;
- direct `pulumi up` cannot bypass preparation;
- secret values remain outside Pulumi state;
- controller storage is protected, and GCE application changes never replace the controller VM;
- manual break-glass rollback remains convergent with the next intentional rollout.

Confidence is high for the first migration. Native CoreWeave ownership is feasible with those gates, but it is a separate lifecycle refactor; GCE should continue using the in-place SSH restart mechanism behind the same command.

### Handoff

No PR was opened because this request was an investigation. The next decision is whether to implement the first migration as scoped above and track native CoreWeave resource ownership separately.

🤖 ### Research

`marin-deploy iris rollout` calls the controller provider's preflight before checkpointing or building images. The CoreWeave provider currently resolves only the controller signing key there; it first reads S3 credentials such as `CW_KEY_ID` and `CW_KEY_SECRET` during Kubernetes activation, after the expensive rollout preparation has completed.

Missing variables will fail before the checkpoint and image build. Pulumi activation reads the same operator environment in its separate provider process, keeping secret values out of Pulumi inputs and state. PR #8652 already owns this deploy path; no other open PR overlaps the change.

RL consumes exactly 32 SWE + 32 non-agentic groups per update, eight samples per group (512 trajectories), with maximum staleness of two optimizer updates. Its explicit budget is 10 h from the first completed optimizer step, with a 1,800-second drain margin. Validation and native saves occur every two updates. Selection uses an EMA with span five (alpha 1/3) and requires all 120 validation tasks scored; selected step 20 scored 120/120. Retention is last three plus protected best. ## 10/05 Micro210 baseline

Evaluation-only entry for the frozen 10/05 model; this does not introduce a new SFT or RL training recipe.

Micro210 is Marin’s mixed reasoning, knowledge, coding and agentic evaluation suite.
This recipe supports 200 distinct tasks across 20 sources (Tau3 excluded), expanded to 440 assignments, including 100 Pi assignments.

## Model and evaluation policy

Model: [open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05](https://huggingface.co/open-athena/Grug-67B-A2B-Datakit-SFT-262K-2026.10.05/tree/ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6), immutable revision `ac60d9401820953943f5a56e06f36e13c86b12d6`. The three runs evaluate this same model in existing region-local storage, with no additional training.

The runtime separately selects [marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools](https://huggingface.co/marin-community/marin-tokenizer-tools/tree/3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09), revision `3f6879acdaf3dae7874b2d48c7d11b9d8c6faf09`, with no explicit template override and thinking enabled. The model’s embedded tokenizer provenance is not the selected runtime tools revision.

Current harness: 16 global Harbor slots (four rollout workers × four), one 8 H100 policy worker (TP1/DP8/EP8, max_num_seqs 8) and an independent 8 H100 M3 judge (TP8). Policy/judge caps are 21,600 s; root cap is 25,200 s. Native Pi 0.87; context 65,536, 16,384 generated tokens per turn, temperature 0.7, top-p 0.95. Compilation and CUDA graphs remain enabled. These role budgets are not asserted identical to every historical recipe in this issue.

Pinned policy image request: `13519c59442bd70ed5ec2902869f15094992d6849d7e34e353f1338dec7ff5f8`. The region-control policy image matched that request; its CPU/judge/broker task image was `b5b474d80ca79f996049cc0cf700ab93ab2d41a4d9b8a91afc43ce11bf44d974`, matching the observed cw-us-east-02a reference. Policy/judge runtime pins are `39e62869693c` / `01911be34fac`; judge model revision is `c5454eb03678d8710e54a4e0fc681b9f3b4a3dba`. Images and pins do not independently attest imported module bytes or platform equivalence.

All three produced suite Parquets are 16,401,114 bytes with SHA256 `00cdda0654be66060d3ff77b6b44e3dc6fa470e50625ef61ef24b5d9c778bef7`. Produced-byte/order identity is not live runtime consumption or complete assigned-UID coverage proof.

Native equal-20 is recomputed from the 20 native source averages, whose denominators include excluded assignments. Available-only means omit excluded outcomes. Scores are heterogeneous partial-credit means, not pass@1.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
Four generated Reasoning Gym tasks give full reward to a reply that does not depend on the question. `reasoning_gym_generated` holds 1,000 rows of each.

- `game_of_life_halting`: every non-blank reply scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer compares `bool(reply)` with `bool(answer)`, and every answer is the string `True` or `False`. [The generator](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/generate.py#L77-L86) records the reward of the fixed wrong answer `definitely wrong` for every row. For these 1,000 rows the recorded reward is 1.0, and [`convert_generated`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/d83e7766c5a5b9bec43cdd26eccc71a54dcf9bfd/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym/tasks.py#L256-L271) stores the record without reading it.
- `complex_arithmetic`: the reply `NaN` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 entries. The scorer returns `min(1.0, math.exp(-distance))`, which is 1.0 when the distance is NaN.
- `coin_flip`: the reply `0` scores 1.0 on 939 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 gives partial reward for a matching prefix and divides by the length of the shorter string, so the one-character reply `0` matches every answer that starts with `0.`.
- `propositional_logic`: the reply `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on 820 of the 1,000 entries. The scorer accepts any conclusion that follows from the premises, and a disjunction that names a premise follows from it.

Reproduce:

1. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   PYTHONHASHSEED=0 uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra reasoning-gym python - <<'EOF'
   import sys

   sys.path.insert(0, "experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/reasoning_gym")
   import generate
   import reasoning_gym

   replies = (
       ("game_of_life_halting", "x"),
       ("complex_arithmetic", "NaN"),
       ("coin_flip", "0"),
       ("propositional_logic", "P ∨ Q"),
   )
   for task, reply in replies:
       data = reasoning_gym.create_dataset(task, size=generate.ROWS_PER_TASK, seed=generate.task_seed(task))
       score = reasoning_gym.get_score_answer_fn(task)
       print(task, repr(reply), sum(score(reply, data[index]) == 1.0 for index in range(generate.ROWS_PER_TASK)))
   EOF
   ```

2. It prints `game_of_life_halting 'x' 1000`, `complex_arithmetic 'NaN' 1000`, `coin_flip '0' 939` and `propositional_logic 'P ∨ Q' 820`.

Expected: a constant reply does not earn full reward.

The recorded wrong answer scores 0 on `complex_arithmetic` and `coin_flip` and 0.05 or 0.25 on `propositional_logic`, so that record shows only the first of the four. Two of the four are in the Nemotron blend's part of the released validation panel (`open-athena/Snowball-Smartie-RL-2026.10.15.32-Data`): with the panel's own grade script, `P ∨ Q` scores 1.0 on six of its seven `propositional_logic` tasks and `NaN` on its one `complex_arithmetic` task.

I tried 44 constant replies on the first 100 entries of every generated task. No fifth task gives the full reward on more than a quarter of the entries to a constant that is not the entry's answer.

comments.author: XiaoyuanWang111
comments.body:
🤖 A fifth task belongs on this list: `puzzle24`. The reply `1*2*3*4` scores 1.0 on all 1,000 of its generated entries. The scorer of `reasoning-gym` 0.1.25 (`reasoning_gym/games/puzzle24.py` L114-L132) checks that the reply evaluates to 24 and contains four numbers between 1 and 10. It does not read the entry's numbers. Five of the 1,000 entries have the numbers 1, 2, 3 and 4. The recorded wrong answer `definitely wrong` scores 0.01 on every entry, so that record does not show it.

The last paragraph of the issue says that no fifth task pays a constant on more than a quarter of its entries. None of the 44 constants I tried evaluates to 24, so that sweep could not find this task.

To check, add `("puzzle24", "1*2*3*4")` to `replies` in the script above. It prints `puzzle24 '1*2*3*4' 1000`. `puzzle24` is not in the released validation panel.

spillover_issues.author: XiaoyuanWang111
spillover_issues.body:
14,062 of the 65,559 tasks of `NeMo:predicted-action` (21.4%) expect a string argument of 10 or more words that occurs nowhere in the request. The source scores a reply 1 only for the exact function name with exact JSON arguments ([`nemo_tool_calls.py` L37](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/nemo_tool_calls.py#L37), [`grade_predicted_action_candidate`](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_predicted_action.py#L47-L61)), so a reply passes such a task only when it writes that string character for character. In 13,738 of the 14,062 tasks the only such arguments are `summary` or `issue_summary`, with a median of 32 words. They belong to calls that hand the conversation to a person, such as `transfer_to_human_agent`.

EvalLite's `agents` family is 165 tasks of this source ([recipe](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/recipes/eval-lite.json#L78-L86)). At the source's rate about 35 of them are such tasks, and every checkpoint scores 0 on them. The recipe's seeded order selects 44 when I apply it to the source without the overlap exclusions; I cannot read the training and development sets that the exclusions use.

Reproduce:

1. One task, row 94,789 of the pinned `train.jsonl`. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-verifyit python - <<'EOF'
   from verifyit.modes.grade_predicted_action import grade_predicted_action_candidate
   from verifyit.spec import FunctionCall, PredictedActionSpec

   expected = (
       "User inherited portfolio with appreciated securities, questions about step-up basis calculation "
       "and tax implications of significant gains."
   )
   spec = PredictedActionSpec(
       expected_calls=(FunctionCall("transfer_to_human_advisor", {"summary": expected, "urgency": "medium"}),)
   )
   replies = (
       expected,
       expected.rstrip("."),
       "The user inherited a portfolio of appreciated securities and asks how the step-up in basis is "
       "calculated and what tax the gains carry.",
   )
   for reply in replies:
       call = FunctionCall("transfer_to_human_advisor", {"summary": reply, "urgency": "medium"})
       print(grade_predicted_action_candidate(spec, (call,)).reward, reply)
   EOF
   ```

   It prints `1.0` for the expected call, `0.0` for the same call without the final period of the summary, and `0.0` for a paraphrase of the summary.

2. The count. The command downloads the pinned `train.jsonl` (1.75 GB) and takes about two minutes:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-taskcompendium python - <<'EOF'
   import json
   import statistics

   from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
   from taskcompendium.identity import canonical_sha256
   from taskcompendium.importers.nemo_predicted_action import DATASET, REVISION, import_row


   def texts(value):
       """Every string in a JSON value, and every string inside a string that is itself JSON."""
       if isinstance(value, str):
           yield value
           try:
               value = json.loads(value)
           except ValueError:
               return
           if not isinstance(value, dict | list):
               return
       for item in value.values() if isinstance(value, dict) else value if isinstance(value, list) else ():
           yield from texts(item)


   tasks, free_rows, long_rows, summary_only, longest = 0, 0, 0, 0, []
   with open(hf_hub_download(DATASET, "train.jsonl", revision=REVISION, repo_type="dataset")) as rows:
       for line in rows:
           row = json.loads(line)
           try:
               task = import_row(row, canonical_sha256(row))
           except ValueError:
               continue
           tasks += 1
           seen = "\n".join(texts(row["responses_create_params"]))
           free = {
               key: len(value.split())
               for call in task.grader.parameters["expected_calls"]
               for key, value in call["arguments"].items()
               if isinstance(value, str) and len(value.split()) >= 2 and value not in seen
           }
           free_rows += bool(free)
           if free and max(free.values()) >= 10:
               long_rows += 1
               summary_only += {key for key, words in free.items() if words >= 10} <= {"summary", "issue_summary"}
               longest.append(max(free.values()))
   print(tasks, free_rows, long_rows, summary_only, statistics.median(longest))
   EOF
   ```

   It prints `65559 15164 14062 13738 32.0`: the tasks, the tasks that expect a string of two or more words that is absent from the request, the tasks where such a string has 10 or more words, the tasks among those where only `summary` or `issue_summary` holds such a string, and the median word count of the longest such string.

Expected: a task whose expected call holds free text is left out of the source, or its free-text arguments are compared by a rule that a correct reply can meet.

NeMo Gym's verifier for this dataset compares strings of two or more words by word overlap, with a threshold of 0.1 ([config L7-L8](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/69a514999667cebee03d8fd8bd0aec996a54a504/resources_servers/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison/configs/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison.yaml#L7-L8), [`_compare_strings`](https://github.com/NVIDIA-NeMo/Gym/blob/69a514999667cebee03d8fd8bd0aec996a54a504/resources_servers/single_step_tool_use_with_argument_comparison/common/verification_utils.py#L597-L634)). The paraphrase of step 1 has an overlap of 0.225 under that rule. The dataset stores 16 rewards per row for Qwen3-235B (`qwen_235b_info`). Their mean is 0.40 on the 14,062 rows and 0.33 on the 46,162 rows whose expected string arguments are all single tokens.

spillover_issues.body:
In `verifyit`'s `math` mode, an equation reference for which SymPy's `solve` returns no solution gives 1.0 to any reply equation that also solves to nothing, such as `1 = 2`. On every 86th row of `MarinSkyRL:numina_math` (9,994 of its 859,494 pinned rows), 588 references contain `=`, are typed EQUATION and score 1.0 as their own reply. 32 of them give 1.0 to both `1 = 2` and `3 = 7`, 32 give 1.0 to the reference with its right-hand side replaced by `-987654.321`, and 35 (6.0%) do one or the other.

Two such references in the source are the boxed conclusions `5 + 3 + 14 = 22` ("Find the quantity of 5-primable integers smaller than 1000") and `f(2008) = 1` ("find f(2008)"). `1 = 2` scores 1.0 against both. The values the problems ask for, `22` and `1`, score 0.0.

The cause is https://github.com/huggingface/Math-Verify/issues/87: `sympy_solve_and_compare` solves both equations for their free symbols and compares the two solution lists pairwise, and two empty lists compare as equal. `_verify_pair` hands a pair of equations to `verify` as it is ([`grade_math.py` L144-L151](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L144-L151)), and its chain branch compares the links of a chain the same way ([L119-L131](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/lib/verifyit/src/verifyit/modes/grade_math.py#L119-L131)): `a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 19` gives 1.0 to `a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 20`. The Evalchemy scorer skips `verify` when the reference and the reply are both relations without free symbols ([`grade_boxed_math` L80-L81](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/lib/taskcompendium/src/taskcompendium/importers/evalchemy/scorers/math.py#L80-L81)). A reference with free symbols can solve to nothing as well: `(10a + 5)^2 = 100a(a + 1) + 25`, another boxed conclusion of the source, is an identity, and `1 = 2` scores 1.0 against it in both graders.

The source's only control is the golden `reference_reply` ([`skyrl/math.py` L27](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/math.py#L27), [L280](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/47383aec90fd93895cf76ea9cad65b84717d8aae/experiments/post_training/task_curation/datasets/skyrl/math.py#L280)), and these references pass it. Neither recipe (`snowball-100k.json`, `eval-lite.json`) names the source today.

Reproduce:

1. Three references from the source, and `x = 5` for comparison. From the repository root, run:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-verifyit --extra math python - <<'EOF'
   from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
   from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

   CASES = (
       ("5 + 3 + 14 = 22", ("5 + 3 + 14 = 22", "5 + 3 + 14 = 23", "1 = 2", "22")),
       ("f(2008) = 1", ("f(2008) = 1", "f(2008) = 99", "1 = 2", "1")),
       ("a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 19", ("a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 19", "a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 20", "1 = 2", "19")),
       ("x = 5", ("x = 5", "x = 6", "1 = 2", "5")),
   )
   for reference, replies in CASES:
       spec = MathSpec(expected=reference, math_type=MathType.EQUATION)
       print(reference, "|", ", ".join(f"{reply}: {grade_math_candidate(spec, reply).reward}" for reply in replies))
   EOF
   ```

   It prints:

   ```
   5 + 3 + 14 = 22 | 5 + 3 + 14 = 22: 1.0, 5 + 3 + 14 = 23: 1.0, 1 = 2: 1.0, 22: 0.0
   f(2008) = 1 | f(2008) = 1: 1.0, f(2008) = 99: 1.0, 1 = 2: 1.0, 1: 0.0
   a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 19 | a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 19: 1.0, a+b+c = 6+2+11 = 20: 1.0, 1 = 2: 0.0, 19: 0.0
   x = 5 | x = 5: 1.0, x = 6: 0.0, 1 = 2: 0.0, 5: 1.0
   ```

2. The count. The command downloads the five pinned shards (1.2 GB) and takes about three minutes:

   ```bash
   uv run --package marin-taskcompendium --extra pipeline python - <<'EOF'
   import pyarrow.parquet as pq
   from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
   from taskcompendium.convert.answers import math_type
   from verifyit.grade import GradingInfraError, InvalidTask
   from verifyit.modes.extract import extract_boxed
   from verifyit.modes.grade_math import grade_math_candidate
   from verifyit.spec import MathSpec, MathType

   REPO, REVISION, STRIDE = "AI-MO/NuminaMath-CoT", "9d8d210c9f6a36c8f3cd84045668c9b7800ef517", 86


   def reward(spec: MathSpec, reply: str) -> float | None:
       try:
           return grade_math_candidate(spec, reply).reward
       except (InvalidTask, GradingInfraError):
           return None


   equations = contradictions = replaced = either = index = 0
   for shard in range(5):
       path = hf_hub_download(REPO, f"data/train-{shard:05d}-of-00005.parquet", revision=REVISION, repo_type="dataset")
       for solution in pq.read_table(path, columns=["solution"])["solution"].to_pylist():
           index += 1
           expected = extract_boxed(solution) if index % STRIDE == 0 else None
           if not expected or "=" not in expected or math_type(expected) is not MathType.EQUATION:
               continue
           spec = MathSpec(expected=expected, math_type=MathType.EQUATION)
           if reward(spec, expected) != 1.0:
               continue
           equations += 1
           first = reward(spec, "1 = 2") == 1.0 and reward(spec, "3 = 7") == 1.0
           second = reward(spec, expected.rsplit("=", 1)[0] + "= -987654.321") == 1.0
           contradictions += first
           replaced += second
           either += first or second
   print(index, equations, contradictions, replaced, either)
   EOF
   ```

   It prints `859494 588 32 32 35`: the rows read, the equation references among every 86th row, those that give 1.0 to both `1 = 2` and `3 = 7`, those that give 1.0 to the replaced right-hand side, and those that do either. The count asks for both contradictions because a reference that math-verify reads as the number 2 gives 1.0 to `1 = 2` by its right-hand side.

Expected: a reply that states a different equation scores 0.0 against these references, or conversion rejects the references that the comparison cannot check.
spillover_issues.title: [verifyit] 32 of 588 numina_math equations give 1.0 to `1 = 2` and to `3 = 7`

spillover_issues.body:
🤖 **Marin Belay intake: post research ideas for [Marin Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/) here.**

Marin Belay is a human-guided, agent-executed experiment loop that hill-climbs the grug `fast_track` scaling ladder (Paloma macro loss).

**Start with the [contributor guide](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/blob/marin_belay_v1_recipe/experiments/belay/CONTRIBUTING.md)**: how to check an idea against the recipe, pick a Track, follow its runs, and take it up the ladder.

1. **Post one idea per comment**, with a paper link or a short rationale. Add a `Track:` line to pick the baseline; the default is `speedrun` (the 8-minute d512 run). The Belay page lists the Tracks.
2. **A maintainer reviews it** on the Belay admin page and approves it for an agent session, or declines it with a reason.
3. **👀 on your comment means it has been reviewed.** Nothing else is posted here. Plans, results and decline reasons are on the Status page.

**The usual path for an idea:** optionally a `vanilla-*` Track first, for a radical idea or a stronger signal; then `speedrun`, for fast iteration and to check it fits the current recipe; then `hero-mfu` if it will change MFU a lot; then `ladder`. Maintainers promote ideas into the recipe from those results.

**Tracks** (the `Track:` line):

| Track | Runs against | Hardware |
|---|---|---|
| `speedrun` (default) | The 8-minute d512 run of the current recipe; judged at equal data, then equal time if the step time changes | 1× 8×H100 |
| `competitive-d512` … `competitive-d1280` | The current recipe at one ladder rung, compared with its finished baseline run | 8×H100; d1280 on 4 nodes |
| `ladder` | All four `competitive-*` rungs at once, at the baseline's step count. After a `hero-mfu` result, each rung's steps are adjusted for the MFU change (better MFU, more steps). Without one, the verdict is provisional: the idea needs a `hero-mfu` result before it joins the recipe | as above |
| `moe-d512` … `moe-d1280` | A basic MoE at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `vanilla-d512` … `vanilla-d1280` | A dense baseline at that rung | 8×H100 |
| `hero-mfu` | Step time of the hero GB200 stack; a maintainer runs it | 1 GB200 rack |
| `custom` | A study: runs on other Tracks, then an analysis report with no win/loss verdict; needs a node and hours budget | per study |

Wins are judged on Paloma macro loss with a noise band of 0.005 (`hero-mfu`: step time, ±0.5%).

**Example comments**

> Try warming the MuonH momentum up from 0.85 to 0.98 over the first 10% of training, as modded-nanogpt does.

> Track: moe-d768
> Replace the router's sigmoid combine weights with softmax over the top-8 experts.

> Track: ladder
> Take X0221 (CPLM Plus) up the ladder with the settings of its speedrun win.

> Track: custom
> Measure how the stable rank of each attention projection changes over a full d512 run, from checkpoints every 1,000 steps.

**The Belay app** ([public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-…](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/)):

- **[Belay](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/):** the project. It covers the current recipe, the scaling ladder and its projection, the timeline, the gates an idea passes, the Tracks, the data and the starter kit.
- **[Status](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#status):** every idea and its results across the gates (Dense, speedrun, Hero MFU, projection, recipe), live runs and queue, and the agent log with one thread per idea (`#status/X####`).
- **[Hero MFU](https://public.applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#mfu):** hero-scale throughput, with each MFU change on the GB200 stack and its branch.
- **[Admin](https://applets.marina.oa.dev/a/33801d46-e280-46f9-b994-2c78603cdf15/#admin)** (maintainers, signed in to Marina): review and approve or decline ideas, with instructions and node, hours and priority grants. It also sets the node cap, dispatch and GitHub reactions.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
In latentMoE, we can try initializing the up/down projections as semi-orthogonal matrices and either:

A: using an orthogonality-preserving optimizer such as the one introduced in https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.06218 to update them
or
B: freezing them, keeping them semi-orthogonal and not updating them at all, while relying the rest of the NN to adapt

Rationale: up/down projections in latentMoE are themselves small, shared by all experts of the same layer, therefore not really having the capability to do meaningful computation for the whole NN. We should see them as information-preserving maps instead, and worry more about gradient pathology/distortion, rather than the potential loss of the degree of freedom/expressivity by using semi-orthogonal matrices.
Also if we take the "no meaningful computation" hypothesis really seriously, option B should only have negligible performance degradation compared to A. And if we use B, no new optimizer and no new hyperparameter tuning are needed.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body: 🤖 Second intake test (end-to-end on main, scheduled run): this comment should be copied into #9451 within a few minutes of its 👍, then get a 🚀. Not a research suggestion.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Tune muonh lr and nesterov momentum for q/k projections separately from the rest of the matrix parameters.

Rationale: I always thought tuning the optimizer hyperparameters of all different components of a neural network, although mundane, is the right thing to do. Falcon H1's way of doing things (Table 8 in https://arxiv.org/pdf/2507.22448) is closer to what we should do if we have enough tuning budget.

But if we don't want to risk wasting a lot of experiments on possibly nonexistent gains, we should rely on our intuitions on which components might benefit the most from a separate set of hyperparameters in order to narrow the targets, and my best guesses are q/k projections. They historically caused trouble by being much less tolerant to high lr, and people had to invent qk norm to help with that. However, after qk norm was introduced, now we don't know which one is true:

1. qk norm is a partial alleviation, and q/k projections should still be optimized with a more conservative setting
2. qk norm stabilizes things so much that it opens the opportunity for q/k projections to be optimized with a more aggressively setting

And we may find out by tuning their optimizer setting separately.

The suggestion above is based on the GQA/MQA arch with qk norm. For MLA, the naive first guess about which parameters should be optimized with a separate set of hyperparameters is W_q, W_dkv and W_uk, though excluding W_dkv or including W_uv seems to be equally convincing.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Attention residuals q embedding:
In addition to a data independent q vector for each layer, we also use a per-layer embedding q_e, similar to the value embedding, and add it to q before computing the dot product with k, so the attention residual formula before normalization turns from

exp(q^T RMSNorm(k))

into

exp((q + q_e(token_index))^T RMSNorm(k))

q_e should be initialized as all 0.

Rationale: In the attention residuals paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.15031), the authors ablated input dependent q in Table 4, and showed that it could further decrease loss, but excluded it from the default implementation because of extra compute and overhead. The "token dependent q" in this proposal is a compromise between cheap "data independent q" and expensive "q calculated from internal states using a dxd projection".

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Reconsider per-element attention gate, and either variant seems viable.

1. a linear projection with the same shape of the W_v projection, followed by sigmoid, like how Kimi K3 does it.
2. a down projection to a smaller vector, followed by a Swish nonlinearity, an up projection, then sigmoid, like how the current GatedNorm does it.

Rationale: the current Marin recipe has reduced the total number of MLA layers, by using a KDA+MLA hybrid, therefore the extra overhead of per-element gates compared to per-head ones becomes smaller.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Log and analyze some of these statistics during training (if some of these are too expensive then do it every tens or hundreds of steps):

1. Stable rank of each projection-like parameter matrix. If it gets very low over time, the frobenius norm which muonh controls no longer serves as a good proxy of spectral norm, and it may be a pathology case when scaling up.
2. Max row norm vs mean row norm of each projection-like parameter matrix. Unusually large row norm is a cause of large (element-wise)activations.
3. RMSNorm gains that become very far away from the initial 1.
4. Max element vs element rms of each layer's output.

Rationale: these indicators may provide some information to help us in both ways:

1. If we decide some of the anomalies are undesirable, we can come up with mitigations, and if the anomalies are local to some of the layers, mitigations can be local too.
2. If we decide some of the anomalies are desirable, we can try inducing the desired effects via explicit ways and prevent the side effects of the implicit behavior, like how the GatedNorm paper discovered that activation outliers are implicitly used for scaling down other activations, and came up with explicit gating to do that instead.

These are just a few indicators I can think of right now, and there has to be much more. When we have other aspects of the model we are interested with, we can add them to the list.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Add an extra loss term to counter the indefinite stretching effect to s, or normalize s and y in the original aux term, in the experiments of Batch 178 (MLP compression).

Choice 1: Instead of lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) we should use lambda * ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) + lambda_1 * ||s||^n
where n can be 2 or (4 and higher) depending on whether we want the counter force to be smoother or more "hard cap like".

Choice 2: let s' = s / ||s|| and y' = y / ||y||, and the aux term should become lambda * ||s' - sg(y')||^2
where y = s + r

Rationale: in the aux loss in batch 178, under the random vector assumption, s and r are approximately orthogonal because they are high dimensional, therefore by pythagorean theorem ||s + r||^2 has a very high probability of being larger than ||s||^2, no matter what training phase we are at. In order for the aux loss to minimize ||s - sg(s + r)||^2 / sg(||y||^2) it would both rotate s to be more aligned to (s + r) and stretch s longer to match the norm of (s + r). This optimization pressure of raw norm stretching would never stop at any phase of training. This seems to be the opposite of what we want for a regularized neural network, and might be the real reason why Batch 178 didn't show improvements.

Of course now in choice 1, lambda_1 also needs tuning and my intuition is to start with a value smaller than lambda.

comments.author: RavnaBergsndot
comments.body:
Try warmup of muonh nesterov momentum, and see if it could shift the optimal momentum from 0.95 to higher ones.

Like how modded-nanogpt introduced it since record 9, start with a lower momentum like 0.85, and linearly increase it to the value we want over the warmup period. Spend more steps in the momentum warmup (like 10% or 20% of total) than common lr warmup settings (<5%). Try higher final momentum such as 0.98 and see whether the momentum warmup schedule could make them better than the default 0.95.

Rationale: 0.95 is a safe number that's widely used, and the kimi paper reported that tuning it makes minimal difference. However, the lack of success from a a higher momentum may be caused by the early-late training dynamic discrepancy, and if this problem is alleviated, it might have some extra potential after training reaches the stabilized phase. A momentum warmup can help with the discrepancy by forgetting gradient information quicker in the early phase. The ademamix optimizer paper has some empirical evidence that the momentum warmup period should be sufficiently long. Since the update size is at the same scale after the short lr warmup finishes, long momentum warmup doesn't have the problem of "too little accumulated update" so it wouldn't require retuning lr and its schedule.

comments.author: bethehand
comments.body:
**Report the Paloma macro without `ptb` and `wikitext_103` next to the macro, and prefer it for calls near the bar.**

I paired each d512 Belay run (`lc1-*` in `marin_moe`) with its `-s1` twin, which has the same config apart from `trainer.seed`: 404 pairs from Sept 25 to Oct 8. These numbers are for the 305 configs near the frontier, i.e. within 0.01 of their batch median.

- **`ptb` is 1/16 of the macro but carries about a third of its seed noise** (35%). With `wikitext_103` the two carry 42%, by a covariance split.
- **Dropping the two cuts the noise much more than the signal.** Averaging the other 14 subsets cuts the noise SD of a paired Δ by 20%, while real differences between configs shrink by 3%. Signal-to-noise rises 1.4–1.5× (main estimate 1.48×, 95% CI 1.2–1.8), about what 1.5× as many seeds would buy.
- **`ptb`'s differences between configs barely reproduce across seeds:**

| Metric | Seed-to-seed correlation | Noise SD of a 2-seed paired Δ |
|---|---|---|
| Paloma macro, 16 subsets | 0.81 | 0.0016 |
| Without `ptb`, `wikitext_103` | 0.86 | 0.0013 |
| Uncheatable macro | 0.87 | 0.0014 |
| `ptb` alone | 0.10 | 0.013 |

The 0.0016 fits your "two-seed noise of ±0.004" (about 2.5 SD).

**This keeps the objective.** Near the bar, the 14-subset Δ estimates the full macro's true Δ better than the measured macro Δ does: the two-seed RMSE is 0.0009 vs 0.0011. For large changes the two can diverge, so the full macro stays the reference there.

**Two fixed-time calls** (seed 0 / seed 1):

| Call | Macro | Without the two | Uncheatable | `ptb` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Batch 174: candidate 11 vs 10 (same math, 3.5% faster) | −0.0058 / −0.0047 | −0.0075 / −0.0067 | −0.0072 / −0.0070 | +0.013 / +0.029 |
| Batch 200: candidate 12 vs 11 | −0.0001 / −0.0000 | +0.0017 / +0.0045 | +0.0043 / +0.0063 | −0.020 / −0.055 |

- In batch 174, `ptb` hid about a quarter of the gain.
- In batch 200, the exact tie was a fixed-time loss on the other 14 subsets and on Uncheatable. Its two sides ran on different clusters, but candidate 11's equal-step runs on the two clusters agree within 0.002 on these metrics.

**Why these two subsets.** They are the subsets with copies in the hero's training data (#9874), and I picked them before looking at Belay. Choosing subsets by their noise would be fitting the metric. Uncheatable works about as well.

**The bar.** You can keep 0.005 on the 14-subset Δ, for fewer false wins. Or you can lower it to about 0.004, which keeps today's false-win rate; with the observed tails the matching value is 0.0042.

Method, code and per-run numbers: https://github.com/bethehand/marin-hero-forecast/tree/main/belay-noise. I left out 6 pairs whose two seeds differ by 0.03–0.21 on the macro and by as much on Uncheatable (broken or diverged runs). Kept in, they swamp the overall variance, but the near-frontier numbers above barely move: for example, the gain is 1.38× instead of 1.48×.

comments.author: Helw150
comments.body:
**Try numerically stable cross-entropy from [arXiv:2610.31642](https://arxiv.org/html/2610.31642).**

The paper identifies a numerical problem with standard softmax cross-entropy called **Softmax Collapse**. When the correct logit becomes sufficiently larger than the others, floating-point rounding makes its softmax probability exactly 1, zeroing its gradient while leaving non-target gradients nonzero. This breaks the zero-sum gradient invariant (the gradients across all logits should sum to zero) and can cause optimization instability, including sudden spikes in training loss.

The proposed fix is simple: exclude the correct class from the log-sum-exp calculation and use `softplus` to combine the result with the correct class's logit.

```python
import jax
import jax.numpy as jnp

def cross_entropy(logits, targets):
    target_logits = jnp.take_along_axis(
        logits, targets[..., None], axis=-1
    )
    is_target = jax.nn.one_hot(
        targets, logits.shape[-1], dtype=jnp.bool_
    )

    others = jnp.where(is_target, -jnp.inf, logits - target_logits)
    return jax.nn.softplus(
        jax.scipy.special.logsumexp(others, axis=-1)
    )
```

This is mathematically equivalent to standard cross-entropy but avoids prematurely zeroing small gradients.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try replacing top-k routing with ReMoE’s ReLU routing and adaptive, load-aware sparsity regularization. Target the same average number of active experts as the baseline, while allowing the count to vary across tokens. Use the paper’s unnormalized nonnegative routing weights.

Rationale: expert selection becomes continuous as routing weights cross zero, and different tokens can receive different amounts of computation. ReMoe (https://arxiv.org/html/2412.14711v2) reports improved language-model loss across several scales. Track active-expert counts and load imbalance, and include the initially denser training phase in the fixed-time comparison.

comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
**Try adding CPLM Plus from #10678 to the Belay experiment ladder.** It extends the copy head with predecessor-conditioned keys and normalized case-class emissions, adding only d² + 2d + 1 parameters over ordinary CPLM.

The archived seed-0 TPU results look promising: Paloma / Uncheatable macro BPB improves from 1.184407 / 0.960857 to 1.181649 / 0.953552 at d512, and from 1.093305 / 0.853946 to 1.091306 / 0.850160 at d768, compared with ordinary CPLM. At d1024, Plus also improves over Belay (1.021640 → 1.014601 Paloma; 0.772050 → 0.767052 Uncheatable).

These runs approximately match analytical useful FLOPs, not wall time, and use one seed, so I think this is worth testing against the current recipe under Belay's fixed-time evaluation with paired seeds. The PR is stacked on #10260 and includes the implementation and results; throughput for the current PR revision still needs validation.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Try causal token-level capacity routing in front of the MoE (Mixture-of-Depths style ([arXiv 2404.02258](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02258)) ), keeping top-k + QB for expert choice.

Following @ClassicLarry's [comment 1](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6411175364) and  [comment 2](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5862159670) that dynamic compute likely matters more at scale.

Each MoE sublayer gets a small per-token router score. Tokens above a learned threshold go through the routed experts with a larger top-k; the rest go through the shared expert and the residual only. For routed tokens, expert ranking stays as in the current recipe (QB-adjusted logits, same combine weights); only k changes. Mean active experts per token matches the current recipe, e.g. with today's k = 10: 80% of tokens routed at k = 12 or 13, so the average stays ≈ 10.

Rationale: X0220 ([batch](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-6409675987)) showed ReMoE's failure came from the ReLU gates themselves: dead experts (40–278 per layer), 3–8% drops and load imbalance. Its allocation was already adaptive (easiest loss decile ≈ 7.4 experts, rest ≈ 12). This proposal keeps that adaptive allocation but separates the two decisions: *which tokens get more compute* (new router) and *which experts serve them* (top-k + QB, already stable here), so no expert can die from a zero gate. Mixture-of-Depths uses the same capacity idea for whole blocks.

FYI: the original MoD picks the top-k tokens over the whole sequence during training, so whether position t is routed depends on later tokens. Use a causal version instead: each token is routed by comparing its own score to a learned threshold (or a running causal quantile), with the same rule in training and eval.

comments.author: TimS-ml
comments.body:
Revisit MTP as a low-weight, decaying auxiliary loss computed on a subset of positions, with a block-head variant.

Batch 18 ([comment](https://github.com/marin-community/marin/issues/9451#issuecomment-5843750617)) tried one MTP configuration: a depth-1 head (h_t + W·norm(embed(t+1)) through the shared lm_head), weight 0.3 for the whole run. 

Rationale: MTP results in the literature come from much longer token budgets, so an equal-steps vs fixed-time pair on this ladder says whether the Batch 18 loss came from the configuration or from the objective at this budget. 

Here are some things worth trying:
1. **Lower weight:** 0.05 and 0.1 instead of 0.3.
2. **Decay to zero:** linearly to 0 by 50% or 80% of training, so the late phase optimizes next-token loss only. One extra arm turns MTP off entirely after the first 50%.
3. **Block head:** replace the linear head with one lightweight Transformer block (local attention + dense FFN) that reads norm(h_t) and norm(embed(t+1)) and feeds the shared lm_head, as in DeepSeek-V3 ([arXiv 2412.19437](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.19437)). 
Also, in a recent interview ([video, ~1:30:00](https://youtu.be/V9eI-t3TApE?t=5396)), MiMo-V2.6 leader Fuli Luo said they added MTP in pre-training because it improves the base model, and only later, while designing inference for their hybrid-SWA model, found enough spare decode compute to use MTP for speculative decoding. She also said teams that put too much faith in MLA missed this path; my reading is that MLA leaves less spare decode compute for MTP drafting. That is an inference-side hypothesis without published measurements, and I am not sure if this (spare compute) applies to our situation.
4. **(optional) Subsampled positions:** compute the t+2 logits and loss on a random 25% of positions per batch, still through the shared lm_head. If the cost scales with scored positions, the slowdown drops to about a quarter of 8.6%.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
Try adding **spelling-normalised byte embeddings** to the input. Each token's input embedding row gets a learned sum over the first 8 UTF-8 bytes of its surface string, one 256 x d table per byte position. Read the bytes after stripping leading spaces and lowercasing, so " The", "the" and "The" share every byte row. Add two small feature rows to keep what the normalisation removes: leading space (0/1) and case (lower, capitalised, all caps, mixed). Zero-init the tables so the model starts identical to the baseline. Add the byte sum to the vocab table before the token gather, so there is no per-token cost and no extra communication. Input side only: do not share byte rows on the lm_head. Keep 8 byte positions and table width d_model at every rung.

Rationale: tokens that are spelling or case variants of each other start with unrelated embeddings and have to learn their similarity from context. Sharing byte rows gives the model that information directly, and it is information the body cannot compute from token ids. This is close to Spelling Bee Embeddings (https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.18030); the space/case normalisation is the addition.

comments.author: xTimeCrystal
comments.body: Track: speedrun Similar to https://arxiv.org/pdf/2608.08888, try implementing a Full Bandwidth Transformer (FBT): the trunk runs K parallel passes over the sequence, and pass p's input at token t is fused from that token's embedding and the previous pass's output at token t-1: `x^{(p)}_{t} = norm(x_t + W_fuse norm(h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}))` - Use this formula, not the paper's. This is more stable. - `x_t` is the pass-1 input of token t (its embedding). - `h^{(p-1)}_{t-1}` is the final layer's output of pass `p-1` at position `t-1` (what the LM head reads), not that pass's input. - `norm` is parameter-free RMSNorm. - `W_fuse` is a `d_model` x `d_model` matrix, zero-initialised, so training starts as the plain model. - Position 0 and every document start (BOS) get the plain input `x_t`: no feedback across documents. - Gradients flow through all passes; do not detach or no-grad any pass. - Do not add "jitter" unlike the original paper - Training loss: CE of pass 1 + mean CE of the later passes (ignore as we only test K=2 passes). Evaluation: the last pass only. Sweep the fraction of training steps that use K=2 passes, the rest using K=1: 0.25, 0.5, 0.75 and 1.0 (always 2 passes). Never use K=3. Evaluate every run with K=2. Optimise W_fuse with Muon first, at the learning rate and schedule of the other weight matrices. Then sweep 0.7x and 1.4x to bracket the optimal W_fuse lr using Muon. Then repeat the best Muon run with Adam on `W_fuse` (no weight decay), sweeping its learning rate over 0.7x, 1x, 1.4x. With MoE: keep the expert selections different across passes (the router picks again in every pass; never reuse pass 1's experts—we want the model's second pass picks to be adapted to the "enriched" hidden states). Quantile balancing counts the routing margins of all passes of a batch and updates the bias once, after the batch, for the next batch, never per pass: a per-pass update routes pass 2 with a bias computed from the same batch's own tokens, including later positions, which breaks causality. Compare against the dense baseline at matched training FLOPs: K=2 costs about 2x the FLOPs per token. Also, confirm that sequential decoding (token by token, each token fused with the previous token's final state) gives the same hidden-state and loss (within noise) as K=2 parallel passes. In our nanochat run they agreed to within 0.0003 bpb. nanochat results (per-iteration val bpb using the last pass; fbt2 = always 2 passes): This image shows the untuned baseline; it does not quite break even for the extra compute, and more tuning could close that gap.

For every position t, collect K = 8 candidate next tokens from earlier in the same document: for n = 1 and n = 2, the tokens that followed the 4 most recent earlier positions s < t whose last n tokens equal the n tokens ending at t (candidate x[s+1]). Mix them into the output: p(y) = (1 - G) p_vocab(y) + open * sum_k pi_k [c_k = y], where (pi_0, pi_1..pi_K) = softmax(0, l_1..l_K) over the candidates that exist, l_k = h . w_k + 8 * b[k, a_k] - 2 with h the lm_head input and a_k the number of other slots proposing the same token, G = open * sum_k pi_k, open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1). w [d_model, 8], b [8, 8] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. comments.author: WhenWen
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

Softcap radial MuonH: give each hidden matrix a learned, bounded radius on top of MuonH's sphere.

(Generated by an automated research harness. Edited to replace the earlier evidence with the completed results; bottom line first.)

**Bottom line**
- On Belay's 8-minute d512 speedrun, softcap beats the recipe's MuonH beyond the 0.005 band (below).
- That edge shrinks with size: on Belay's ladder recipe it is inside the band by d768 (one seed).
- Softcap does **not** beat a fairly tuned MuonW-family baseline. Once MuonW gets a tuned head LR and schedule-scaled decay (MuonC, Defazio, arXiv 2506.02285), that baseline matches or beats softcap.
- So we are not proposing softcap as a ladder improvement on current evidence. d1024/d1280 are still running.

**Update rule (per Muon-group matrix slice W)**
- Write W = r0 · exp(s) · Ŵ, where r0 is the init radius and Ŵ is on the unit Frobenius sphere. Ŵ takes the usual MuonH hyperball step.
- s (a scalar log-radius per slice) is stepped by Adam on the radial gradient g = <∂L/∂W, W>, at the same LR and schedule as the matrix LR.
- Bound: outward steps are scaled by (1 − (s/c)²) and inward steps are taken in full. With c = 2 the radius is capped at e² ≈ 7.4× init.
- Slices whose output passes through a scale-removing norm keep a fixed radius (plain MuonH). Head and fallback groups are unchanged.

**d512 speedrun (Belay recipe, same-commit MuonH control)**
- Equal data, six paired GB200 seeds: softcap − MuonH mean −0.0083, one-sided 95% upper bound −0.0059, 6/6 seeds better. Three H100 seeds agree (mean −0.0082).
- An equal-time check gave smaller margins on the seeds read (about −0.004).
- learnable_qk_mult adds nothing (control + lqk +0.0002). The radius gain does transfer under the recipe's MLA q/k norms.

**Ladder (Belay recipe, one seed per rung; single-run gaps under 0.005 are ties)**
- Against MuonH: d512 −0.0103 (seed 1; −0.0057 on seed 0), d768 −0.0030 (a tie).
- Against the best MuonW-family run (MuonC, head LR ×0.35): d512 tie (−0.0025 on averaged reruns), d768 −0.0049 (a tie at the band edge).
- Same-seed reruns of identical settings at d512 differ by up to about 0.003, so one-seed margins below the band carry little weight.

**KMA d768 target (where the method was developed)**
- Softcap leads MuonW tuned on LR and decays by −0.0044 (seeds 2-11, held-out agreeing).
- That MuonW was under-tuned:
  - With MuonW's AdamW head LR tuned as well (×0.25-0.5), the lead drops to about −0.002, inside noise.
  - MuonC with a tuned head (2.4944, seed 0) beats every weight-normalized variant we tried, including softcap's best (2.5013).

**What we learned**
- Weight-normalized radial MuonH's apparent edge over MuonW came mostly from two things a fair MuonW also gets:
  - the AdamW head LR being too large;
  - plain decoupled decay shrinking the matrices late.
- MuonC's scheduled decay fixes the second, which matches the paper's prediction (flat late weight norm, bounded grad/weight ratio).

comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Document n-gram count cache mixed into the output. For each position t with label y, count over earlier positions s < t of the same packed document: c1 = number of s with x_s = x_t, n1 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y, c2 = number of s with (x_{s-1}, x_s) = (x_{t-1}, x_t) and n2 = number of those with x_{s+1} = y. Let q1 = n1 / c1 and q2 = n2 / c2 (each is a distribution over the vocabulary). Gate logits l_n = h . w_n + 8 * b_n * log2(1 + c_n) / 12 - 2 for n = 1, 2, where h is the lm_head input; (pi_0, pi_1, pi_2) = softmax(0, l_1, l_2) over the orders with c_n > 0; open = clip(8 * o, 0, 1); G = open * (pi_1 + pi_2). The model's distribution is p(y) = (1 - G) * p_vocab(y) + open * (pi_1 * q1(y) + pi_2 * q2(y)). w [d_model, 2], b [2] and the scalar o are zero-initialised and trained in the plain Adam group with no weight decay, so the model starts as the control. Train and evaluate on the mixture loss ce - log((1 - G) + M * exp(ce)), where ce is the lm_head's per-token cross-entropy (plus z-loss in training) and M = open * (pi_1 * q1(label) + pi_2 * q2(label)). Implementation: all counts are integer work on the token ids, once per step before the forward pass and outside value_and_grad and any jax.checkpoint region. Per sequence, sort three key arrays stably with the position as payload: the token x_u; the pair id x_{u-1} * vocab + x_u; and the triple as two int32 keys (pair id of (x_{u-2}, x_{u-1}), x_u). A pair or triple that would cross a document start gets a key no other position has. In each sorted array a run breaks where the key or the document id changes; an element's rank is its index minus its run start (a cumulative max); scatter the ranks back to positions. Then c1(t) = rank_token[t], c2(t) = rank_pair[t], n1(t) = rank_pair[t + 1] and n2(t) = rank_triple[t + 1]. Take ce from the existing fused cross-entropy kernel with per-token reduction; no second pass over the vocabulary, no [batch, seq, vocab] tensor, no lm_head row gather. Target step time within 1% of the control. Same settings at every rung.

comments.body:

Track: speedrun

MuonC: replace MuonH's hyperball step with Muon plus AdamC-corrected weight decay (Defazio 2025, arXiv 2506.02285, which scales the decay by lr_t^2 / lr_max) for every matrix in the MuonH group. For each MuonH sphere slice W (the slices MuonH already uses: each 2-D matrix, or each leading index of a stacked leaf), store r0 = ||W||_F at init. Each step, take U = O / ||O||_F, where O is the Newton-Schulz output MuonH already computes, and update W <- W - lr_t * r0 * U - (lr_t^2 / lr_max) * lambda * W, with no projection back to the sphere. lr_t is the current MuonH learning rate from the existing schedule and lr_max is its peak. Set lambda = lr_max / 2: for independent steps this makes the init radius the steady state, and the model starts as the control. The KDA write-strength group, lm_head and output_proj (AdamH) and the Adam group are unchanged. There are no new parameters (r0 is one stored scalar per slice). If a second arm fits, run lambda = 5 * lr_max / 2. Target step time within 1% of the control. At every rung, lambda is taken from that rung's own lr_max.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0243: the same MuonC update with a 25x stronger decay. Keep everything from X0243 (Muon plus AdamC-corrected decay on every MuonH-group sphere slice, r0 = ||W||_F at init stored per slice, U = O / ||O||_F from the Newton-Schulz output MuonH already computes, W <- W - lr_t * r0 * U - (lr_t^2 / lr_max) * lambda * W, no projection back to the sphere, lr_t the MuonH schedule and lr_max its peak) and change only lambda: set lambda = 25 * lr_max / 2 instead of lr_max / 2. The KDA write-strength group, lm_head and output_proj (AdamH) and the Adam group are unchanged. No new parameters. Target step time within 1% of the control. At every rung, lambda is taken from that rung's own lr_max.

comments.author: armorfaye
comments.body:
🤖 Posted on behalf of @armorfaye.

Track: speedrun

Follow-up to X0244: keep X0244's MuonC exactly (every MuonH-group sphere slice W steps W <- W - lr_t * r0 * U - (lr_t^2 / lr_max) * lambda * W with lambda = 25 * lr_max / 2, r0 the slice's init norm, U the normalized Newton-Schulz output, no projection) and apply the same AdamC-corrected decay to three more places. (1) lm_head / output_proj: replace AdamH with AdamC. Per head slice, store r0 = ||W||_F at init, take U = the Adam direction AdamH already computes, normalized per slice, and update W <- W - lr_t * r0 * U - (lr_t^2 / lr_max) * lambda * W with no projection back to the sphere, where lr_t is the head's current learning rate (the same schedule AdamH uses), lr_max its peak, and lambda = 25 * lr_max / 2. (2) MoE router weights (the router matrices only, not the router bias and not attn_gate): keep Adam's update and replace their decoupled decay with (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.1 * W per step, where adam_lr_t is the Adam group's current learning rate and adam_lr_max its peak; this replaces the existing annealed router decay. (3) The input token embedding table token_embed: keep Adam's update and add the same decay, (adam_lr_t^2 / adam_lr_max) * 0.1 * W per step. Every other group is unchanged. The head needs one stored scalar per slice and no new parameters; the decays are elementwise terms in the existing optimizer update. Target step time within 1% of the control. At every rung, lambda and the decay schedules are taken from that rung's own peak learning rates.

comments.author: ClassicLarry
comments.body:
Track: speedrun

At each step of training, we estimate the gradient against the 'weights', where the weights is a weighted sum over all prior gradients. However this weighted sum has a restricted set of options because we only modify it via new_update + modifier*all_prior_updates. A richer set is possible. Try this:

Implement linear init removal in our Hyperball optimizer. For every weight matrix Hyperball constrains (attention and MLP matrices; leave embeddings and norm gains alone), keep a scalar b, the coefficient of the initial weights W₀ in the current weights. It starts at 1.0. Regenerate W₀ from the init seed rather than storing a copy. On every step, keep b updated as b ← a·b, where a = R/‖W − ηV‖ is Hyperball’s projection factor. From step N/3 to step 2N/3, subtract a fixed amount of the init before projecting: W ← W − ηV − d·W₀ with d = min(δ, b), then project back to radius R, and update b ← a·(b − d). Pick δ so b reaches exactly 0 at step 2N/3. A good start is δ ≈ b(N/3) divided by the number of steps in the window, then adjust slightly to account for the shrinking from projection. Outside that window the optimizer is unchanged.
